Proposal for Astaxanthin (Sigma-Aldrich A9465)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Astaxanthin is a naturally occurring carotenoid belonging to the xanthophyll subclass, first discovered from marine sources such as lobsters and various microalgae, notably Haematococcus pluvialis (Yang & Wang, 2022, pp. 1–2). This red-orange pigment exhibits exceptional antioxidant properties that have been exploited both in natural extraction and through large‐scale synthetic production, with approximately 95% produced synthetically for enhanced economic viability (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–3). Its amphipathic structure, characterized by a long polyene chain terminated with polar functional groups, allows it to integrate into both hydrophilic and hydrophobic environments, a property that is fundamental to its ability to span and stabilize cell membranes (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–4; Rodella et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Astaxanthin is a representative member of a broader class of antioxidants that have historically been used as nutraceuticals and dietary supplements, targeting a range of conditions including cardiovascular, dermatologic, and neurodegenerative diseases. Over the decades, the unique biochemical properties of astaxanthin have motivated extensive research into its therapeutic potential, particularly for conditions associated with oxidative stress. Its regulatory approval as a food supplement in the early 1990s, together with subsequent studies demonstrating its anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic capabilities, have established astaxanthin as a promising candidate for further exploration in the context of ocular diseases (Yang & Wang, 2022, pp. 1–2; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, astaxanthin has been investigated and utilized in various biomedical contexts due to its robust antioxidant function. Clinical research and preclinical models have repeatedly shown that astaxanthin improves retinal function and visual acuity in patients with ocular diseases, including both early and nonadvanced stages of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). In addition to its application in AMD, astaxanthin has been evaluated for therapeutic effects in conditions such as diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and dry eye syndrome, demonstrating broad-spectrum protective activities against the oxidative and inflammatory insults commonly underlying these disorders (Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 2–5; Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10). Animal models have provided evidence that dietary supplementation with astaxanthin can mitigate photoreceptor degeneration, reduce choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in models of exudative AMD, and suppress retinal cell apoptosis induced by light or xenobiotic stress (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–7; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5). Despite being explored predominantly for ocular applications, astaxanthin’s history is not limited to ophthalmology alone; its neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory properties have been leveraged in studies addressing broader neurodegenerative and systemic conditions, emphasizing a solid profile for safety and translational potential (Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 2–5). Clinical studies have been encouraging in demonstrating that astaxanthin, when administered as a dietary supplement, exhibits an excellent safety profile with minimal adverse effects, thereby facilitating its clinical translation for chronic, age-related ocular conditions (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5, 13–14). Despite these promising reports, it is important to note that while most available studies indicate significant benefits, the literature also highlights the necessity for further research to determine optimal dosages and to overcome challenges related to bioavailability (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic potential of astaxanthin in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) is thought to stem from its unparalleled antioxidant activity, which is mechanistically linked to its lipophilic and hydrophilic properties. On a molecular level, astaxanthin integrates into cellular membranes—including those of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) mitochondria—where it acts as a chain-breaking antioxidant, quenching reactive oxygen species (ROS) and scavenging free radicals efficiently (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–5). Its mechanism involves the neutralization of lipid peroxidation, a process wherein polyunsaturated fatty acids in the cell membrane are damaged by ROS, ultimately leading to the formation of malondialdehyde (MDA) and other toxic aldehyde species that compromise membrane integrity (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Maiuolo et al., 2022, pp. 8–9). By inhibiting lipid peroxidation, astaxanthin stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), an essential parameter for maintaining proper mitochondrial function and for preventing the initiation of apoptosis via intrinsic death pathways (Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).  

At the molecular level, studies indicate that astaxanthin modulates key intracellular signaling pathways. It downregulates inflammatory mediators by suppressing the NF-κB pathway, thereby reducing the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 3–5). Additionally, astaxanthin has been shown to enhance the activity of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and glutathione peroxidase (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–3; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5), which together help restore cellular redox balance under chronic oxidative stress conditions. Its role in modulating mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt pathways further contributes to cellular survival by reinforcing anti-apoptotic signaling and inhibiting caspase activation, thereby reducing retinal ganglion cell death (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5).  

The hypothesis under consideration—that astaxanthin integrates into RPE mitochondrial membranes to quench lipid peroxidation and stabilize Δψm—is supported by its molecular configuration, which allows the compound to embed itself at the interface of membrane lipids without disrupting the bilayer structure (Rodella et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–4). Once incorporated, astaxanthin acts as a “molecular rivet” that not only prevents oxidative damage but also helps maintain membrane fluidity and structural integrity. This is particularly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where chronic oxidative stress leads to the degeneration of the RPE, a critical cell layer whose dysfunction is central to the pathogenesis of the disease (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–5). Additionally, the ability of astaxanthin to traverse cellular and mitochondrial membranes enhances its efficacy in neutralizing ROS, thereby preserving both mitochondrial function and cellular viability within the retina (Manresa et al., 2016, p. 5; Rodella et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  

Expected Effect:  
In the assay proposed for the evaluation of dry AMD treatment, the primary expectation is that astaxanthin supplementation will lead to a marked reduction in oxidative stress markers and preservation of mitochondrial function in RPE cells. Specifically, the anticipated effects include a decrease in MDA formation, indicative of attenuated lipid peroxidation, and stabilization of Δψm, which is critical for preventing loss of mitochondrial integrity and the subsequent cascade of apoptotic signaling (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). Based on its molecular actions, astaxanthin is expected to enhance cellular antioxidant defenses by upregulating enzymes such as SOD and glutathione peroxidase, ultimately leading to improved cell survival under conditions of chronic oxidative insult typical of dry AMD (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–3; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).  

RPE cells are known to express high levels of antioxidants and genes responsive to oxidative stress, such as those regulated by the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway (Manresa et al., 2016, p. 5). In vitro assays, therefore, should reveal that astaxanthin treatment results in enhanced Nrf2 activation and subsequent transcription of phase II detoxifying enzymes, which in turn protects against oxidative damage. Furthermore, electrophysiological assessments, such as electroretinograms (ERG), are expected to show functional improvements in retinal activity, corroborating the cytoprotective effects observed at the cellular level (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 5–7).  

In addition to cellular antioxidants, astaxanthin’s anti-inflammatory properties are likely to mitigate the secretion of inflammatory cytokines from RPE cells and reduce the activation of microglial cells in the retina. Such a reduction in the inflammatory milieu is crucial, as chronic inflammation is known to exacerbate retinal degeneration in AMD by promoting pathological angiogenesis and further oxidative damage (Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 2–5). Hence, a combinatorial effect of decreased oxidative stress, improved mitochondrial stability, and reduced inflammation is anticipated to confer significant protection to retinal structures, ultimately delaying or preventing the progression of dry AMD (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 12–14).

Overall Evaluation:  
The collective body of evidence suggests that astaxanthin holds considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. One of its principal strengths lies in its multifaceted action: as a potent antioxidant, it effectively quenches reactive oxygen species and prevents lipid peroxidation, while its ability to integrate into cellular membranes, particularly those of RPE mitochondria, ensures that mitochondrial membrane potential is preserved even under chronic oxidative conditions (Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10; Rodella et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). The convergence of biochemical, cellular, and clinical data highlights its capacity to improve retinal function, as evidenced by improvements in electroretinogram outcomes and visual acuity measurements in clinical trials (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). Moreover, its favorable safety profile—as demonstrated through extensive use as a dietary supplement—provides an added advantage in terms of translational potential, facilitating the design and execution of clinical studies aimed at validating its efficacy in dry AMD (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5).

Another strength is the well-documented anti-inflammatory property of astaxanthin, which complements its antioxidant activity. By downregulating NF-κB and associated pro-inflammatory mediators, this compound mitigates the inflammatory processes that contribute to RPE degeneration and retinal neuronal loss (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 3–5). This dual action is particularly significant given the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis, where both oxidative stress and chronic inflammation play aggravating roles. The integration of these effects suggests that astaxanthin may not only slow disease progression but also restore aspects of retinal function, representing a comprehensive therapeutic approach.

However, several challenges and weaknesses also warrant consideration. Despite the promising mechanistic profile, the translational efficacy of astaxanthin in clinical settings remains to be fully established. Although numerous preclinical models have demonstrated cytoprotective effects in vitro and in animal models, the optimal dosing regimen and formulation for achieving sufficient bioavailability in the human retina are still under investigation (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). As a lipophilic compound, astaxanthin’s stability and absorption in the gastrointestinal tract can be variable, potentially limiting its effective concentration at the target site. Recent studies have suggested that innovative drug delivery systems, such as nano-based lipophilic carriers, may be necessary to enhance its bioavailability and achieve consistent therapeutic outcomes (Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10; Yang & Wang, 2022, pp. 4–5).

Furthermore, while its safety profile is favorable, long-term clinical trials are required to ensure that chronic administration does not lead to unforeseen adverse effects, particularly when used in high doses over extended periods. Variability in patient response based on genetic factors or baseline antioxidant status may also affect clinical outcomes, necessitating personalized approaches to dosing and supplementation (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 3–5). Additionally, while the molecular mechanisms such as the stabilization of Δψm and quenching of lipid peroxidation are well-documented in controlled experimental settings, the complexity of dry AMD—characterized by a combination of degenerative, inflammatory, and vascular processes—means that astaxanthin may need to be part of a multifactorial therapeutic strategy rather than a stand-alone treatment (Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 2–5).

In summary, astaxanthin stands out as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD on several fronts. Its remarkable antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, combined with its ability to stabilize mitochondrial membrane potential and prevent lipid peroxidation, directly address key pathogenic mechanisms implicated in dry AMD (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–5; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5). The extensive preclinical and clinical data on its ocular applications, alongside its established safety profile as a dietary supplement, provide a solid foundation for further investigation. Nonetheless, the challenges associated with optimizing its bioavailability, determining the optimal dosing regimen, and confirming its long-term efficacy in diverse patient populations highlight areas where additional research is critically needed (Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5).

From the perspective of a drug development team leader focused on repurposing agents for dry AMD, the evidence supports the incorporation of astaxanthin into further preclinical testing and potential early-phase clinical trials. A multi-pronged approach that includes detailed pharmacokinetic studies, the exploration of enhanced delivery systems, and the evaluation of combination treatments with complementary agents might maximize its therapeutic potential. In conclusion, while certain hurdles remain to be overcome, the overall strengths of astaxanthin—its potent antioxidant activity, favorable safety profile, and mechanistic relevance to RPE mitochondrial stabilization—render it a highly promising candidate for inclusion in the therapeutic armamentarium against dry age-related macular degeneration (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–7; Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10).

To recapitulate, astaxanthin’s natural origin as a marine-derived carotenoid, its extensive historical use as a nutraceutical, and its documented molecular mechanisms that include inflammation suppression, ROS scavenging, and stabilization of vital mitochondrial functions all contribute to its strong candidacy for repurposing in dry AMD (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–3; Yang & Wang, 2022, pp. 1–2; Maiuolo et al., 2022, pp. 8–9). The expected outcomes of integrating astaxanthin into RPE mitochondrial membranes—particularly the reduction of lipid peroxidation, decrease in MDA formation, and stabilization of Δψm—are directly aligned with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD patients. Despite the necessity for further research to optimize formulation and dosing, the body of evidence suggests that astaxanthin merits serious consideration as a component of future therapeutic regimens aimed at mitigating the multifactorial pathology of dry age-related macular degeneration (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Overall, the current literature provides a comprehensive rationale for advancing astaxanthin into a translational research pipeline focused on dry AMD. With its robust antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective actions, astaxanthin may fill a critical gap in the current therapeutic landscape, addressing both the symptomatic and pathogenic progression of the disease. The scientific hypothesis that it integrates into RPE mitochondrial membranes to quench lipid peroxidation and stabilize Δψm finds substantial support in the biochemical and clinical studies referenced above (Bakac et al., 2023, pp. 9–10; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 12–14). While additional investigations are warranted to resolve issues relating to bioavailability and long-term efficacy, the convergence of preclinical, clinical, and biochemical evidence indicates that astaxanthin is a compelling and promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 5–7).

In conclusion, the evaluation of astaxanthin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD underscores its exceptional potential to mitigate oxidative stress-induced mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE. Its natural origin, extensive therapeutic history in ocular and other diseases, detailed molecular mechanisms of action, and expected beneficial effects on mitochondrial stability collectively provide a strong scientific basis for further development. The challenges regarding bioavailability and optimal dosing are recognized; however, these are not insurmountable with current advances in pharmaceutical formulation and drug delivery technologies. Based on the extensive literature reviewed, the evidence overwhelmingly supports moving forward with additional targeted preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials to validate astaxanthin’s efficacy and safety in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–4).

Proposal for Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone; Cayman Chemical #700105)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), also known as ubiquinone, is a naturally occurring lipophilic molecule synthesized endogenously via the mevalonate pathway. It is a quinone class compound that was originally discovered as a crucial component of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) and is essential for adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production. Chemically, CoQ10 contains a benzoquinone ring and a long isoprenoid side chain, which confers its lipid solubility and allows integration into mitochondrial and other cellular membranes. As a therapeutic candidate, it is available commercially (e.g., Cayman Chemical #700105) as a pure formulation that can be used for research purposes and has been repurposed in several settings to address oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Its widespread use as a dietary supplement and as an adjunct therapy in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and metabolic disorders underlines the extensive clinical experience with this class of compounds. The rationale for its repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on the compound’s natural role as a coenzyme, its potent antioxidant properties, and its ability to modulate mitochondrial energy metabolism—all of which are critically compromised in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of the aging eye (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Maiuolo et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past decades, CoQ10 has been evaluated in multiple experimental and clinical contexts. Biochemical studies have consistently demonstrated its ability to protect mitochondrial structure and function by facilitating electron transport and scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS). In vitro, CoQ10 treatments have been shown to improve mitochondrial respiration and ATP production in various cell types, including ARPE-19 cells, a widely used human RPE model. These studies utilized oxidative stress challenges (e.g., H₂O₂ exposure) to simulate conditions similar to those present in dry AMD, and showed that CoQ10 supplementation lowered levels of apoptotic markers such as caspase-3 and TUNEL staining, effectively reducing cell death (Hernandez et al., 2024). In the clinical arena, several studies have explored the use of CoQ10, sometimes in combination with other nutritional compounds, for early stages of AMD. For instance, combination therapies incorporating CoQ10 with agents such as acetyl-L-carnitine and n-3 fatty acids have resulted in improvements in visual function and fundus appearance among early AMD patients, demonstrating its potential impact in slowing disease progression (Feher et al., 2005). Moreover, its established safety profile in chronic use and its history of use as a metabolic booster and antioxidant in various degenerative conditions further support its potential repurposing for dry AMD, where similar mitochondrial and oxidative stress mechanisms underlie disease pathology (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kiliç, 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, CoQ10 exhibits a dual mechanism of action that is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Firstly, it functions as an obligatory electron carrier within mitochondria. In the ETC, CoQ10 shuttles electrons from complexes I (NADH dehydrogenase) and II (succinate dehydrogenase) to complex III (cytochrome bc₁ complex), thereby driving the proton gradient needed for ATP synthesis by ATP synthase. Its redox-active benzoquinone ring is capable of reversible oxidation and reduction, enabling it to accept and donate electrons during the process of cellular respiration (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024). This electron-transfer activity is critical in tissues with high metabolic demands such as the retina, where the maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (mt∆ψ) and ATP production are indispensable for cell survival. A second and equally important aspect of CoQ10’s mechanism is its potent antioxidant property. Through its reduced form, ubiquinol, CoQ10 directly scavenges free radicals and prevents lipid peroxidation of cell membranes. This antioxidant activity extends to the regeneration of other lipid-soluble antioxidants such as vitamin E, thereby reinforcing a broader cellular antioxidant defense network (Manzar et al., 2020; Hernandez et al., 2024).

In the context of RPE cells, the protective effects of CoQ10 extend to the stabilization of mitochondrial proteins and prevention of oxidative damage-induced mtDNA release. Notably, CoQ10 has been shown to modulate the expression of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase-2 (SOD2), which further contributes to the reduction of intracellular ROS levels. Additionally, CoQ10 influences mitochondrial dynamics by reducing the activation of pro-fission proteins like DRP-1, thereby inhibiting excessive mitochondrial fragmentation—a phenomenon that has been associated with increased apoptosis in oxidative stress conditions (Hernandez et al., 2024). Its capacity to dampen inflammatory mediators, including the restoration of cytokines such as TNFα and caspase-1 to their baseline levels following oxidative insult, underscores its role in mitigating the inflammatory cascades implicated in AMD pathology (Hernandez et al., 2024). These combined actions—preservation of electron transport efficiency, reduction in ROS-mediated damage, and stabilization of mitochondrial integrity—are central to the hypothesis that exogenous supplementation of CoQ10 can counteract the underlying cellular stress mechanisms in dry AMD (Hernandez et al., 2024; Maiuolo et al., 2022).

Expected Effect in the Assay and Mechanistic Rationale:  
Given the proposed experimental approach—using H₂O₂-challenged ARPE-19 cells as a model to simulate oxidative stress encountered in dry AMD—the expected effect of exogenous CoQ10 supplementation would be multi-fold. Firstly, by increasing the mitochondrial pool of ubiquinone, the supplemented CoQ10 is expected to enhance electron transport efficiency within RPE cells, thereby sustaining ATP production under stress conditions. The repletion of CoQ10 levels would counteract the age-associated decline in endogenous CoQ10 and restore mitochondrial membrane potential, which is critical for normal cell metabolism (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Maiuolo et al., 2022). Secondly, due to its antioxidant properties, CoQ10 is anticipated to directly scavenge ROS generated by H₂O₂ exposure, thereby reducing oxidative lipid peroxidation and preventing damage to mitochondrial membranes and proteins. As a result, key apoptotic markers—such as caspase-3 activity and TUNEL-positive cell counts—should be decreased, reflecting improved cell viability and reduced progression toward cell death (Hernandez et al., 2024).

Moreover, it is expected that CoQ10 may influence the expression of genes related to mitochondrial defense and redox balance, such as those encoding for SOD2 and other antioxidant enzymes, ultimately leading to a more robust cellular response against oxidative insults. Since ARPE-19 cells express the protein machinery integral to both oxidative phosphorylation and antioxidant defense, the modulation of these pathways by CoQ10 would provide a mechanistic basis for its protective effects in vitro (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024). In addition, the expected synergistic benefits when CoQ10 is combined with a nutritional complex—such as Nutrof—has been documented, where the combination was more effective at reducing oxidative stress markers and apoptosis than CoQ10 alone (Hernandez et al., 2024). This synergistic effect likely arises from the complementary actions of CoQ10 in regenerating other antioxidants and its specific targeting of mitochondrial dysfunction—a key driver of dry AMD pathology (Hernandez et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The comprehensive review of the literature provides strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical evidence to support the repurposing of CoQ10 for dry AMD. One of the primary strengths of CoQ10 as a candidate is its dual role—facilitating electron transport and exerting antioxidant effects—which addresses two critical pathological features in dry AMD: mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Its ability to preserve mitochondrial integrity by maintaining the electron transport chain and reducing mitochondrial depolarization directly aligns with the needs of RPE cells, which have high energy demands and are vulnerable to oxidative damage (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024).

Furthermore, numerous in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation leads to reduced apoptosis, lower ROS generation, and improved cell viability following oxidative challenges. These studies provide robust biochemical evidence that CoQ10 can counteract cellular stresses that mimic early events in AMD pathogenesis (Hernandez et al., 2024). From a therapeutic history standpoint, the extensive clinical experience with CoQ10 in other degenerative and mitochondrial disorders lends additional credibility to its safety and potential efficacy for ocular applications. Its long history of use as an adjunct supplement in various conditions enhances its attractiveness as a repurposed drug candidate from a regulatory and translational perspective (Feher et al., 2005).

However, several challenges must also be considered. One key weakness is the issue of bioavailability. CoQ10 is a large, lipophilic molecule, and its effective delivery to the retina following systemic or topical administration remains a significant technical hurdle. Although studies have shown that exogenous CoQ10 can elevate retinal levels to some extent, optimizing its formulation for enhanced tissue penetration and sustained release is critical for therapeutic success (Manzar et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2009). Additionally, the variability observed in clinical responses in AMD studies suggests that patient-specific factors or differences in the progression of mitochondrial dysfunction may influence the therapeutic outcomes. Therefore, while the preclinical data are promising, rigorous clinical studies are needed to determine optimal dosing regimens, delivery methods (such as oral versus topical administration), and combination strategies with other antioxidants or mitotropic agents (Feher et al., 2005).

Another important consideration is the multifactorial nature of dry AMD, which involves not only mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress but also chronic inflammation, complement dysregulation, and genetic predispositions. As such, CoQ10 monotherapy may not fully address the complex pathological processes underlying the disease. Combination therapies that target multiple pathways simultaneously, such as those combining CoQ10 with nutritional complexes that include other antioxidants and anti-inflammatory agents, are likely to yield better clinical outcomes. In this regard, CoQ10 appears to be particularly well-suited for inclusion in combination regimens designed to synergistically reduce oxidative stress and support mitochondrial health (Hernandez et al., 2024; Feher et al., 2005).

The mechanistic data support the hypothesis that elevating RPE mitochondrial ubiquinone pools can enhance electron transport efficiency and reduce ROS accumulation. Detailed biochemical analyses have shown that CoQ10 prevents lipid peroxidation and stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane potential, which in turn decreases the release of pro-apoptotic factors such as cytochrome c and prevents the activation of caspases (Hernandez et al., 2024). These effects are particularly relevant to dry AMD, where RPE cell death and the subsequent degeneration of photoreceptors play a central role in disease progression (Hernandez et al., 2024).

Overall, the aggregate evidence from biochemical, in vitro, and early clinical studies strongly supports the continued investigation of CoQ10 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its established role in mitochondrial function and cellular antioxidant defense mechanisms, combined with a favorable safety profile, provides a firm scientific basis for clinical translation. The expected benefits in ARPE-19 assays—namely, enhanced cell viability, reduced ROS levels, and the attenuation of apoptosis—reflect the direct mechanistic impacts of CoQ10 on key aspects of dry AMD pathology. Moreover, the potential to modulate mitochondrial dynamics via regulation of proteins such as DRP-1 and maintain mtDNA integrity further underscores its therapeutic relevance (Hernandez et al., 2024).

In conclusion, while CoQ10 is not without its challenges—primarily related to its delivery and the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD—the strengths of its molecular mechanism and supportive preclinical data render it a highly promising candidate. The potential for topical and systemic administration to elevate retinal levels, combined with its dual action as both a metabolic enhancer and a free radical scavenger, aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD patients. Nonetheless, further research is warranted to optimize formulations, validate efficacy in larger clinical trials, and explore its integration into multi-targeted therapeutic strategies. Given the existing biochemical and clinical literature, CoQ10 represents a rational and mechanistically sound approach for addressing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in dry AMD, making it a candidate worthy of further development and investigation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024; Feher et al., 2005; Qu et al., 2009).

Proposal for Alda-1 (Selleck S8274)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Alda-1 is a synthetic small molecule discovered through target-directed screening for modulators of mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), originally identified as “ALDH2 activator 1” with the chemical name N-(1,3-benzodioxol-5-ylmethyl)-2,6-dichlorobenzamide and first demonstrated to reduce myocardial ischemic injury in rodents by directly activating ALDH2 (i.e., increasing its catalytic activity and rescuing function of the common inactive ALDH2*2 variant) (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019). Structurally and mechanistically, Alda-1 binds at the substrate entrance tunnel of ALDH2 and extends toward the active site, where it enhances dehydrogenase activity by favorably altering local dynamics, improving NAD+ engagement, and acting as a chemical chaperone that preserves the functional conformation of critical active-site loops and α-helices, while shielding key catalytic cysteines from irreversible electrophilic adduction by reactive aldehydes such as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). In vitro biophysical and enzymology work shows Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 activity approximately twofold and markedly rescues activity of the common East Asian mutant ALDH2*2 (Glu504Lys), restoring heterotetramer activity to near wild-type levels; importantly, Alda-1 is selective against several other ALDHs in original profiling, although later biochemical work suggests some degree of cross-activation of ALDH1A1 under specific assay conditions (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013).

Alda-1 belongs to the pharmacologic class of enzyme activators/allosteric agonists targeting mitochondrial ALDH2; the class is characterized by its ability to catalytically enhance clearance of reactive aldehydes generated by oxidative and nitrosative stress (e.g., 4-HNE, malondialdehyde [MDA], acrolein, and catecholamine-derived DOPAL), thereby acting as indirect antioxidants that reduce downstream carbonyl stress, proteotoxicity, and mitochondria-dependent cell death without directly scavenging ROS (Kimura et al., 2019; Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Wang & He, 2018). This mechanism has been applied preclinically across multiple organ systems to mitigate ischemia–reperfusion injury, chronic heart failure, metabolic and neurodegenerative toxicities, and toxin-induced organ damage, providing a consistent translational thread: activation of ALDH2 accelerates detoxification of stable electrophilic products of lipid peroxidation, interrupting aldehyde-driven positive feedback loops that amplify mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS generation, and apoptosis (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
Across cardiovascular models, Alda-1 has repeatedly demonstrated robust cytoprotection in vivo. In rat and mouse myocardial ischemia–reperfusion and infarction models, Alda-1 administration prior to or during ischemia reduced infarct size by approximately 60% and improved long-term survival following myocardial infarction, associating efficacy with increased ALDH2 activity, reduced 4-HNE-protein adducts and protein carbonyls, preserved mitochondrial respiratory control ratio (RCR), reduced mitochondrial H₂O₂ release, protection against Ca²⁺-induced mitochondrial permeability transition (MPT), and decreased cytochrome c release (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014). In a chronic post-MI heart-failure model with established aldehydic overload, sustained Alda-1 treatment increased cardiac ALDH2 activity by ~2.7-fold, lowered 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, normalized uncoupler responsiveness, improved RCR by preserving State 3 respiration, lowered mitochondrial ROS emission, and corrected MPT sensitivity; organ-level outcomes included increased contractility, reduced LV dilation, diminished hypertrophy and fibrosis, and anti-remodeling benefits (Gomes et al., 2014). In vitro, Alda-1 shielded isolated cardiac mitochondria from 4-HNE–induced respiratory inhibition, demonstrating direct aldehyde-dependent protection at the mitochondrial level (Gomes et al., 2014).

Hepatic and other organ systems provide convergent evidence. In a mouse acetaminophen hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 pretreatment substantially reduced liver injury biomarkers (ALT/AST), histologic necrosis, 4-HNE adduct burden, mitochondrial depolarization, and cell death without altering upstream NAPQI bioactivation or JNK phosphorylation, demonstrating that protection is downstream via aldehyde detoxification and preservation of mitochondrial polarization and MPT control (Wimborne et al., 2020). Additional preclinical reports document Alda-1 efficacy in models of lung ischemia/reperfusion, intestinal I/R, kidney injury, neurotoxic injuries, and alcohol-related hepatic injury, again with mechanistic ties to accelerated clearance of reactive aldehydes, restoration of mitochondrial function, and modulation of stress/apoptosis pathways (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).

Retina-focused data, while more limited and not in dry AMD models, are directionally supportive. In streptozotocin-induced aged diabetic rats (an early diabetic retinopathy model), systemic Alda-1 improved ERG parameters, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) and total retinal thickness on OCT at 7–30 days, increased retinal SOD activity, and decreased retinal TNF-α and IL-6 across multiple timepoints; concurrent upregulation of ALDH2, Nrf2, and Sirt1 was observed by immunofluorescence and Western blot, suggesting that ALDH2 activation engages antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways in the retina under hyperglycemic oxidative stress (He et al., 2018). In a separate in vivo retinal degeneration study (MNU-induced photoreceptor damage), systemic Alda-1 preserved ERG amplitudes, mitigated photoreceptor degeneration (OCT, histology), increased retinal ALDH2 and SIRT1 protein, and reduced markers of ER stress (GRP78) and apoptosis (PARP1), supporting the hypothesis that enhancing aldehyde detoxification ameliorates retinal cellular stress downstream of lipid peroxidation (Yan et al., 2020; Carullo et al., 2020). Although neither model recapitulates RPE-centric dry AMD (drusen, complement activation, geographic atrophy), they provide proof-of-principle that ALDH2 activation can protect neural retina under oxidative/aldehydic stress in vivo (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Clinical translation status remains nascent. No human proof-of-concept trials of Alda-1 have been reported, and authoritative reviews note the absence of clinical efficacy data for ALDH2 activators like Alda-1, despite extensive rodent evidence across organs; moreover, no ALDH2 activators are in clinical use at present (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019). Safety experience is therefore limited to preclinical settings: chronic Alda-1 dosing in naïve rats (10 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks) demonstrated acceptable tolerability (no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight changes), whereas a separate report described crystalline nephropathy and renal function deterioration after I/R under specific Alda-1 dosing/formulation conditions, suggesting potential tissue-specific or formulation-dependent risks requiring evaluation (Gomes et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2023). With respect to ophthalmology, existing Alda-1 studies are limited to rodent retina in DR and MNU models; there is no published use in dry AMD patients or preclinical AMD-like RPE atrophy models, and there is no reported ocular delivery pharmacokinetics or long-term ocular safety data in the provided literature (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action  
ALDH2 is a mitochondrial, NAD⁺-dependent dehydrogenase that catalyzes the oxidation of reactive aldehydes—most notably acetaldehyde, 4-HNE, MDA, acrolein, and DOPAL—to their corresponding carboxylic acids, thereby detoxifying electrophiles that otherwise form covalent Michael adducts and Schiff bases with cysteine, histidine, and lysine residues on proteins and nucleic acids (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009). The enzyme’s catalytic mechanism involves NAD⁺ binding in the Rossmann fold and activation of the catalytic cysteine (Cys302 in ALDH2), nucleophilic attack on the aldehyde to form a thiohemiacetal, hydride transfer to produce a thioacyl-enzyme intermediate, and Glu268-mediated hydrolysis to release the acid product and NADH; this canonical chemistry underlies ALDH2’s role as an indirect antioxidant via aldehyde clearance rather than direct ROS scavenging (Parajuli, 2013; Wang & He, 2018). Importantly, ALDH2 is highly susceptible to oxidative and electrophilic inactivation—its active-site cysteine cluster (Cys301–Cys303) can be adducted by 4-HNE at micromolar concentrations (>10 µM), establishing a pathogenic feed-forward loop in which lipid peroxidation products both injure proteins and progressively compromise the aldehyde-detoxifying capacity of mitochondria (Karan et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009).

Alda-1 engages this system at multiple mechanistic levels. Structurally, Alda-1 binds to the substrate entrance tunnel and active site of ALDH2, altering the local environment to increase effective substrate/catalytic-cysteine proximity and improve NAD⁺ binding (lower Kₘ), while simultaneously acting as a molecular chaperone to stabilize conformational elements disrupted in the ALDH2*2 variant (e.g., restoring α-helix and active-site loop structures toward wild-type) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). Functionally, Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 catalytic activity approximately two-fold, but the effect is more pronounced in ALDH2*2 (10-fold or more in homotetramers), which is clinically relevant in East Asian populations; Alda-1 does not affect ALDH1/ALDH5 in initial selectivity panels, though subsequent biochemical reports indicate potential ALDH1A1 activation under specific conditions (i.e., DOPAL-inactivation assays), a detail that warrants further isozyme-specific profiling in ocular tissues (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013). Crucially, Alda-1 also reduces aldehyde access to catalytic cysteines (Cys302/301/303), protecting ALDH2 from 4-HNE–induced inactivation, thereby sustaining endogenous detoxification under aldehyde stress; in direct assays Alda-1 prevents rapid 4-HNE-mediated ALDH2 inactivation and shifts the enzyme to a higher-efficiency state (Gao et al., 2022; Kotraiah et al., 2013). The net biochemical outcome is enhancement of mitochondrial clearance of 4-HNE to the less reactive 4-hydroxynonenoic acid (4-HNA), alongside accelerated metabolism of other toxic aldehydes, which interrupts aldehyde-driven proteotoxic cascades (e.g., proteasomal inhibition, protein carbonyl accumulation) and preserves mitochondrial respiratory function (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014).

Systems-level consequences of ALDH2 activation by Alda-1 have been delineated extensively in heart and liver. In failing hearts with elevated aldehydic load, Alda-1 decreased 4-HNE-protein adducts and total carbonyls without altering ALDH2 protein abundance, demonstrating a purely catalytic detoxification effect (i.e., activity increase without expression change) (Gomes et al., 2014). Mitochondrial bioenergetic protection is robust: Alda-1 preserved State 3 respiration, increased RCR, normalized uncoupler responses (CCCP), reduced absolute and relative H₂O₂ release, decreased cytochrome c release, and corrected MPT sensitivity, indicating mitigation of mitochondria-centered death signaling under chronic oxidative/aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014). In isolated mitochondria, pre-incubation with Alda-1 prevented 4-HNE–induced declines in respiratory control and State 3 oxygen consumption, further supporting a direct anti-aldehyde effect on mitochondrial electron transport chain function (Gomes et al., 2014). In the APAP hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 reduced tissue 4-HNE adduct burden by an order of magnitude, preserved mitochondrial polarization, and reduced cell death, consistent with detoxification of lipid peroxidation products downstream of parent electrophile formation (Wimborne et al., 2020).

Retinal and neuronal contexts provide complementary mechanistic observations. In cultured endothelial cells exposed to amyloid-β₁–₄₀, Alda-1 restored mitochondrial function, reduced 4-HNE adducts and ROS, and rescued angiogenic responses, indicating that ALDH2 activation can directly blunt aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction in non-cardiac cells (Chen & Joshi, 2016; Roy, 2022). Within the retina, ALDH2 localizes across layers with predominant co-localization to CRALBP-positive Müller glia, and its expression diminishes with age; transgenic upregulation protects against retinal aging by decreasing oxidative-stress–related apoptosis and enhancing the unfolded protein response (UPR) in the ER, indicating that increased ALDH2 activity has cytoprotective effects in vivo in the aging retina (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020). In diabetic retinopathy rodent studies, Alda-1 increased retinal ALDH2, SIRT1, and Nrf2 signaling, decreased proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6), and improved electrophysiologic and structural outcomes, suggesting that ALDH2 activation enlists antioxidant and proteostasis pathways beyond direct aldehyde detoxification to preserve retinal function (He et al., 2018). In photoreceptor degeneration, Alda-1 upregulated SIRT1 and decreased ER stress/apoptotic markers, again consistent with mitigation of downstream stress signaling when aldehyde load is reduced (Yan et al., 2020).

Finally, the disease biochemistry underpinning our hypothesis—aldehyde toxicity as a conserved driver downstream of oxidative lipid peroxidation—is well defined in neurodegeneration and retinal biology. 4-HNE forms adducts that impair proteasome activity, promote accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and inflammation, covalently modify and crosslink amyloid peptides, impair ion pumps and transporters, and directly kill neurons at low micromolar concentrations; ALDH2 loss-of-function (including ALDH2*2) exacerbates accumulation of 4-HNE adducts and age-dependent neurodegeneration in rodent models (Chen & Joshi, 2016). In retinal disease, the RPE and photoreceptors operate in a high-oxygen, PUFA-rich environment, with continuous photo-oxidation and phagocytosis of outer segments generating lipid peroxides and aldehydes, and oxidative stress is a central driver of AMD pathogenesis; therapeutic strategies that augment endogenous detoxification (e.g., via Nrf2) have been proposed as rational approaches to bolster RPE resilience (Chen et al., 2023). Collectively, Alda-1’s biochemical action—activation of a mitochondrial enzyme that eliminates 4-HNE/MDA—integrates tightly with the pathophysiology of aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial and proteostatic injury that characterizes oxidatively stressed retinal tissues (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009).

Expected Effect  
In RPE mitochondria subjected to chronic oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, the proposed mechanism predicts that Alda-1 will (i) increase ALDH2 catalytic activity and resilience to aldehyde-induced inactivation, (ii) accelerate metabolic clearance of 4-HNE and related long-lived electrophiles to non-reactive acids, (iii) reduce covalent adduction/carbonylation of mitochondrial and cytosolic proteins, (iv) preserve oxidative phosphorylation (increased State 3 respiration and RCR), (v) lower mitochondrial H₂O₂ production, (vi) increase resistance to Ca²⁺-induced MPT and decrease cytochrome c release, and (vii) therefore reduce apoptotic signaling and downstream inflammation in RPE, which in aggregate should attenuate RPE dysfunction and slow progression of dry AMD (Gomes et al., 2014). While direct ALDH2 expression in RPE has not been demonstrated in the provided texts, ALDH2 is present across retinal layers (notably Müller glia) and declines with age, and increasing ALDH2 conferred protection in the aged mouse retina in vivo, supporting the rationale that ALDH2 activation in retinal tissue can be beneficial under oxidative stress; confirming ALDH2 expression and activity in human and murine RPE will be a critical enabling experiment (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020). The retina’s documented vulnerability to lipid peroxidation (PUFA-rich outer segments, high O₂ consumption, chronic light exposure) and the centrality of oxidative stress to AMD pathogenesis further support that increased mitochondrial aldehyde detoxification should reduce toxic aldehyde burden in RPE and adjacent cells (Chen et al., 2023).

Assay expectations and readouts for validation align closely with prior Alda-1 literature. In isolated RPE mitochondria or permeabilized cells, Alda-1 should preserve ADP-stimulated State 3 oxygen consumption and increase RCR versus vehicle under aldehydic load (e.g., exogenous 4-HNE) or oxidative stress conditions; decreased H₂O₂ release and normalization of uncoupler (CCCP) responses would be predicted based on cardiac mitochondria data (Gomes et al., 2014). Under Ca²⁺ challenge, Alda-1 should increase the threshold for MPT and reduce cytochrome c release; in intact RPE, Alda-1 should maintain Δψm under oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, NaIO₃, HOHA lactone), paralleling hepatocyte in vivo imaging under APAP (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). At the biochemical level, 4-HNE-protein adduct quantification (IHC/ELISA/LC-MS) and protein carbonylation assays should show significant reductions with Alda-1 pretreatment; mitochondrial respiratory chain complex activities may be preserved relative to vehicle under electrophile exposure (Gomes et al., 2014; Cheng, 2019). Downstream stress responses (e.g., ER stress markers such as GRP78, UPR activation; SIRT1 and Nrf2 activity; inflammatory cytokines TNF-α/IL-6) should reflect improved homeostasis, consistent with diabetic retina and MNU data (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). Methodologically, the respiratory chain enzymology and aldehyde reactivity analytics described for RPE systems (e.g., complex I–IV assays in 96-well format, reverse-phase HPLC quantitation of aldehyde scavenging, LC-MS/MS quantitation of aldehyde uptake) are directly applicable to evaluating Alda-1’s effects on mitochondrial function and aldehyde handling in RPE models (Cheng, 2019).

A critical caveat is that ALDH2 distribution within the retina emphasizes Müller cells rather than RPE in available reports, and ALDH2 can be inactivated by high aldehyde levels (>10 µM 4-HNE), implying that the therapeutic window may be constrained under extreme aldehydic stress; Alda-1 is explicitly reported to reduce 4-HNE accessibility to catalytic cysteines and reverse 4-HNE–mediated inhibition, which should mitigate this concern but does not obviate the need to quantify ALDH2 activity and 4-HNE load in RPE during oxidative stress (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022). Given that dry AMD pathobiology includes chronic oxidative stress, complement-driven inflammation, lysosomal/lipofuscin pathology, and lipid/protein debris accumulation (drusen), the expected benefit of Alda-1 would likely be most pronounced on the oxidative–aldehydic damage axis (mitochondrial and proteostatic integrity) rather than directly addressing complement or lipid trafficking, suggesting it would be a mechanistically complementary therapy potentially combined with agents targeting other AMD pathways (Chen et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic coherence with AMD pathophysiology: Dry AMD is driven in part by oxidative stress in RPE with accumulation of lipid peroxidation products; ALDH2 is a mitochondrial enzyme that detoxifies 4-HNE/MDA and is susceptible to inactivation by aldehydes, establishing a feed-forward injury loop that Alda-1 is designed to interrupt (Chen et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009; Karan et al., 2023).  
- Direct mitochondrial mechanism with robust preclinical performance: Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity, reduces 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, preserves State 3 respiration and RCR, reduces mitochondrial H₂O₂ emission, raises MPT thresholds, and decreases cytochrome c release under chronic aldehydic stress; these endpoints directly match the mitochondrial failure features observed in stressed RPE (Gomes et al., 2014).  
- Retinal in vivo signals: In diabetic and photoreceptor degeneration models, Alda-1 improved ERG, preserved retinal structure, increased SIRT1/Nrf2 signaling, reduced inflammatory cytokines, and diminished ER stress/apoptotic markers, collectively supporting retinal tissue benefit under oxidative stress (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020).  
- Protective breadth across organs and insults via aldehyde clearance: Repeated demonstration that Alda-1 reduces 4-HNE accumulation and preserves mitochondrial function in heart, liver, lung, intestine, and neuronal contexts increases confidence that the aldehyde-clearance mechanism is conserved and translatable (Wimborne et al., 2020; Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Pharmacogenetic upside: Alda-1 rescues ALDH2*2 activity, suggesting potential efficacy in East Asian ALDH2*2 carriers, a large at-risk population for aldehyde-mediated diseases; this also provides a biomarker-based stratification opportunity in trials (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Safety signs in chronic rodent dosing: Six-week daily Alda-1 in naïve rats showed no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight toxicity, supporting tolerability for longer-term therapy (Gomes et al., 2014).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of dry AMD/RPE-specific data: No direct evidence in RPE-focused dry AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy, complement dysregulation models, aging-driven GA models) is presented in the context, and ALDH2 expression has not been explicitly demonstrated in RPE here; expression across retina with Müller co-localization and protection in aged retina is encouraging but not definitive for RPE (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020).  
- Clinical translation gap: No human proof-of-concept for Alda-1 or class; no ALDH2 activator currently in clinical use; ocular PK, distribution, and chronic safety are uncharacterized (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Potential safety concerns: A preclinical report of Alda-1–associated crystalline nephropathy after I/R cautions that formulation, dosing, or off-target deposition may cause tissue-specific toxicity; comprehensive toxicology and formulation work are essential, especially for chronic ocular indications (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biological complexity and compensatory pathways: Chronic acceleration of aldehyde clearance could theoretically blunt electrophile-mediated adaptive antioxidant signaling (Keap1/Nrf2, PPAR), potentially reducing hormetic protection; the balance of detoxification versus adaptation requires careful evaluation in chronic degenerative settings (Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Enzyme inactivation at high aldehyde loads: ALDH2 is inactivated by >10 µM 4-HNE; although Alda-1 protects ALDH2 from 4-HNE and enhances activity, in extreme aldehydic states therapeutic efficacy might be limited, necessitating combination with upstream ROS control or lipid peroxidation inhibitors (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022).  
- Isoform selectivity: Some reports suggest Alda-1 can modulate ALDH1A1 activity, while others report inconclusive cross-activation; off-target activation or inhibition in ocular tissues could have unanticipated effects on retinoid metabolism or cellular differentiation, especially given ALDH1A1’s role in retinaldehyde metabolism and Müller cell biology (Kotraiah et al., 2013; Karan et al., 2023).  
- Delivery challenges: Systemic dosing achieves retinal effects in rodent DR/MNU models, but the optimal route for chronic dry AMD (topical, intravitreal, suprachoroidal, systemic) is unknown; achieving therapeutic mitochondrial concentrations in RPE with acceptable safety will be nontrivial and requires PK/PD studies (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Decision-oriented recommendations  
- Mechanistic validation in human/murine RPE: Quantify ALDH2 mRNA/protein/activity and subcellular localization in primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE; test whether Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity and protects against 4-HNE–induced ALDH2 inactivation in RPE mitochondria; measure 4-HNE/ACR/MDA adduct load ±Alda-1 under blue-light/NaIO₃/HOHA lactone stress (Karan et al., 2023; Cheng, 2019).  
- Mitochondrial function endpoints in RPE: Using established microplate assays and Seahorse OCR, test Alda-1’s effects on State 3 respiration, RCR, Δψm, H₂O₂ release, CCCP response, MPT susceptibility, and cytochrome c release under aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014; Cheng, 2019).  
- Retinal disease models aligned to dry AMD: Progress to NaIO₃-induced RPE injury, photo-oxidative stress, and aging/complement models relevant to geographic atrophy; evaluate RPE survival, autofluorescent lipofuscin, drusen-like deposits, inflammatory markers, and photoreceptor secondary degeneration with functional readouts (ERG/OCT) under Alda-1 (Chen et al., 2023).  
- Formulation and delivery: Develop ocular formulations (e.g., intravitreal, sustained-release) and conduct ocular PK/PD to quantify RPE mitochondrial exposure; evaluate chronic ocular and systemic safety with renal monitoring given crystalline nephropathy risk (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biomarkers and patient stratification: Consider ALDH2 genotype (ALDH2*2 carriers), circulating/ocular 4-HNE-adduct biomarkers, and retinal imaging endpoints as stratification and PD markers; Alda-1’s rescue of ALDH2*2 suggests a precision-medicine angle (Budas et al., 2009; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Combinations: Given AMD’s multifactorial pathobiology, test Alda-1 alongside Nrf2 activators or lipid peroxidation suppressors to determine additive/synergistic effects on RPE resilience while monitoring for suppression of adaptive electrophile signaling (Chen et al., 2023; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Overall, Alda-1 presents a mechanistically compelling, enzyme-directed strategy to alleviate aldehyde-driven mitochondrial and proteostatic injury in oxidatively stressed retinal tissues, with in vivo retinal efficacy already demonstrated in DR and photoreceptor degeneration contexts, albeit without RPE-centric dry AMD models to date (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). The totality of evidence across organ systems (cardiac, hepatic) underscores that Alda-1 reliably reduces 4-HNE load and preserves mitochondrial function in vivo—precisely the biology we seek to modulate in RPE for dry AMD—making this candidate worthy of structured, stepwise validation in RPE-specific systems and AMD-relevant models (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). Key risks reside in translational gaps (RPE expression, ocular PK/safety), potential toxicity signals (renal crystalline nephropathy under certain conditions), and the possibility that aldehyde detoxification alone will be insufficient to arrest complex AMD progression without adjunctive modulation of complement, lipid trafficking, or lysosomal pathways (Jin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). With these caveats, Alda-1 merits advancement to focused preclinical validation for dry AMD, with an emphasis on RPE mitochondrial protection endpoints, aldehyde-adduct burden, and rigorous ocular safety assessment before considering first-in-human studies.

Proposal for Metformin (Sigma-Aldrich D150959)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Metformin is a well‐known therapeutic agent belonging to the biguanide class, originally derived from guanidine compounds found in the plant Galega officinalis. The molecule is a synthetic derivative of naturally occurring galegine and has been refined into a modern oral antihyperglycemic agent (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). This class of compounds has historically been used as a first-line oral treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus, with metformin being one of the most prescribed drugs worldwide for managing hyperglycemia. Its synthesis did not follow the classical target‐driven design path but instead emerged from an adaptation of naturally occurring structures into a chemically optimized, orally bioavailable, and generally well-tolerated drug (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021). Given its long clinical history starting from the 1950s and subsequent FDA approval in the 1990s, metformin has accumulated a significant amount of safety data and clinical experience, which collectively make it an attractive candidate for repurposing into other disease areas, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) characterized by geographic atrophy (Amin et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, metformin has been used extensively as an antidiabetic agent to lower hepatic glucose output and improve peripheral insulin sensitivity. Its beneficial pleiotropic effects beyond glycemic control have been recognized over the years; these include anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antiangiogenic properties, which have been observed in both biochemical and clinical investigations. Multiple epidemiologic studies have examined the association between metformin use and ocular outcomes. Retrospective analyses in predominantly diabetic cohorts have indicated that metformin use correlates with reduced odds or hazard for developing age-related macular degeneration and other retinal diseases, although some studies report mixed results depending on cumulative dose, exposure timing, and concomitant diabetes-related complications (Moir et al., 2023; Amin et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2022). Notably, while metformin has not historically been approved for any ocular indication, several preclinical studies using retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell models have demonstrated that metformin may protect against oxidative damage and improve mitochondrial function. Moreover, a Phase II single-blind randomized trial was initiated to assess the efficacy of metformin in slowing the progression of geographic atrophy among non-diabetic patients with advanced dry AMD (Shen et al., 2024), suggesting that the concept of repurposing metformin for dry AMD is already under active clinical investigation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, metformin’s primary mechanism of action involves the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I of the electron transport chain, resulting in a decrease in ATP production and a concomitant increase in the intracellular AMP:ATP ratio. This metabolic shift leads to the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a master regulator of cellular energy homeostasis that orchestrates shifts in metabolism under conditions of energy deficit (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). AMPK activation exerts multiple downstream effects that are particularly relevant to RPE cell function and the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy. First, AMPK activation promotes autophagy, including mitophagy, a quality-control mechanism that ensures the removal of dysfunctional mitochondria. Preclinical studies in RPE cell models, such as those using ARPE-19 cells, have provided evidence that metformin increases autophagosome formation, reduces intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), lowers apoptosis rates, and helps maintain the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) under oxidative stress conditions (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, the activation of AMPK in RPE cells has been associated with upregulation of protective pathways including enhanced nitric oxide (NO) production and increased expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors such as PGC-1α, which together contribute to improved mitochondrial quality control (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).  

Furthermore, metformin is known to activate both AMPK-dependent and AMPK-independent signaling pathways. The AMPK-independent effects may include inhibition of NF-κB activation, leading to a reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α, which are implicated in chronic inflammation observed in the aging retina (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). From a biochemical standpoint, the inhibition of complex I by metformin also directly reduces the leakage of electrons that can form ROS, thereby lowering mitochondrial oxidative stress—a key aspect in the progression of dry AMD pathogenesis (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). It is important to note, however, that several reports have highlighted the concern that activation of AMPK in vivo or in vitro appears to require suprapharmacological doses of metformin, casting uncertainty on whether standard clinical dosing is sufficient to achieve these retinal effects (Moir et al., 2023). Nonetheless, the preclinical evidence supports a model whereby metformin’s inhibition of mitochondrial complex I—thereby reducing ROS and enhancing autophagy—provides a rationale for its potential use in protecting RPE cells from oxidative stress-induced damage (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis driving the repurposing of metformin for dry AMD is predicated on its ability to activate AMPK and inhibit mitochondrial complex I leakage in RPE cells, leading to reduced ROS production and enhanced mitochondrial quality control. In the context of geographic atrophy, RPE dysfunction and death play a central role in the degeneration of photoreceptors and the progression of AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that metformin can protect ARPE-19 cells (an established human RPE cell line) from oxidative insults by lowering intracellular ROS levels, augmenting autophagic processes, and preserving mitochondrial membrane potential (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, through the activation of AMPK, metformin is expected to stimulate the expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors, leading to improved mitochondrial function, which is critical given the high metabolic demands of the RPE (Moir et al., 2023). 

Epidemiologically, several retrospective cohort and case-control studies have observed associations between metformin use and a reduced risk of developing AMD. Some studies even suggest that these associations are dose- and timing-dependent, with earlier or sustained use of metformin correlating with greater protective effects (Moir et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Therefore, in an assay designed to measure the effects of metformin on mitochondrial function and oxidative stress in RPE cells, one would expect to see an enhancement in autophagic flux, decreased markers of oxidative stress, and preservation or restoration of Δψm. These cellular effects would ideally translate into a slower progression of geographic atrophy in vivo, as suggested by the decreased degeneration of the retinal layers that has been observed in certain mouse models of retinal damage (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). RPE cells are known to express AMPK and other components of the autophagy machinery, which further supports the rationale for targeting these pathways in the treatment of dry AMD (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Moir et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
Metformin shows considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly for geographic atrophy, due to several key strengths. First, its long and well-documented clinical history in the management of type 2 diabetes provides a robust safety profile and widespread clinical familiarity, which is a significant advantage when considering repurposing strategies (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021; Amin et al., 2022). Second, the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which metformin acts—namely, the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, subsequent activation of AMPK, and promotion of autophagy—are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. The ability of metformin to reduce ROS and promote mitochondrial quality control addresses one of the core aspects of RPE dysfunction and degeneration seen in geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Jiang et al., 2022).

Furthermore, the epidemiologic data showing associations between metformin use and a reduced incidence of AMD lend additional support to its potential utility in this setting (Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023). The possibility that metformin’s protective effects might be independent of its glycemic control properties is particularly intriguing, as it expands the target population to non-diabetic AMD patients—a group that represents the majority of those affected by geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2024). On a mechanistic level, the detailed understanding of metformin’s interaction with AMPK and mitochondrial pathways not only provides a clear therapeutic target but also offers multiple biomarkers for assessing efficacy in both preclinical and clinical studies.

Despite its strengths, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. One significant concern is whether standard clinical doses of metformin are sufficient to activate the AMPK pathway in retinal tissues, given that some in vitro studies indicate suprapharmacological doses are required to see a robust effect (Moir et al., 2023). This raises questions of retinal bioavailability and whether alternative delivery strategies, such as local ocular administration or formulation enhancements, might be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Additionally, while the epidemiologic studies are promising, they are not uniformly consistent; some retrospective analyses have reported no association or even conflicting results depending on dosing and timing parameters (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2019; Amin et al., 2022). These discrepancies underscore the inherent limitations of observational data, including potential confounding factors such as the presence and severity of diabetes, concomitant medications, and the challenges of accurately classifying AMD subtypes using administrative coding.

Another consideration is that although metformin’s broad mechanism of action (i.e., modulation of inflammation, oxidative stress, and autophagy) is advantageous in addressing multifactorial diseases like AMD, it may also lead to off-target effects or systemic side effects such as vitamin B12 deficiency or, in rare instances, lactic acidosis (Jiang et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). In elderly populations—who are generally most affected by dry AMD—these risks must be carefully weighed against the potential benefits. Moreover, the heterogeneity in study designs and patient populations in the available epidemiologic literature means that prospective, well-designed clinical trials remain essential to definitively determine whether metformin can meaningfully slow the progression of geographic atrophy in AMD (Shen et al., 2024).

In summary, the overall evaluation of metformin as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Its well-established safety profile, combined with mechanistic data that align closely with the underlying pathology of geographic atrophy, make it a compelling candidate. The strengths lie in its ability to activate AMPK, thereby reducing mitochondrial ROS, promoting autophagy, and potentially preserving RPE function—molecular actions that directly address key pathological features of dry AMD. However, critical questions regarding dosing, ocular bioavailability, and the variability in epidemiologic outcomes necessitate further rigorous investigation in controlled clinical settings. Moving forward, clinical trials designed to specifically assess metformin’s efficacy in non-diabetic populations with early to intermediate stages of geographic atrophy will be crucial to validate its repurposing potential. Overall, while metformin has significant promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional studies are needed to resolve questions about its optimal dosing regimen, delivery method, and long-term efficacy in preserving retinal structure and function (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022).
