Proposal for Tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA; Sigma-Aldrich 12399)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) is an endogenous bile acid, a taurine conjugate of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), that was originally isolated from bear bile and is now produced synthetically for laboratory and clinical research (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). As a member of the bile acid family, TUDCA has a dual role: its traditional function in lipid digestion is accompanied by potent signaling activities that provide chemical chaperoning properties. This property enables TUDCA to stabilize misfolded proteins and alleviate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. In addition, TUDCA exerts anti-apoptotic effects by modulating the mitochondrial cell death pathway. Its application as a neuroprotectant has emerged over the last decade, and its favorable ocular safety profile in preclinical studies has invited consideration for repurposing in retinal degenerative conditions such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TUDCA and related bile acids have been evaluated in several models of neurodegeneration and retinal degeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that TUDCA protects retinal cells against both oxidative injury and ER stress. In vitro, TUDCA treatment of ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) not only attenuated cell death but also reduced markers of oxidative damage, increased cell viability, and modulated antioxidant gene expression (Alhasani et al., 2020). In parallel, multiple in vivo studies have reported that systemic administration of TUDCA reduces photoreceptor apoptosis and preserves retinal structure and function in animal models of inherited retinal degeneration including retinitis pigmentosa and in models of exudative AMD such as laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Although the bulk of these preclinical investigations has been conducted in models focusing on photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells, or vascular endpoints, the underlying mechanisms of TUDCA’s cytoprotective activity raise the possibility that its benefits may extend to the RPE—the cell type that is centrally involved in dry AMD and geographic atrophy. Importantly, little direct evidence exists from dedicated geographic atrophy models or experiments that solely target RPE mitochondrial endpoints; however, the promising biochemical and electrophysiological data from rodent models suggest that the candidate’s safety and overall neuroprotective profile are well established in ocular systems (Alhasani et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanistic basis of TUDCA’s therapeutic potential is multifaceted. A central theme is its ability to reduce ER stress in cells that are undergoing chronic protein-folding challenges. Under conditions of sustained stress, the unfolded protein response (UPR) is activated, and key transcription factors such as CHOP (CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein homologous protein) become upregulated to drive cell death when the stress is unmanageable. TUDCA has been shown in various cell models to act as a chemical chaperone, thereby reducing ER stress and suppressing CHOP induction (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020). For instance, in ARPE-19 cell models treated with thapsigargin to induce ER stress, TUDCA treatment led to a marked decrease in CHOP expression and reduced apoptosis (Alhasani et al., 2020). This suggests that TUDCA modulates the ER stress response, possibly by stabilizing protein folding and facilitating the proper trafficking of misfolded proteins.  

In addition to its ER‐related effects, TUDCA exerts anti-apoptotic actions by stabilizing the mitochondrial membrane. Under stress conditions, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) triggers the intrinsic apoptosis pathway, characterized by the translocation of pro-apoptotic proteins such as Bax, the release of cytochrome c, and subsequent caspase activation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kusaczuk, 2019). Evidence from neuronal models and some retinal studies indicates that TUDCA prevents the depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, thereby preserving Δψm, and reduces downstream apoptotic events. This effect has been linked to a reduction in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), which are produced excessively when mitochondrial integrity is compromised. TUDCA’s actions in reducing overall intracellular ROS levels, as reported in H₂O₂-exposed RPE cells, further support the idea that improved mitochondrial function may contribute to cell survival (Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Moreover, TUDCA can modulate additional cellular pathways that are pertinent to retinal health. It has been reported to up-regulate antioxidant defenses via increased expression of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) and enhancement of glutathione (GSH) levels. These effects likely contribute to the reduction in both cytosolic and mitochondrial oxidative stress (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Other studies have highlighted TUDCA’s influence on phagocytic pathways in the RPE—for example, by promoting MerTK-mediated phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—which, although not directly linked to ER or mitochondrial stress, represent an important aspect of RPE physiology that could indirectly improve cell survival in degenerative conditions (Murase et al., 2015).  

Taken together, the biochemical and molecular data indicate that TUDCA’s mechanism of action is well aligned with addressing the cellular stress observed in dry AMD. By inhibiting CHOP induction, preserving Δψm, and reducing mtROS, TUDCA could feasibly stop or slow the progression of RPE cell death that underpins geographic atrophy (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect:  
The proposal hypothesizes that TUDCA will reduce ER stress in the RPE, thereby preventing secondary mitochondrial dysfunction and the associated production of reactive oxygen species. In the proposed assay, RPE cells (either ARPE-19 or primary RPE cultures) subjected to an ER stressor (such as thapsigargin or H₂O₂) are expected to exhibit elevated markers of ER stress, particularly CHOP, along with signs of mitochondrial distress including decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased mtROS production. On treatment with TUDCA at appropriate dosages (often in the 100 μM range in similar in vitro assays), one expects to observe a significant reduction in CHOP induction along with the preservation or restoration of Δψm, as measured by fluorescent indicators such as JC-1 or TMRM, and a concomitant decrease in mitochondrial ROS as assessed by probes such as MitoSOX. These effects are expected because prior in vitro studies in retinal cells have shown that TUDCA can ameliorate cell death by modulating oxidative stress and apoptosis, and similar outcomes have been observed in neuronal and non-retinal cell models (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Furthermore, given that dry AMD is characterized by chronic ER stress and secondary mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE, the ability of TUDCA to reduce these stress responses may translate into improved RPE survival and function. RPE cells express high levels of ER stress markers under pathologic conditions, and proteins such as CHOP are known mediators of apoptosis in these cells. It is therefore expected that TUDCA will attenuate the cascade of events initiated by ER stress—reducing apoptotic signaling, preserving mitochondrial function, reducing mtROS, and ultimately leading to enhanced cell viability. As such, the anticipated outcome in the proposed assay is a clear biochemical and functional improvement in RPE cultures challenged with ER stressors, supporting the use of TUDCA in dry AMD (Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
TUDCA presents as a promising candidate for drug repurposing in dry AMD due to its well-documented roles as an ER stress inhibitor and mitochondrial stabilizer. One of the major strengths of TUDCA is its dual mechanism of action: it not only functions as a chemical chaperone to reduce ER stress and inhibit the pro-apoptotic effector CHOP but also stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane to prevent the cascade of events leading to cell death. These effects are complemented by its ability to reduce overall reactive oxygen species and bolster antioxidant defenses, which are critical in tissues affected by chronic oxidative stress such as the RPE in geographic atrophy (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).  

In terms of therapeutic history, TUDCA has been used extensively in preclinical models of retinal degeneration, with multiple studies demonstrating its protective effects on photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells. Its prior use in ocular contexts and a favorable safety profile in animal models provide important translational support. However, one potential weakness in repurposing TUDCA for dry AMD is that most of the preclinical evidence is derived from models of photoreceptor degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, or choroidal neovascularization rather than from targeted assessments in RPE cells or dry AMD models. While there is suggestive evidence from several studies that TUDCA benefits RPE function—such as improved phagocytosis via MerTK activation—the direct demonstration of its ability to inhibit CHOP induction, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, or specifically reduce mitochondrial ROS in RPE is less robust (Alhasani et al., 2020; Murase et al., 2015).  

Furthermore, although mechanistic data in other tissue and neuronal models strongly support TUDCA’s capacity to modulate both ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kusaczuk, 2019), these endpoints have not been unequivocally established in RPE cells within the context of geographic atrophy. This gap highlights the need for further targeted preclinical studies. For example, experiments using polarized primary RPE cultures or RPE-specific animal models of dry AMD should be undertaken to directly measure CHOP expression, mitochondrial membrane potential via JC-1/TMRM assays, and mtROS levels via MitoSOX or equivalent assays following TUDCA treatment. Additionally, while in vitro assays have established its general safety in retinal cells, chronic dosing studies in appropriate AMD models will be important to establish long-term efficacy and safety.  

Another consideration is that the multifaceted nature of dry AMD pathogenesis extends beyond ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. While TUDCA’s actions on these pathways are compelling, resistance or compensatory mechanisms in RPE cells could limit its efficacy in the complex environment of geographic atrophy. Nonetheless, the broad-spectrum anti-apoptotic and anti-oxidative actions of TUDCA provide a strong rationale for its further examination in dry AMD.  

In summary, TUDCA is a highly attractive candidate for repurposing as a therapy for dry AMD based on its natural origin as a bile acid, its established use as a chemical chaperone and mitochondrial stabilizer, and its demonstrated neuroprotective and cytoprotective effects in multiple retinal models. Its capacity to reduce ER stress—with particular inhibition of CHOP induction—and to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential and lower oxidative stress aligns well with the proposed mechanism underlying RPE degeneration in geographic atrophy. However, critical gaps remain in the direct evidence for its efficacy in RPE-specific systems and AMD/dry AMD models. The next steps should include rigorous experimental validation in relevant in vitro and in vivo models to establish that TUDCA indeed preserves Δψm and suppresses mitochondrial ROS in ER-stressed RPE cells while reducing pro-apoptotic markers such as CHOP. If these endpoints can be achieved in targeted preclinical studies, TUDCA could represent a promising, safe, and mechanistically rational therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).

Proposal for Olaparib (Selleckchem #S1060)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Olaparib is a small‐molecule, synthetic inhibitor originally discovered and developed for oncology indications, particularly in cancers harboring BRCA mutations. It belongs to the class of PARP (poly[ADP‐ribose] polymerase) inhibitors that function by binding to the catalytic domain of PARP enzymes, competitively inhibiting the binding of NAD+ and thereby blocking poly‐ADP‐ribosylation reactions. Olaparib was discovered through high‐throughput screening and subsequently optimized chemically to yield a compound with high potency and selectivity for PARP1 and PARP2. As a synthetic chemotherapeutic agent, olaparib has been extensively characterized and approved by regulatory agencies for the treatment of various malignancies such as ovarian and breast cancer. Its mechanism involves “trapping” PARP on damaged DNA, although in nononcologic applications the key therapeutic action is related to the inhibition of overactive PARP1 activity in conditions of oxidative DNA damage. In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), the hypothesis is that olaparib will inhibit PARP1‐mediated NAD+ consumption in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby preserving both the cellular energy status and, indirectly, the activity of NAD+‐dependent enzymes such as the mitochondrial sirtuin SIRT3. This candidate falls within a larger class of repurposed drugs that are being re‐evaluated for neurodegenerative and retinal disorders, where dysregulated PARP activity is thought to be a key driver of cellular dysfunction under chronic oxidative stress (Jang et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Olaparib’s primary therapeutic history is rooted in oncology. It has been used clinically to target cancers that are deficient in homologous recombination repair, where its PARP‐inhibitory action leads to synthetic lethality in malignant cells. Over recent years, growing experimental evidence has implicated hyperactivation of PARP1 in a number of non-neoplastic conditions characterized by oxidative DNA damage and subsequent energetic collapse. Various studies carried out in retinal cell lines such as ARPE-19 under oxidative stress (e.g., H2O2 exposure) have demonstrated that pathological PARP1 activation leads to a depletion of NAD+ and ATP, mitochondrial depolarization, altered mitochondrial morphology, and ultimately, cell death; these studies have employed olaparib to effectively block PARP1 activity and thereby rescue the cells from these metabolic defects (Jang et al., 2018). In animal models that mimic features of dry AMD, such as sodium iodate (SI)-injected mice or rabbits, pharmacologic inhibition of PARP1 with olaparib resulted in preservation of retinal morphology including maintenance of outer nuclear layer thickness and improvements in electrophysiological readouts (Jang et al., 2018). To date, while significant preclinical evaluation has been performed in models of oxidative injury and retinal degeneration, olaparib has not yet been trialed clinically in dry AMD patients. However, the repurposing approach is supported by extensive literature in which PARP inhibitors have been proposed as a therapeutic approach to mitigate oxidative injury in neurodegenerative disorders, with the underlying rationale being the restoration of cellular NAD+ levels as well as improved mitochondrial bioenergetics (Jang et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The well-established mechanism of action of olaparib is based on the inhibition of the PARP enzyme family, primarily targeting PARP1. Under conditions of oxidative stress, DNA strand breaks activate PARP1, which catalyzes the transfer of ADP-ribose units from NAD+ to several nuclear and mitochondrial proteins. This process, known as poly-ADP-ribosylation, normally plays a role in DNA repair; however, when overactivated—as is observed in conditions of persistent oxidative damage—PARP1 consumes enormous amounts of cellular NAD+, leading to ATP depletion and an ensuing collapse of cellular energy metabolism. Olaparib binds to the catalytic domain of PARP1, thereby preventing the excessive transfer of ADP-ribose moieties and preserving intracellular NAD+ levels. This preservation of NAD+ is critical because NAD+ is a necessary cofactor not only for PARP activity but also for the function of a range of NAD+-dependent deacetylases, including the sirtuin family.

Within the context of dry AMD, RPE cells subjected to oxidative stress exhibit PARP1 hyperactivation, resulting in NAD+ depletion that compromises cellular bioenergetics and contributes to mitochondrial dysfunction. While much of the literature has focused on the interplay between PARP1 and nuclear sirtuin SIRT1 in the context of autophagy, emerging hypotheses posit that similar mechanisms extend to the mitochondria. SIRT3, a key mitochondrial deacetylase, requires NAD+ to catalyze the deacetylation of multiple mitochondrial proteins. One well-characterized substrate is manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), whose deacetylated, active form is responsible for detoxifying reactive oxygen species (ROS) within the mitochondria. The proposed mechanism is that by inhibiting PARP1, olaparib preserves NAD+ pools in RPE cells, which in turn sustains SIRT3 activity. Active SIRT3 would ensure proper deacetylation of mitochondrial proteins, including MnSOD, thus reducing mitochondrial protein hyperacetylation, curtailing mtROS production, and ultimately mitigating oxidative damage (Jang et al., 2018; Lin & Apte, 2018).

Notably, while multiple studies have documented that olaparib effectively reduces NAD+ depletion, preserves ATP levels, and maintains mitochondrial membrane potential in ARPE-19 cells under H2O2 challenge (Jang et al., 2018), direct assessments of SIRT3 activity and the acetylation state of mitochondrial proteins remain to be specifically reported. Several excerpts unequivocally state that although the biochemical cascade from PARP1 hyperactivation to NAD+ loss is well-documented, explicit data connecting PARP inhibition by olaparib to restored SIRT3-mediated mitochondrial deacetylation have not been presented (Jang et al., 2018). Thus, the mechanistic rationale is largely built on the inference that a well-maintained NAD+ pool under olaparib treatment will naturally support the activity of all NAD+-dependent enzymes, including SIRT3 (Jang et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
The expected effect of olaparib in experimental models of dry AMD is multifaceted. First, by inhibiting PARP1, olaparib should significantly reduce the accumulation of poly-ADP-ribose (PAR) polymers that are normally generated in response to oxidative DNA damage. This reduction in PARP1 activity would result in preservation of intracellular NAD+ and ATP levels, thereby preventing the energy collapse characteristic of parthanatos—a form of cell death distinct from classical apoptosis that has been implicated in RPE degeneration (Jang et al., 2018).

In in vitro assays using ARPE-19 cells, olaparib is expected to block H2O2-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, as evidenced by improved mitochondrial membrane potential measurements and normalized rates of ATP production. Functionally, such bioenergetic stabilization should correlate with increased cell survival and improved resistance to oxidative stress. Moreover, given the central role of NAD+ as a substrate for mitochondrial sirtuins, it is anticipated that olaparib treatment will indirectly sustain SIRT3 activity within the mitochondria. Although direct measurements of SIRT3 activity and mitochondrial protein acetylation were not explicitly given in the reviewed studies, the biochemical paradigm suggests that when NAD+ concentrations are conserved, SIRT3 maintains the deacetylated and therefore active state of key proteins. For example, the deacetylation of MnSOD by SIRT3 is crucial for controlling mtROS levels. A reduction in mitochondrial protein hyperacetylation would likely result in lower levels of mitochondrial oxidative stress, improved mitochondrial respiration, and an overall protective effect on both the metabolic and structural integrity of RPE cells (Jang et al., 2018; Lin & Apte, 2018).

In animal models designed to mimic the degenerative environment of dry AMD—such as the sodium iodate (SI) induced retinal degeneration model—olaparib has been shown to preserve retinal morphology. For instance, olaparib-treated animals exhibited maintenance of outer nuclear layer thickness and more robust electroretinogram (ERG) wave amplitudes compared to SI-treated controls (Jang et al., 2018). Thus, the expected effect of olaparib extends from the biochemical (preservation of NAD+ and suppression of PAR polymer formation) to the functional (preservation of retinal structure and function) levels. In assays that measure oxidative damage, assays of mitochondrial function, and endpoint assessments of RPE survival, olaparib treatment is therefore predicted to yield significant improvements relative to untreated, oxidatively stressed controls.

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of olaparib as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD proceeds from its well-characterized mechanism of action and a robust body of preclinical evidence, while also acknowledging certain gaps that need to be addressed in future research.

Strengths:  
1. The Mechanism Is Well-Established in Related Contexts: Olaparib’s ability to inhibit PARP1 has been incontrovertibly demonstrated both biochemically and in various disease models. Preclinical studies in ARPE-19 cells have repeatedly shown that olaparib can mitigate PARP1-dependent NAD+ depletion and restore cellular ATP levels under oxidative stress conditions (Jang et al., 2018). This is especially relevant in dry AMD, where RPE loss and mitochondrial dysfunction are driven by oxidative insults and chronic PARP activation.  
2. Preservation of NAD+ Pools: By blocking PARP1 overactivation, olaparib helps preserve the intracellular NAD+ pool, which is critical for maintaining the activity of NAD+-dependent enzymes. Although most studies have focused on the nuclear deacetylase SIRT1, the biochemical logic extends to mitochondrial sirtuins such as SIRT3. Given SIRT3’s essential role in deacetylating enzymes involved in the detoxification of ROS—most notably MnSOD—its preservation is of potential therapeutic importance in the context of dry AMD (Jang et al., 2018).  
3. Preclinical Efficacy in Retinal Models: Several studies have used olaparib in retinal oxidative injury models, demonstrating improvements in mitochondrial potential, cellular bioenergetics, and even in in vivo retinal function as measured by ERG. These data support the notion that PARP inhibition can translate into a meaningful rescue of retinal structure and function (Jang et al., 2018; Akkaya et al., 2025).  
4. Established Clinical Use in Oncology: Olaparib is already approved by major regulatory agencies for several cancer indications, meaning that its pharmacokinetics, safety profile, and manufacturing processes are well characterized. This facilitates the drug repurposing pathway and may allow for a head start in clinical development for dry AMD, provided that formulation and ocular delivery challenges can be overcome (Jang et al., 2018).

Weaknesses and Considerations:  
1. Incomplete Evidence on SIRT3 and Mitochondrial Deacetylation: While the preservation of NAD+ is well documented, direct evidence linking olaparib treatment to sustained SIRT3 activity and the corresponding maintenance of mitochondrial protein deacetylation is sparse in the current literature. Several studies explicitly note that measurements of SIRT3 activity or assessments of mitochondrial protein acetylation status were not performed in the RPE/retinal models reviewed (Jang et al., 2018; Du et al., 2016). Given that the hypothesis specifically posits that olaparib preserves SIRT3 activity—and, by extension, proper mitochondrial deacetylation—this represents a critical gap that must be filled by targeted experimental studies.  
2. DNA Repair and Long-Term Safety: PARP1 plays an important role in normal DNA repair processes. Chronic inhibition in a non‐oncologic setting such as dry AMD raises concerns about potential cumulative genomic instability in retinal cells. Therefore, long-term dosing regimens must be carefully optimized to balance neuroprotection against the risk of impairing physiologic DNA repair mechanisms (Jadeja et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018).  
3. Delivery and Bioavailability Challenges: Although olaparib is effective systemically in oncology, its bioavailability in ocular tissues following systemic administration may be suboptimal. Successful repurposing for dry AMD may require the development of novel ocular delivery formulations, such as topical eye drops or intravitreal injections, to achieve therapeutic concentrations at the level of the RPE without incurring off-target systemic toxicities (Kovacs et al., 2019; Jang et al., 2018).  
4. Translational Gap: Most of the available evidence for olaparib’s efficacy derives from preclinical models, including in vitro experiments in ARPE-19 cells and in vivo studies in animal models of retinal degeneration. There is currently no clinical trial data for olaparib in dry AMD, which increases the uncertainty associated with its translational potential. Furthermore, the pathophysiology of dry AMD is multifactorial and may involve additional pathways that are not fully addressed by PARP inhibition alone (Jang et al., 2018).  
5. Potential Off-Target Effects: While olaparib is selective for PARP enzymes, the extent to which off-target effects may impact retinal homeostasis is not fully understood. Ocular cells might have unique metabolic or repair requirements that differ from those in oncologic tissues, necessitating careful preclinical toxicology studies.

Overall, the repurposing of olaparib for dry AMD is supported by a robust mechanistic rationale—namely, that excessive PARP1 activation under oxidative stress depletes NAD+ reserves, leading to energy collapse and retinal cell death. By inhibiting PARP1, olaparib rescues NAD+ levels and has been shown to restore mitochondrial integrity and preserve retinal function in preclinical models. This fundamental mechanism is highly relevant to dry AMD pathogenesis, where oxidative stress-mediated damage to the RPE is a central feature. Moreover, given that NAD+ is required for the activity of sirtuins (including nuclear SIRT1 and mitochondrial SIRT3), ultimately ensuring proper deacetylation of key enzymes and maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis, the overall therapeutic cascade proposed by the hypothesis is well grounded in established biochemistry (Jang et al., 2018).

Nevertheless, while there is convincing evidence regarding the ability of olaparib to inhibit PARP1 and rescue bioenergetic failure in RPE under oxidative stress, a crucial aspect of the proposal—that PARP inhibition preserves SIRT3 activity and thus maintains mitochondrial deacetylation—remains largely inferential. Several studies have noted the absence of direct measurements of SIRT3 activity or mitochondrial protein acetylation status after olaparib treatment in RPE models (Jang et al., 2018; Du et al., 2016). It is conceivable that, if NAD+ pools are restored, SIRT3 function will inherently be maintained; however, without direct experimental validation, this remains an unproven aspect of the therapeutic mechanism. Moreover, the potential consequences of long-term PARP inhibition—particularly with respect to DNA repair fidelity—and the challenges of delivering adequate concentrations of the drug to the retina without systemic toxicity cannot be overlooked.

In addition, while preclinical studies using SI-induced retinal degeneration models have shown promising results with olaparib in terms of improving retinal morphology and function (as per improvements in ERG wave amplitudes and preservation of outer nuclear layer thickness), these models do not capture the full complexity of dry AMD in humans. Dry AMD is a chronic, multifactorial disorder with contributions from inflammation, drusen formation, and cumulative RPE dysfunction over years; thus, short-term protective effects observed in animal models, while encouraging, might not directly translate to robust clinical efficacy.

Taking into account both the strengths and the weaknesses, the overall potential for olaparib as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is promising but not yet definitive. The strengths lie in its well-documented ability to inhibit PARP1, prevent NAD+ depletion, and improve mitochondrial bioenergetics in models of retinal oxidative injury. These effects are directly relevant to the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying dry AMD, where RPE degeneration is driven by chronic oxidative stress. Furthermore, the fact that olaparib is already an approved drug for other indications offers a strategic advantage in terms of repurposing and regulatory approval. However, the lack of direct evidence linking olaparib treatment to the restoration of mitochondrial SIRT3 activity and normalization of mitochondrial protein acetylation is a significant gap in the current literature. Addressing this gap would require focused studies that assess SIRT3 enzyme activity, evaluate the acetylation status of mitochondrial proteins such as MnSOD, and determine whether these molecular endpoints correlate with improved RPE survival and function. Additionally, long-term safety studies that investigate the potential risk of impaired DNA repair in retinal cells under chronic PARP inhibition are warranted. Finally, developing an appropriate ocular delivery system that ensures effective local concentrations of olaparib while minimizing systemic exposure will be critical for translating these preclinical findings into a viable clinical candidate.

In conclusion, olaparib’s repurposing for dry AMD has significant mechanistic and preclinical support. Its ability to inhibit PARP1 offers a means to preserve NAD+ levels in RPE cells, thereby potentially maintaining mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative injury—a cascade that is highly attractive for a disease characterized by chronic oxidative stress. Although the evidence for PARP inhibition in rescuing NAD+ and ATP levels in the RPE is strong (Jang et al., 2018), the specific link between NAD+ preservation and the maintenance of mitochondrial sirtuin SIRT3 activity remains to be directly demonstrated. Addressing this knowledge gap through targeted biochemical assays will be essential before advancing olaparib into clinical trials for dry AMD. Overall, given the compelling preclinical data, existing clinical experience in oncology, and the critical need for novel therapeutics in dry AMD, olaparib represents a promising candidate that merits further investigation. Future studies should focus on elucidating its effects on mitochondrial deacetylation in RPE, optimizing ocular drug delivery, and carefully assessing long-term safety in the context of chronic retinal disease (Jang et al., 2018; Du et al., 2016; Lin & Apte, 2018).

Proposal for Urolithin A (Sigma-Aldrich SML1791)

1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Urolithin A (UA) is a naturally occurring polyphenolic metabolite that is generated in humans via the microbial transformation of dietary ellagitannins, which are abundant in pomegranates, berries, walnuts, and other fruits and nuts. UA belongs to the class of gut-derived α-benzocoumarin compounds and is produced through the specific metabolic activities of intestinal bacteria on ellagitannins and ellagic acid. The discovery of UA emerged from studies aimed at understanding the beneficial effects of diets rich in polyphenols on aging and cellular health, and its structure was elucidated as a 6H-dibenzopyran-6-one derivative. In general, compounds of this class are known for their anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, and pro-mitophagic properties. Over time, UA has been investigated increasingly for its ability to modulate mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis, garnering interest in its potential applications beyond traditional nutritional supplementation. Its multifaceted biological activities have been documented in several preclinical studies where it enhanced mitochondrial quality control, improved muscle endurance in aging populations, and mitigated neurodegenerative processes by clearing dysfunctional mitochondria, lending support to its candidacy as a repurposed drug for chronic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Makarov & Korkotian, 2023).  

Historically, naturally derived compounds with similar mechanisms of action have been used to address age-related cellular dysfunction. UA, however, stands out by virtue of its dual ability to invoke both mitophagy and lysophagy, which are critical for the removal of damaged organelles—key processes implicated in aging and neurodegeneration. This compound is not synthesized chemically in the traditional pharmaceutical sense; rather, its production relies on the interplay between dietary intake and the gut microbiota, reinforcing the concept that natural metabolic products can be harnessed as therapeutic agents. Its inclusion in the spectrum of therapeutics aimed at cellular rejuvenation has sparked significant interest, particularly because its widespread availability in the human diet and favorable safety profile, as observed in early clinical trials, set a promising foundation for further drug development (Maksimović et al., 2025; Liu, 2022).

2. Therapeutic History  
Urolithin A has been extensively studied in the context of aging and degenerative diseases, and its therapeutic history spans several biomedical, clinical, and biochemical investigations. Preclinical studies have shown that UA is effective in enhancing mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria. In animal models, UA supplementation has been correlated with improved mitochondrial function and increased muscle endurance, which has led to its exploration as an “anti-aging” agent. Notably, several clinical trials have confirmed its safety in elderly populations, with doses up to 2,500 mg/day being well tolerated and associated with improvements in mitochondrial biomarkers in skeletal muscle (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Liu, 2022).  

In the realm of neurodegeneration, UA has been recognized for its neuroprotective activities. Studies have demonstrated that UA can ameliorate cognitive impairment and reduce inflammatory markers, suggesting benefits in neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Fehér et al., 2022). Importantly, recent investigations have extended the focus to ocular health. Preclinical models of retinal degeneration—particularly those mimicking dry AMD—have emerged as critical systems in which UA’s multifactorial actions are being tested. In models employing sodium iodate (SI) to induce retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) damage, UA treatment resulted in enhanced RPE cell survival, restoration of autophagic flux, and preservation of visual function (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). These studies underscore UA’s potential in mitigating geographic atrophy, a defining feature of dry AMD.  

Beyond its direct mitochondrial effects, UA has been evaluated for its impact on lysosomal function. Some reports indicate that UA exerts potent neuroprotective benefits by promoting SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy, leading to the clearance of damaged lysosomes and restoration of cellular proteostasis. This lysophagy mechanism appears to be crucial in maintaining retinal cellular homeostasis and preventing RPE atrophy, a process that is marked by an accumulation of dysfunctional organelles and consequent oxidative stress in AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Although direct clinical use of UA in the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular diseases has not yet been fully realized, the wealth of preclinical evidence—particularly from relevant animal models—provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in this context. In summary, UA’s therapeutic history demonstrates its utility across multiple age-related pathologies, with growing evidence supporting its potential application in dry age-related macular degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

3. Mechanism of Action  
The molecular mechanisms underpinning the actions of Urolithin A are multifaceted and involve intricate interactions across several cellular pathways. Central to UA’s mechanism is its ability to induce selective autophagy, a process that includes both mitophagy and lysophagy, leading to the clearance of damaged mitochondria and lysosomes, respectively. Under normal physiological conditions, mitochondria that lose membrane potential become marked for degradation through the action of PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1), which accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane. This accumulation results in the recruitment and activation of Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates mitochondrial surface proteins, thereby flagging them for autophagic degradation. UA has been shown to upregulate the PINK1/Parkin pathway, thereby enhancing the clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria and ensuring mitochondrial quality control (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024; Jayatunga et al., 2021).  

In addition to its role in mitophagy, UA has been demonstrated to elicit pronounced effects on lysosomal recycling processes through the promotion of SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy. This pathway is critical because damaged lysosomes, if not effectively removed, can contribute to cellular toxicity and inflammation. The engagement of p62 in the targeting of these vesicles for autophagosome formation has been observed as a necessary step in the restoration of autophagic flux within RPE cells (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). The dual activation of mitophagy and lysophagy by UA helps mitigate the accumulation of damaged organelles, thereby reducing the levels of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and subsequent oxidative stress.

At the biochemical level, UA influences several upstream signaling pathways. Notably, it activates the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/ULK1 axis—a key regulator of autophagy. Activation of AMPK leads to phosphorylation of ULK1, kick-starting the autophagy process, and is associated with improved energy balance and mitochondrial turnover. This activation is complemented by an upregulation of factors such as PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha), which is instrumental in mitochondrial biogenesis. Together, these events not only promote the removal of impaired mitochondria but also support the generation of new, functional mitochondria, thereby restoring mitochondrial homeostasis (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the anti-inflammatory properties of UA are closely tied to its capacity to modulate oxidative stress. By clearing mitochondria that are prone to leaking mtROS, UA indirectly diminishes the activation of pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB and AP-1, which have been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. UA’s activation of SIRT1, SIRT3, and AMPK also play a role in upregulating antioxidant defenses; for instance, the enhanced transcription of Nrf2-dependent genes contributes to a robust antioxidative response. These molecular interactions collectively participate in mitigating the inflammatory milieu that is characteristic of neurodegenerative conditions and retinal disorders (Makarov & Korkotian, 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Jayatunga et al., 2021).

In the context of retinal degeneration, several studies have delineated how UA’s molecular actions translate into cytoprotective outcomes. In SI-induced retinal injury models, the re-establishment of autophagic flux by UA is correlated with reduced RPE cell death and preservation of photoreceptor function. Although some findings suggest that UA’s neuroprotective effects in these models are independent of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, there is substantial evidence that UA comprehensively enhances cellular quality control mechanisms through both mitophagy and lysophagy. This dichotomy might reflect the compound’s capability to engage multiple parallel pathways to ensure the efficient clearance of damaged organelles (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Fehér et al., 2022). Given that the retina is especially sensitive to oxidative stress and that impaired mitochondrial dynamics are a hallmark of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD, these molecular mechanisms underscore UA’s therapeutic potential.

At a more granular level, it is worth noting that UA appears to influence the expression levels of key mitophagy-related proteins not only at the post-translational level but also transcriptionally. For instance, treatment with UA has been associated with increased expression of Parkin and proteins involved in the formation of autophagosomes, such as BECN1, further reinforcing its role in maintaining mitochondrial and lysosomal integrity. This transcriptional regulation may be mediated by the activation of transcription factors such as FOXO, which have been implicated in cellular stress responses and longevity pathways. As mitochondrial dysfunction contributes significantly to the pathology of dry AMD, the ability of UA to simultaneously promote the degradation of damaged mitochondria and stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis positions it as a strong candidate for addressing the underlying etiologies of RPE degeneration (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

In summary, the detailed biochemistry of UA illustrates that its mechanism of action involves a well-coordinated activation of autophagic processes through both the PINK1/Parkin axis for mitophagy and the SQSTM1/p62 pathway for lysophagy, with auxiliary support from AMPK/ULK1 and SIRT-mediated signaling. This comprehensive modulation of cellular clearance pathways is critical in contexts where mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal impairment drive disease progression, such as in dry age-related macular degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

4. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis behind repurposing Urolithin A for dry AMD posits that the compound enhances PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby accelerating the clearance of damaged mitochondria that contribute to excessive mtROS production. In the cellular assays designed to evaluate this therapeutic intervention, the expected effect would be a measurable reduction in mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress within RPE cells, ultimately leading to improved cellular viability and resistance to atrophy.  
 
Experimental models of RPE degeneration, particularly those utilizing sodium iodate (SI) as a toxic insult, have provided a platform for assessing the cytoprotective properties of UA. In these models, UA treatment leads to a restoration of autophagic flux—a critical determinant of cellular health—by enhancing both the degradation of impaired mitochondria and the recycling of damaged lysosomes through the p62-dependent pathway. The net effect is a significant decrease in RPE cell death and, consequently, the preservation of photoreceptor cells and visual function. This outcome is particularly relevant for dry AMD, a condition characterized by geographic atrophy of the RPE and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024).

At the molecular level, the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway by UA is expected to facilitate the tagging of dysfunctional mitochondria for autophagic removal. Consequently, a reduction in mtROS levels would follow, as damaged mitochondria are a major source of these reactive species. In parallel, the activation of AMPK/ULK1 signaling by UA further promotes autophagosome formation, ensuring that the cell’s degradative capacity is optimized to handle the increased load of dysfunctional organelles. The coordinated activation of these pathways not only improves mitochondrial quality control but also indirectly suppresses downstream inflammatory cascades that are typically exacerbated by oxidative stress. For instance, by reducing mtROS levels, UA is anticipated to attenuate the activation of pro-inflammatory transcription factors such as NF-κB, thereby contributing to a more quiescent cellular environment supportive of RPE survival (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

More specifically, in the assay proposed by the research team, RPE cells would be evaluated for changes in markers of mitophagy and lysophagy as well as for functional readouts of mitochondrial health. Biochemical assays might include quantification of PINK1 and Parkin recruitment to mitochondria, measurement of autophagic flux using LC3 conversion assays, and assessment of p62 levels. Furthermore, evaluation of mitochondrial membrane potential and ROS production through fluorometric assays would provide additional functional evidence for UA’s efficacy. Given that studies in animal models have shown that UA treatment not only restores autophagic flux but also leads to increased cone survival and improved visual function, it is reasonable to expect that similar beneficial effects could be recapitulated in RPE cells in vitro (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Another anticipated effect of UA treatment in RPE cells is the upregulation of mitochondrial biogenesis. The activation of AMPK and the consequent stimulation of PGC-1α are critical steps in fostering the production of new mitochondria, which serve to replace those that have been degraded. This replenishment of the mitochondrial pool is essential for maintaining cellular energy homeostasis in an environment that is otherwise challenged by the metabolic demands of ongoing stress. The dual action of UA in both clearing damaged mitochondria and promoting the biogenesis of healthy ones creates a favorable cellular milieu that could slow, or potentially reverse, the progression of RPE atrophy—a key pathological feature of dry AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Moreover, the expected reduction in mtROS levels upon UA treatment has broader implications for the cellular stress response. High levels of ROS not only cause direct oxidative damage to cellular components but also activate signaling pathways that lead to further inflammation and apoptosis. By mitigating this excessive ROS production, UA is likely to reduce the activation of stress-related kinases and inflammatory mediators that contribute to the degeneration of RPE cells. This protective effect on cellular integrity is anticipated to translate into preserved retinal function, as the health of the RPE is integral to the maintenance of the outer retina and photoreceptor survival (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Fehér et al., 2022).

In summary, the expected effect of UA in the proposed assay is multifactorial:  
– Enhanced clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria via the upregulation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway, as well as p62-dependent lysophagy.  
– A corresponding reduction in mtROS, leading to decreased oxidative stress and lower inflammatory signaling.  
– Improvement in mitochondrial biogenesis and overall cellular energy homeostasis via activation of the AMPK/ULK1 pathway and upregulation of PGC-1α.  
– Ultimately, these molecular changes should culminate in improved RPE cell survival and a delay or reversal of atrophic processes that underpin dry AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

5. Overall Evaluation  
In evaluating Urolithin A as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and potential areas for further investigation emerge. First and foremost, UA offers a robust safety profile supported by both preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials in elderly populations, where it has been administered at relatively high doses without observable toxicity or adverse events (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Liu, 2022). This favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile is critical given the generally conservative approach required when developing treatments for chronic, age-related conditions like AMD.

The molecular versatility of UA is another significant strength. Its capacity to engage multiple autophagic pathways—specifically, the PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy and the SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy—provides a multifaceted approach to mitigating RPE degeneration. Given that the pathogenesis of dry AMD involves a complex interplay of mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation, the ability of UA to target these processes simultaneously renders it a particularly attractive candidate (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Furthermore, the activation of upstream signaling pathways such as AMPK/ULK1 not only enhances autophagic activity but also supports mitochondrial biogenesis, thereby ensuring that the clearance of damaged mitochondria does not result in an energy deficit within RPE cells (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Preclinical data from retinal degeneration models provide compelling evidence that UA can ameliorate pathological features reminiscent of dry AMD. In SI-induced models, UA treatment has resulted in restored autophagic flux, reduced RPE cell death, and preservation of visual function—all of which are promising indicators for its potential to slow or reverse the atrophic processes underlying geographic atrophy in AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Moreover, its ability to mitigate inflammatory signaling and reduce mtROS production adds another layer of protective activity that is critical in managing chronic retinal degeneration.

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges warrant consideration. One area of potential ambiguity concerns the precise mechanistic contributions of the PINK1/Parkin pathway versus the SQSTM1/p62-mediated lysophagy in mediating UA’s protective effects. While some studies emphasize the role of PINK1/Parkin in clearance of damaged mitochondria, others have reported that UA’s neuroprotective benefits are maintained even with genetic manipulations of these proteins, suggesting that p62-dependent lysophagy may be the predominant mechanism in certain contexts (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Fehér et al., 2022). This duality raises questions regarding which pathway is most critical in RPE cells, particularly given that the proposed hypothesis centers on enhanced PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy. Further mechanistic studies in RPE-specific models will be necessary to delineate the relative contributions of these pathways and to optimize dosing and formulation strategies accordingly.

Another potential weakness is the translational gap between preclinical studies and clinical application in dry AMD. Although UA has shown promise in animal models of retinal degeneration, human disease is complex, and dry AMD is known for its multifactorial etiology. The pharmacokinetic properties of UA, including its relatively short half-life and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate ocular bioavailability, might necessitate novel delivery strategies for effective retinal targeting. Formulation development—potentially involving sustained-release systems or ocular-specific delivery vehicles—may be required to overcome these hurdles (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). Additionally, while the evidence from non-ocular (e.g., muscle and neural) studies is robust, direct clinical evidence in AMD patients remains sparse, necessitating carefully designed human trials to confirm efficacy and safety in this specific population.

It is also important to contextualize UA’s potential within the current landscape of AMD treatments. While existing therapies for wet AMD (e.g., anti-VEGF agents) have transformed clinical outcomes, there remains no established treatment for dry AMD. The multifaceted mode of action of UA—targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation—offers a unique therapeutic approach that could complement or, in some cases, provide an alternative to emerging interventions. However, comparative studies against other experimental agents will be critical to fully establish its translational relevance and competitive advantage in the therapeutic space (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Overall, Urolithin A presents several compelling attributes that support its development as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its origin as a naturally derived, gut-microbiota transformation product provides a favorable starting point from a safety perspective. Preclinical studies consistently demonstrate its ability to enhance autophagic clearance mechanisms, reduce oxidative damage, and improve cell survival in models that recapitulate key features of AMD. The ability of UA to simultaneously stimulate both mitophagy and lysophagy—the former via the PINK1/Parkin pathway and the latter via p62-dependent mechanisms—positions it as a multi-targeted intervention capable of addressing the multifactorial pathology of RPE degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Nonetheless, for the successful translation of UA into a clinically effective therapy for dry AMD, several challenges need to be addressed. Detailed mechanistic insights specifically in RPE cells are required to understand the relative importance of the PINK1/Parkin versus the lysophagy pathway. Optimizing drug delivery to ensure sustained retinal bioavailability and addressing potential issues related to its pharmacokinetic profile are also key areas that will require further research. Finally, controlled clinical studies in AMD patients will be essential to validate the promising preclinical findings and to ensure that the observed benefits in animal models translate into meaningful clinical outcomes.

In conclusion, based on the comprehensive literature reviewed from biochemical, clinical, and biomedical sources, Urolithin A demonstrates significant potential as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its established ability to enhance mitochondrial quality control through both mitophagy and lysophagy, alongside its additional anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, offers a novel mechanism to counteract the progressive degeneration observed in RPE cells during AMD. Given the encouraging preclinical data and a robust safety profile already evidenced in other indications, further investigations—particularly those focusing on RPE-specific mechanisms and optimized ocular drug delivery—are warranted to fully ascertain UA’s clinical potential in halting or reversing geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024; Jayatunga et al., 2021).
