Proposal for Melatonin (Sigma-Aldrich M5250)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous indoleamine neurohormone first identified as a pineal product and now recognized to be synthesized in many extrapineal tissues, including the human eye (retina, retinal pigment epithelium [RPE], lens, ciliary body) where it is also delivered via the circulation and acts locally through cognate receptors (MT1, MT2) and the MT3 binding site (quinone reductase 2) (Lundmark et al., 2006; Lundmark et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2024). Ocular melatonin is under circadian control and is produced primarily by photoreceptors, with additional production reported in inner retina and potentially the RPE, consistent with a paracrine neuromodulatory role in retinal physiology; importantly, melatonin synthesis has been localized to mitochondria, linking its biosynthesis directly to the organelle most relevant to retinal oxidative metabolism (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024). Biosynthesis proceeds from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase to serotonin, followed by arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT) and hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase (HIOMT) to generate melatonin, which freely diffuses to act in an autocrine/paracrine manner (Ma et al., 2024). As a chemical class, melatonin belongs to amphiphilic indoleamines; it partitions into both aqueous and lipid compartments, crosses biological barriers (including the blood–retinal barrier), and concentrates in mitochondria, properties that underpin its direct antioxidant, membrane-protective, and mitochondrial-modulatory actions described in multiple ocular contexts (Romeo et al., 2024; Rastmanesh, 2011; Ma et al., 2024).

Melatonin’s pharmacology encompasses receptor-dependent signaling via MT1 and MT2 G protein–coupled receptors (G_i and G_q/11 coupling), and receptor-independent actions as a direct free-radical scavenger with active redox metabolites (e.g., AFMK, AMK) capable of sequential radical quenching (“antioxidant cascade”), allowing a single parent molecule to neutralize multiple reactive species; MT3 corresponds to cytosolic quinone reductase 2 (QR2) and represents a distinct enzymatic interaction relevant to ocular physiology (D’Angelo et al., 2024; Lundmark et al., 2007; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Rastmanesh, 2011). This dual pharmacology (receptor-mediated signaling plus direct ROS/RNS scavenging) provides a mechanistic basis for melatonin’s pleiotropic antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial-protective effects in the retina and RPE, actions widely reported in preclinical models of oxidative retinal injury, diabetic retinopathy, and nonexudative AMD (Crooke et al., 2017; Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Within ophthalmology, melatonin and melatonergic agents have been explored across inflammatory, neurodegenerative, and vascular retinal diseases. Topical melatonin (0.1%) reduced intraocular inflammation and blood–ocular barrier permeability in rabbit uveitis while increasing tear and aqueous antioxidant activity (supporting tolerability and local pharmacodynamic engagement), and multiple melatonin analogs lowered intraocular pressure in glaucoma, with nanomicelles extending hypotensive and neuroprotective effects (Rusciano & Russo, 2024). In diabetic retinopathy models, melatonin reduced retinal oxidative and nitrosative stress, decreased hypoxia-inducible factor-1α and VEGF signaling, protected the blood–retinal barrier, and improved neural survival, aligning with its redox, anti-inflammatory, and anti-angiogenic pharmacology (Crooke et al., 2017).

For macular degeneration, mechanistic and efficacy signals span in vitro RPE studies, in vivo retinal protection in mice, and human observational datasets. A protected in vivo AMD-relevant signal includes a subcutaneous melatonin pellet that preserved visual function and outer retinal structure and limited oxidative stress in a nonexudative AMD mouse model (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Independently, rodent studies demonstrate intravitreal melatonin prevents acute photoreceptor loss (MNU model) by lowering oxidative damage markers (retinal MDA, 8-OHdG), increasing mitochondrial MnSOD and total SOD activities, and reducing photoreceptor apoptosis—evidence of both antioxidant and anti-apoptotic benefits from local delivery (Li et al., 2020). In RPE cell models (ARPE-19), melatonin consistently protected against H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury by lowering ROS and lipid peroxidation, restoring mitochondrial membrane potential, reducing Bax/cytochrome c/caspase-7 activation, and promoting autophagy (increased LC3-II and Beclin-1, reduced p62), with low-nanomolar protective effects blocked by the melatonin receptor antagonist luzindole, implicating receptor mediation at physiologic ranges (Chang et al., 2018; Blasiak et al., 2016).

Emerging ferroptosis-focused work further reports that melatonin rescues Aβ₁₋₄₀–induced RPE degeneration by curbing lipid peroxidation, restoring GPX4 and SLC7A11, and normalizing iron handling, with loss-of-function of MDM2 abolishing protection and positioning PI3K/AKT→MDM2→P53→SLC7A11 as a key axis; in vivo, melatonin preserved RPE structure and ERG responses in Aβ₁₋₄₀ models (Wu et al., 2025). These mechanistic and efficacy themes converge with a high-quality in vivo finding that melatonin “protects the retina from experimental nonexudative age-related macular degeneration” in mice (Diéguez et al., 2020).

Clinical observations are suggestive but not definitive. A large real-world EHR cohort analysis (TriNetX) associated chronic melatonin use with lower incidence of AMD and reduced progression from nonexudative to exudative AMD after propensity matching, while acknowledging potential residual confounding and calling for randomized trials (Jeong et al., 2024a). An editorialized report in JAMA Ophthalmology similarly noted protective associations and biological plausibility (RPE protection, VEGF reduction) while emphasizing exploratory design and the need for confirmatory prospective studies (Jeong et al., 2024b). Earlier case-series reported that 3 mg oral melatonin nightly for three months stabilized or improved macular changes in many AMD patients, but these uncontrolled data lack modern trial rigor (Lundmark et al., 2007; Martínez-Águila et al., 2021). Across aging and AMD, reduced nocturnal melatonin and urinary aMT6s have been documented, providing a pathophysiologic rationale for supplementation in older adults; however, oral melatonin exhibits variable and often low bioavailability, and aqueous/topical formulations must address photostability and posterior-segment delivery challenges (Čolak & Žorić, 2019; Blasiak et al., 2016; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Melatonin’s ocular actions relevant to dry AMD encompass receptor-mediated signaling, direct and indirect antioxidant effects, mitochondrial protection, modulation of apoptosis and autophagy/mitophagy, ferroptosis suppression, and immune/vascular regulation.

- Receptor-mediated signaling (MT1/MT2/QR2): MT1 and MT2 are expressed in retina and RPE; MT1 is present in photoreceptor inner segments and inner retinal neurons, MT2 shows high retinal expression and is reported in RPE, while the MT3 binding site corresponds to QR2, an oxidoreductase implicated in ocular physiology (Lundmark et al., 2006; Lundmark et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2024). In RPE, low-dose melatonin protection against oxidants is blocked by luzindole, indicating MT receptor involvement at physiologic concentrations (≤10⁻⁸ M), whereas higher concentrations (>10⁻⁶ M) exert receptor-independent antioxidant effects (Blasiak et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2018). MT1-dependent signaling maintains mitochondrial function under oxidative stress in RPE, underscoring receptor linkage to mitochondrial homeostasis in relevant models (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

- Direct and cascade antioxidant activity: Melatonin directly scavenges ROS/RNS, including hydroxyl radicals, and via successive metabolism (3-hydroxymelatonin → AFMK → AMK) neutralizes multiple radicals (“antioxidant cascade”), affording broad-spectrum redox control across aqueous and lipid compartments due to its amphiphilicity (Rastmanesh, 2011; Čolak & Žorić, 2019). In retinal tissues it reduces lipid peroxidation (MDA) and oxidative DNA damage (8-OHdG), and its metabolites independently contribute to radical quenching in ocular systems (Li et al., 2020; Romeo et al., 2024).

- Indirect antioxidant signaling (Nrf2, Sirtuins, AKT): Melatonin modulates redox-sensitive transcriptional programs; it maintains or enhances Nrf2 nuclear activity in several ocular contexts (though Nrf2 responses can be model-dependent), leading to upregulation of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutases and glutathione peroxidases; it also engages AKT phosphorylation and related DNA damage responses (Blasiak et al., 2016; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Melatonin regulates sirtuins (SIRT1, SIRT3) which link metabolism to antioxidant gene expression, autophagy, and anti-inflammatory effects, with SIRT1/SIRT3 activation reducing apoptosis and VEGF and promoting autophagy gene programs; modulation is context-dependent but provides additional axes by which melatonin can protect RPE mitochondria and restrain inflammatory signaling (Crooke et al., 2017).

- Mitochondrial protection: Melatonin concentrates in mitochondria, stabilizes the electron transport chain, reduces electron leakage, maintains mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), inhibits the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, and can activate uncoupling proteins; it reduces mtDNA damage and restores respiratory control, thereby curbing ROS generation at its source (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Tong et al., 2022). In vivo retina, intravitreal melatonin increased mitochondrial MnSOD (SOD2) activity and total SOD, aligning with enhanced endogenous antioxidant defenses at the organellar level (Li et al., 2020). In RPE cell models, melatonin preserved Δψm (JC-1/TMRM assays) after H₂O₂ challenge (Chang et al., 2018).

- Anti-apoptotic effects: In ARPE-19 cells, melatonin reduced the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, decreased cytochrome c release and caspase-7 activation, and lowered TUNEL positivity, consistent with inhibition of intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis; this aligns with higher Bcl-2 mRNA and fewer apoptotic photoreceptors in vivo (Chang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020). Mechanistically, mitochondrial stabilization, reduced ROS, and modulation of NF-κB/JAK-STAT signaling contribute to anti-apoptosis (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

- Autophagy/mitophagy regulation: Melatonin increases LC3-II and Beclin-1 and decreases p62 in RPE oxidative stress models, indicating enhanced autophagic flux; MT2-mediated inhibition of mTOR and SIRT1-linked transcriptional control further connect melatonin to autophagy and mitophagy, processes essential for RPE proteostasis and organellar quality control in aging (Chang et al., 2018; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Given that impaired mitophagy is a feature of early AMD, pharmacologic reinforcement of autophagy/mitophagy by melatonin is mechanistically aligned with disease biology (Crooke et al., 2017).

- Ferroptosis suppression: Aβ₁₋₄₀–induced ferroptosis in RPE is attenuated by melatonin via PI3K/AKT-driven phosphorylation and activation of MDM2, which inhibits p53; this derepresses SLC7A11, restores cystine import and GSH synthesis, and rescues GPX4 activity, thereby reducing lipid peroxidation, Fe²⁺ accumulation, and mitochondrial ultrastructural damage; MDM2 knockdown abrogates these effects, functionally linking melatonin to the PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53/SLC7A11 axis (Wu et al., 2025). In vivo, melatonin preserved ERG a-/b-waves and outer retinal integrity after Aβ₁₋₄₀ insult (Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-inflammatory and immune modulation: Melatonin limits NF-κB activation, reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6), and modulates immune cell phenotypes (e.g., promoting macrophage polarization toward tissue-repair M2), contributing to reduced retinal inflammation; it suppresses nitric oxide synthases and decreases NO, relevant to nitro-oxidative stress (Crooke et al., 2017; Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024). In models of choroidal neovascularization, melatonin attenuated angiogenesis via HIF-1α–VEGF inhibition and RhoA/ROCK-mediated macrophage/microglia polarization, suggesting an adjunctive anti-neovascular role even though dry AMD lacks CNV (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Telomere/telomerase and DNA repair: Melatonin modulates telomerase and DNA repair pathways in retinal cells, with reports of stimulated telomerase activity and reduced telomere erosion in senescent contexts, and increased efficacy of oxidative DNA damage removal in RPE, potentially mitigating RPE senescence in AMD (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rastmanesh, 2011).

- Electrophysiologic and circadian effects: Melatonin modulates retinal electrophysiology and ERG amplitude in a dose- and time-dependent manner, interacting with PKC, MAPK/ERK, and cAMP/PKA signaling; while protective effects are seen in nocturnal rodent ERGs, a small human study reported reduced b-wave amplitude after a 10 mg oral dose, highlighting the need for careful dosing and chronotherapy alignment (Lundmark et al., 2006; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Collectively, these mechanisms plausibly converge in RPE to reduce mitochondrial ROS, maintain Δψm, prevent cytochrome c release, lower caspase activation, and support autophagy/mitophagy, aligning directly with the pathobiology of dry AMD driven by oxidative/mitochondrial damage and impaired proteostasis (Blasiak et al., 2016; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis—melatonin scavenges ROS and upregulates mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes in RPE, preserving Δψm and preventing apoptosis in dry AMD—is consistent with reported assay-level outcomes in RPE and retina and yields clear, testable predictions.

- In RPE oxidative-stress assays (H₂O₂, cigarette-smoke constituents, Aβ₁₋₄₀), melatonin should reduce intracellular ROS (DCF/CellROX), lipid peroxidation (MDA, C11-BODIPY), and Fe²⁺ accumulation (FerroOrange), while increasing reduced glutathione (GSH), restoring mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1/TMRM), and rescuing viability (MTT/CCK-8/LDH), effects substantiated in ARPE-19 and primary RPE studies (Chang et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2025).

- Mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme readouts are expected to increase: while direct ARPE-19 measures of SOD2/GPx protein can be added to this program, in vivo retinal data show melatonin increases mitochondrial MnSOD (SOD2) activity and total SOD, and multiple reviews report melatonin-induced upregulation of SOD and GPx in ocular tissues via Nrf2 and related signaling, supporting the enzyme-induction arm of the hypothesis (Crooke et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024).

- Intrinsic apoptosis markers should decline: reduced Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, decreased cytochrome c release, and reduced caspase-7/-3 activation, plus fewer TUNEL-positive nuclei, as already demonstrated in ARPE-19 under H₂O₂ and in photoreceptors in vivo (Chang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020).

- Autophagy/mitophagy engagement should be evident: increased LC3-II and Beclin-1 and decreased p62, with flux confirmed by lysosomal inhibitors; mitophagy markers (e.g., PINK1/Parkin) should be assessed given melatonin’s reported influence on mitochondrial quality control (Chang et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022).

- Ferroptosis control should be demonstrable in Aβ₁₋₄₀ and other ferroptotic stressors: upregulation of SLC7A11 and GPX4, normalization of TFR1/ACSL4/FTH1, reduced lipid peroxidation, and dependence on PI3K/AKT→MDM2→p53 signaling tested by pharmacological inhibitors and siRNA, as shown in recent preclinical reports (Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-inflammatory and transcriptional endpoints should shift: decreased NF-κB nuclear translocation and pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β), increased Nrf2 nuclear retention and target gene expression, and potential SIRT1/SIRT3 upregulation in appropriate contexts (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

- Functional in vivo correlates should include preservation of ERG a-/b-wave amplitudes, photoreceptor/RPE morphology on OCT/H&E, and reduced oxidative tissue biomarkers (MDA, 8-OHdG) under retinal oxidative/AMD-like stressors, consistent with prior animal studies (Diéguez et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2025).

Receptor expression to support target engagement is well documented in retina and RPE, and dependence on MT receptors can be tested with antagonists (luzindole) and MT1/MT2 knockdown, as low-dose protective effects in ARPE-19 are reversibly blocked by luzindole and MT1 knockdown abolishes mitochondrial protective actions under oxidative stress (Blasiak et al., 2016; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Lundmark et al., 2007). Given circadian regulation, repeated dosing aligned with the retinal clock may be necessary to realize full mitochondrial DNA protection and durable antioxidant responses, as suggested by diurnal pretreatment requirements in ARPE-19 (Rastmanesh, 2011).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic convergence on AMD biology: Melatonin’s combined direct scavenging of ROS/RNS, induction of endogenous antioxidant defenses (SODs, GPxs), mitochondrial stabilization (Δψm preservation, mtDNA protection), anti-apoptotic signaling (reduced Bax/cytochrome c/caspases), and autophagy/mitophagy support addresses core pathogenic axes in dry AMD—oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and defective proteostasis in post-mitotic RPE and photoreceptors (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022).

- Demonstrated efficacy in relevant preclinical systems: Protection of RPE from peroxide and Aβ₁₋₄₀ ferroptotic stress in vitro, and preservation of retina/RPE structure and function in AMD-like mouse models, including nonexudative AMD and acute degeneration models, with robust biomarker changes (MDA, 8-OHdG, SOD2 activity) and ERG preservation (Chang et al., 2018; Diéguez et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2025).

- Receptor and nonreceptor pharmacology: Dual mode of action enables efficacy at physiologic concentrations via MT1/MT2 and at higher local concentrations via receptor-independent radical scavenging, offering flexibility across dosing ranges and delivery routes; MT1-linked mitochondrial protection in RPE provides a direct mechanistic link between receptor activation and Δψm preservation (Blasiak et al., 2016; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

- Anti-ferroptotic axis in RPE: PI3K/AKT→MDM2→p53→SLC7A11 mechanism positions melatonin within contemporary cell-death biology relevant to AMD (lipid peroxidation, iron handling, GPX4), offering mechanistic biomarkers and combination opportunities with iron chelators or GPX4-preserving agents (Wu et al., 2025).

- Favorable endogenous safety rationale and clinical signal: As an endogenous molecule with extensive human exposure for sleep disorders, melatonin has a comparatively favorable safety backdrop; observational EHR data provides a clinically relevant association signal for AMD incidence and progression reduction that justifies prospective trials (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Translational feasibility with targeted delivery: Topical ocular and nanocarrier formulations can improve posterior-segment delivery, and intravitreal administration achieves retinal protection with measurable biochemical and functional benefits; nanotechnologies address melatonin’s aqueous instability and enhance tissue penetration (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Li et al., 2020).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Evidence base is predominantly preclinical; clinical efficacy in dry AMD is unproven: Apart from exploratory EHR associations and small uncontrolled case-series, there are no randomized controlled trials in dry AMD demonstrating visual function or structural endpoints with melatonin; reliance on animal models and ARPE-19 limits translatability (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Context- and dose-dependent effects: Nrf2 modulation by melatonin can vary by model, and very high exogenous concentrations can worsen photoreceptor light damage; a small human study showed acute ERG b-wave reduction after 10 mg oral melatonin, indicating potential physiological perturbation at certain doses/times and the importance of chronotherapy and dose finding (Blasiak et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2022; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

- Vascular tone considerations: MT1-mediated vasoconstriction in retinal endothelium could theoretically exacerbate early perfusion deficits in AMD; dose, receptor selectivity, and local exposure will be critical to avoid adverse vascular modulation (Ma et al., 2024).

- Delivery and pharmacokinetics: Oral melatonin exhibits highly variable and often low bioavailability due to first-pass metabolism, and aqueous topical formulations face photostability and posterior-segment penetration barriers; while nanocarriers and intravitreal delivery overcome these, each introduces manufacturing and safety considerations (Jeong et al., 2024b; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

- Aged tissue pharmacodynamics: Age-related declines in retinal melatonin and potential receptor desensitization could diminish responsiveness to exogenous melatonin in elderly AMD populations; some aging-associated retinal rhythms were not rescued by exogenous melatonin in prior studies (Blasiak et al., 2016).

- Safety window for intravitreal dosing: Although protective effects are demonstrated, at least one report cites retinal cell degeneration at high intravitreal doses, underscoring the need for careful dose-range finding and chronic safety assessment (Ma et al., 2024).

- Product-specific gaps: There is insufficient formulation- and impurity-specific information for Sigma-Aldrich M5250 in ocular contexts, and no product-specific ocular PK/PD has been reported in AMD; stability, excipient compatibility, and photostability data must be generated for any clinical candidate (Ma et al., 2024; Romeo et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Assessment against the team’s hypothesis  
Supportive evidence is strong that melatonin reduces ROS, preserves mitochondrial function, and prevents apoptosis in RPE/retina. Multiple ARPE-19 studies demonstrate decreased ROS, increased Δψm, and reduced intrinsic apoptosis markers (Bax, cytochrome c, caspases) under oxidative stress with melatonin, consistent with maintained mitochondrial integrity and suppressed apoptotic cascades (Chang et al., 2018). In vivo, raised mitochondrial MnSOD activity and reduced oxidative biomarkers after intravitreal melatonin substantiate mitochondrial antioxidant engagement in retina (Li et al., 2020). Upregulation of antioxidant enzymes (SOD, GPx) by melatonin in ocular tissues via Nrf2, SIRT1/3, and AKT pathways is reported in leading reviews and experimental models, even though direct SOD2/GPX induction has not been quantified in RPE in all cited primary studies; this constitutes a tractable validation gap for our planned assays (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Ferroptosis suppression via PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 further extends the mitochondrial-protective narrative to lipid ROS and iron metabolism, relevant to RPE stress in AMD (Wu et al., 2025).

Programmatic recommendations  
- Formulation and delivery: Given oral PK variability and ocular delivery constraints, prioritize posterior-segment–targeted strategies: (1) intravitreal melatonin for proof-of-mechanism in large animals (define safety window, ocular distribution, and retinal PD biomarkers); (2) develop stabilized topical nanocarriers (e.g., ethylcellulose, PLGA-PEG, nanomicelles) to improve posterior-segment delivery and residence time for chronic use (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Pharmacodynamic biomarkers: In RPE/retina, quantify Δψm, mitochondrial respiration (OCR), ROS (DCF, MitoSOX), lipid peroxidation (C11-BODIPY, MDA), mtDNA integrity (long-amplicon qPCR), SOD2 and GPX4 protein/activity, Bax/Bcl-2, cytochrome c release, caspase-3/-7 activity, LC3-II/Beclin-1/p62 flux, Nrf2 nuclear localization and target genes, and ferroptosis markers (SLC7A11, GPX4, TFR1, ACSL4, FTH1) with pharmacologic/siRNA controls for MT receptors and PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 (Chang et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2025).

- Dosing and chronotherapy: Incorporate diurnal dosing regimens to align with retinal circadian biology; evaluate low-dose receptor-mediated windows versus higher-dose antioxidant windows, avoiding concentrations shown to potentiate phototoxicity (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rastmanesh, 2011; Tong et al., 2022).

- Safety and off-target risks: Monitor ERG under different dosing/time-of-day schedules, retinal/choroidal vascular caliber (given MT1-mediated vasoconstriction), photoreceptor light injury susceptibility under high-dose exposure, and long-term ocular histopathology in repeat-dose studies (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Tong et al., 2022).

- Clinical translation: Design an adaptive, randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 2 in intermediate dry AMD with multimodal endpoints (SD-OCT GA growth, mesopic microperimetry, dark adaptation, low-luminance VA) and fluid biomarkers (plasma/urine aMT6s, systemic oxidative markers), stratified by baseline melatonin levels and sleep parameters; consider an intravitreal proof-of-concept in high-risk early GA to validate local PD and safety prior to chronic topical development (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Conclusion  
Melatonin is a mechanistically well-justified, low-cost, repurposable candidate for dry AMD: it directly and indirectly controls retinal/RPE redox status, stabilizes mitochondrial function (including Δψm), engages endogenous antioxidant enzymes, prevents intrinsic apoptosis, supports autophagy/mitophagy, and suppresses ferroptosis along a defined PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 axis, with concordant protection in RPE and retina across preclinical models (Chang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Epidemiologic data add a clinically relevant signal for reduced AMD risk and progression with melatonin exposure, and ocular delivery is feasible with modern formulations, though oral PK variability and aqueous instability pose development challenges (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024). Key risks—dose-dependent phototoxicity, potential vasoconstrictive effects, variability of Nrf2 responses, and uncertain responsiveness in aged retinas—can be managed through judicious dosing, chronotherapy, receptor-aware design, and robust safety pharmacology (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Net assessment: advance melatonin into a formal translational program for dry AMD centered on posterior-segment–targeted delivery and rigorous mitochondrial/RPE pharmacodynamic validation, while preparing for a randomized clinical evaluation; the mechanistic breadth and preclinical efficacy merit this investment, contingent on resolving dosing, delivery, and safety windows in aged ocular tissue (Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Proposal for GKT137831 (Setanaxib; MedChemExpress HY-108921)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GKT137831, also known as Setanaxib, is a synthetic small‐molecule drug originally discovered and optimized for its ability to inhibit NADPH oxidase activity, with specificity primarily toward the NOX1 and NOX4 isoforms. It belongs to the dihydropyrazolone chemical class, sharing structural similarity with the free radical scavenger edaravone, and has been further refined from earlier analogues such as GKT136901 through structure–activity relationship studies to improve its potency, selectivity, and oral bioavailability (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). The compound was originally developed by Genkyotex as a dual NOX1/NOX4 inhibitor; however, it possesses additional but lower potency activity against NOX2 and even shows some partial inhibition of NOX5 in certain settings (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30). The initial discovery was based on high-throughput screening methods that targeted NADPH oxidase-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—a process that has been linked to multiple pathological conditions including fibrotic, vascular, and inflammatory diseases. As a representative of its class, GKT137831 exemplifies a modern approach to drug design wherein inhibition of the primary enzymatic source of ROS is favored over conventional antioxidant strategies, which often suffer from non-specificity and poor clinical translation (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26).

Therapeutic History:  
GKT137831 has a distinguished preclinical and clinical history rooted in its application to diseases characterized by oxidative stress and inflammation. In preclinical models, it has been shown to significantly reduce the generation of ROS and the downstream activation of pro-inflammatory signaling. In primary cultured human retinal endothelial cells, for instance, treatment with GKT137831 reduced both ROS generation and VEGFA expression, indicating its potential utility in limiting vascular dysfunction in ocular diseases (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). Beyond ocular applications, the compound has been evaluated in several preclinical models of fibrotic and vascular pathologies including diabetic kidney disease, hypertensive cardiac remodeling, and liver fibrosis, wherein its administration lowered the levels of ROS, inflammatory cytokines, and markers of tissue injury (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Cipriano et al., 2023, pp. 22–23). Clinically, GKT137831 has advanced to Phase II trials in diabetic nephropathy and primary biliary cholangitis, demonstrating both safety and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties in human subjects (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26; Buglak et al., 2018, Art. 2468457). Although it has not been tested directly for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) in clinical trials, several preclinical studies using models of ischemic retinopathy and diabetic retinopathy have provided supportive evidence that NOX inhibition may attenuate oxidative stress and inflammation in retinal tissues (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 15–17). The repurposing rationale for dry AMD hinges on the observation that oxidative stress plays a central role in the degeneration of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and the subsequent progression of AMD—pathophysiological processes that have been effectively modulated by GKT137831 in other experimental disease models (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 1–7).

Mechanism of Action:  
From a molecular perspective, GKT137831 has been characterized as a dual inhibitor of NOX1 and NOX4, enzymes that catalyze the transfer of electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen and thereby generate superoxide or hydrogen peroxide, respectively (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 4–6). Unlike classical antioxidants that scavenge ROS after they are generated, GKT137831 aims to prevent ROS formation at its source by directly inhibiting NOX enzyme activity. One study demonstrates that it can bind to the extracellular region of the catalytic subunit of NOX enzymes in an allosteric manner, distinct from the NADPH binding site, which leads to a decrease in NADPH-dependent superoxide generation and hydrogen peroxide production (Gorin et al., 2015, pp. 16–20). In addition to its enzyme inhibitory actions, the dihydropyrazolone scaffold confers an inherent ROS scavenging property, enabling the compound to neutralize peroxynitrite and hydrogen peroxide through redox-mediated chemical mechanisms (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 8–9). This dual property—direct enzyme inhibition coupled with ROS scavenging—is theorized to offer a more comprehensive approach to modulating oxidative stress in target tissues. However, there are conflicting reports in the literature regarding the specificity of its NOX inhibition, with some studies suggesting that measured low Ki values may be artifactual due to interference with assay components such as horseradish peroxidase, raising questions about whether the observed effects are entirely attributable to NOX inhibition or, in part, to non-specific redox modulation (Vincent, 2021, pp. 79–80; Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 12–13). Notwithstanding these concerns, the prevailing hypothesis remains that by dampening NOX activity, GKT137831 reduces both cytosolic and mitochondrial ROS. In the context of RPE cells, which are rich in mitochondria and subject to high oxidative loads due to constant light exposure and high metabolic activity, the inhibition of NOX4 is expected to be particularly beneficial for mitigating oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and preserving the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 24–28).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of GKT137831 for the treatment of dry AMD is that its inhibition of NOX4—and, by extension, NOX1—leads to a substantial reduction in the generation of reactive oxygen species within the retinal pigment epithelium. Oxidative stress in RPE cells is a key driver of mitochondrial dysfunction, particularly impairment of electron transport chain complexes, which in turn leads to decreased cellular energy production and the eventual onset of apoptosis. By pharmacologically reducing the burden of ROS, GKT137831 is expected to prevent the oxidative damage to mitochondrial ETC components, thereby preserving the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and ensuring continued ATP production and cellular viability under conditions of oxidative stress (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 24–28). In vitro assays utilizing RPE cells exposed to high-glucose or other oxidative stress conditions have shown that treatment with GKT137831 can dampen ROS levels, reduce caspase-3 activity (a marker of apoptosis), and decrease the expression of inflammatory molecules (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). Given that the pathogenesis of dry AMD involves chronic, low-grade oxidative damage and inflammation leading to RPE degeneration, the expected therapeutic effect of GKT137831 would be to attenuate these processes at a cellular level, thereby slowing or halting disease progression. Moreover, the expression profile of NOX enzymes—particularly NOX4 in RPE cells—provides a sound molecular basis for this approach, with several studies documenting increased NOX activity under conditions that mimic AMD pathogenesis (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kulbay et al., 2024, pp. 2–5). Furthermore, the oral formulation of GKT137831, validated in other disease contexts, offers a practical advantage because it facilitates long-term administration, which is essential for a chronic condition like dry AMD where sustained drug exposure is necessary to counteract cumulative oxidative damage (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating the potential of GKT137831 as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge. Among its major strengths is the robust preclinical evidence that supports the concept of targeting NOX enzymes to mitigate oxidative stress. The dual mode of action—combining direct enzyme inhibition with ROS scavenging—provides a theoretically advantageous approach to protecting RPE cells from both cytosolic and mitochondrial oxidative insults (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 8–9). This is particularly pertinent in dry AMD, a disease where oxidative stress is a driving force behind RPE dysfunction, drusen formation, and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 1–7). Furthermore, GKT137831’s progression into Phase II clinical trials for other indications such as diabetic nephropathy and primary biliary cholangitis demonstrates that the compound is orally bioavailable and has an acceptable safety profile in human subjects (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26; Buglak et al., 2018, Art. 2468457). This reduces the developmental risk when considering repurposing for dry AMD since chronic administration is feasible and the regulatory pathway may be accelerated based on existing human data.

On the other hand, significant concerns related to the specificity of GKT137831’s mechanism remain. Conflicting evidence suggests that some of the in vitro inhibitory effects attributed to the compound may be partly due to assay artifacts or non-specific redox-modulating activities rather than bona fide NOX inhibition (Vincent, 2021, pp. 79–80; Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 12–13). These findings raise critical questions regarding the extent to which the protective effects observed in retinal and other disease models are directly mediated by diminution of NOX-derived ROS. Additionally, while preclinical studies in diabetic and ischemic retinopathy models have provided promising results, there is a paucity of data directly linking GKT137831 to improved outcomes in dry AMD specifically. The absence of studies evaluating blood–retinal barrier permeability, retinal tissue pharmacokinetics, and direct effects on RPE mitochondrial function in the context of AMD remains a notable gap (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 15–17). Moreover, some reports indicate that the antiproliferative or cytoprotective effects observed with GKT137831 are independent of NOX1/4 expression, suggesting that its mechanism of action in certain cell types may be more complex than initially postulated (Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 2–3, 12–13).

Given these considerations, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. GKT137831, with its favorable oral bioavailability and established safety profile from Phase II clinical trials in non-ocular indications, represents a promising candidate for repurposing given the central role of oxidative stress and NOX-mediated ROS production in dry AMD. Its capacity to reduce ROS levels, modulate inflammatory responses, and potentially preserve mitochondrial function in RPE cells offers a compelling therapeutic rationale (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 1–7; Shi, 2024, pp. 21–24).  

Furthermore, detailed mechanistic studies employing genetic knockdown approaches in RPE cells, coupled with advanced imaging techniques to monitor mitochondrial dynamics, would be critical to discern whether the expected effects are indeed mediated via NOX inhibition or through alternative, non-NOX-related redox pathways (Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 2–3, 12–13). Given that some reports have reported paradoxical increases in ROS in other cell types treated with GKT137831, it is imperative to understand its cell-type-specific and context-dependent effects to mitigate unintended pro-oxidant consequences in the delicate retinal environment (Demircan et al., 2022, p. 13; Vincent, 2021, pp. 13–17).

In summary, the strengths of GKT137831 lie in its dual functional profile as both a NOX inhibitor and an ROS scavenger, its documented efficacy in preclinical models of oxidative stress-induced pathologies, and its demonstrated oral bioavailability with favorable safety outcomes in human trials for other indications (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Buglak et al., 2018, Art. 2468457; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26). These attributes strongly support the rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD, where oxidative stress is a key pathogenic driver. Nonetheless, weaknesses including unresolved mechanistic ambiguities, potential off-target effects, and limited direct evidence in AMD-relevant models call for rigorous additional research before clinical translation can be confidently pursued (Vincent, 2021, pp. 79–80; Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 2–3, 12–13). Overall, while there is considerable promise in targeting NOX-mediated oxidative stress in the RPE with a compound like GKT137831, the current evidence base necessitates further specific validation within the context of dry AMD. Such an approach would ideally involve a series of well-designed in vitro and in vivo experiments to ascertain pharmacodynamics, tissue distribution within ocular compartments, and ultimately, the functional outcome measures relevant to RPE health and retinal integrity under conditions that closely mimic the human disease state (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 15–17; Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11).  

The next steps for our research team should include initiating experiments using cultured RPE cell lines exposed to oxidative stress paradigms (e.g., high-glucose, light-induced stress) to determine whether GKT137831 effectively preserves mitochondrial function and decreases apoptotic markers. Parallel studies in animal models of dry AMD, particularly those that recapitulate key features such as drusen formation, RPE degeneration, and subsequent photoreceptor loss, will be essential to elucidate the in vivo efficacy of the compound (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 24–28). Ultimately, while the translational potential is high given its clinical safety record and oral formulation, the mechanistic uncertainties must be thoroughly addressed to confidently advocate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. In conclusion, GKT137831 remains an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, provided that further targeted research can unequivocally demonstrate its beneficial effects on RPE mitochondrial health and overall retinal preservation (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26; Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11).

Proposal for AICAR (5-Aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide; Sigma-Aldrich A9978)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐Aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide) is a synthetic nucleoside analog originally developed as an AMP mimetic agent that is capable of activating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) across a range of cell types. It is produced by chemical synthesis and is available commercially (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich A9978), having been studied for several decades in the context of cellular energy metabolism and stress signaling. As a member of a class of compounds that mimic the natural intracellular messenger AMP, AICAR is taken up into cells via adenosine transporters and is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its active metabolite, ZMP (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate), which then mimics AMP in its interactions with AMPK (Efstathiou et al., 2020). This compound belongs to a well‐established class of metabolic modulators, and similar agents have been used in experimental settings to modulate glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, and overall energy homeostasis in both basic science and translational research contexts (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). In addition, several preclinical studies have evaluated AICAR’s potential as an “exercise mimetic” due to its ability to enhance energy metabolism in muscle and other tissues, and its synthetic nature allows for reproducible and scalable dosing in research models (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR was developed primarily as an agent to activate AMPK in metabolic studies and has been investigated in a variety of preclinical models ranging from cancer to cardiovascular disease. In the oncology field, for example, AICAR has been shown to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce cell cycle arrest, and promote programmed cell death in several cancer types via AMPK-dependent modulation of pathways such as PI3K-Akt and mTOR (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rattan et al., 2005). Clinical studies, particularly those in the cardiovascular arena, have also evaluated AICAR’s safety profile in the context of ischemia-reperfusion injury, including human trials during cardiac surgery, demonstrating that it can be administered safely in humans (Rattan et al., 2005). In the context of ocular research, AICAR has been studied for its effects on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular cell types; several studies have demonstrated that AICAR suppresses the production of pro-inflammatory complement components such as complement factor 3 (C3) and complement factor B (CFB) in RPE cells under inflammatory conditions (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017). Although there is no established clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) to date, these preclinical observations, combined with its well-known pharmacological profile, have spurred interest in repurposing AICAR for treating retinal diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Furthermore, studies examining AMPK activators in the eye – including those using AICAR in animal models of uveitis or oxidative stress-induced RPE damage – support the notion that activating this metabolic pathway can protect against retinal degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Mechanism of Action:  
AICAR exerts its biological activity primarily through the activation of AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy balance that responds to alterations in the AMP/ATP ratio. Once AICAR is imported into cells through adenosine transporters, it is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to form ZMP, an analog of AMP. ZMP binds to the regulatory γ subunit of AMPK, causing a conformational change that facilitates AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172 by upstream kinases such as LKB1, thereby fully activating the kinase (Efstathiou et al., 2020). Activated AMPK then phosphorylates a series of downstream targets involved in energy metabolism, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and elements of the mTOR signaling pathway. In RPE cells, this activation is particularly important because AMPK phosphorylates and activates ULK1, a kinase critical for initiating autophagy and mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2017).  

A central component of the rationale for using AICAR in dry AMD is its ability to stimulate the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α. AMPK-mediated phosphorylation of PGC-1α enhances its activity and nuclear translocation, which in turn drives the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and metabolic adaptation (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This mechanism is particularly attractive in dry AMD because mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells is thought to contribute significantly to disease pathogenesis by impairing oxidative phosphorylation, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and triggering cell senescence or death (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). In addition to these AMPK-dependent effects, some studies have reported that AICAR exerts certain effects independent of AMPK activation. For instance, AICAR has been shown to suppress TNF-α-induced complement factor expression by mechanisms that do not involve AMPK, suggesting that alternative signaling pathways or direct modulation of transcription factor activity might also contribute to its overall activity profile (Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These AMPK-independent actions could either broaden the therapeutic potential of AICAR in modulating inflammatory responses or introduce complexity into its activity profile that will need to be carefully isolated and understood (Kirchner et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2024).  

Furthermore, AICAR has been observed to affect mitochondrial dynamics not only by stimulating biogenesis through PGC-1α activation but also by modifying autophagic flux through mTOR inhibition. In models of RPE oxidative stress, where excessive ROS levels lead to mitochondrial fragmentation and accumulation of dysfunctional organelles, AICAR-induced AMPK activation facilitates the clearance of damaged mitochondria via mitophagy, thus restoring mitochondrial quality and energy production (Fisher et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2024). Moreover, experimental evidence suggests that AICAR can modulate the balance between cellular glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation by shifting metabolism toward a more energy-efficient, oxidative phenotype, thereby increasing the overall oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and potentially improving cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Chan et al., 2020; Fisher, 2022).  

Expected Effect:  
Given its mechanisms of action, the expected effect of AICAR in an assay aimed at treating dry AMD would be multifaceted. In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD—AICAR treatment is expected to lead to robust activation of AMPK, as measured by increased phosphorylation of both AMPK and its downstream substrates such as ACC and ULK1 (Guo et al., 2018; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This activation should in turn upregulate PGC-1α, resulting in enhanced transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, improved mitochondrial DNA replication, and an increased capacity for ATP production (Hu et al., 2024). As damaged mitochondria are a major source of ROS in stressed RPE cells, the stimulation of autophagy and mitophagy is anticipated to selectively clear these dysfunctional organelles, reducing cellular oxidative stress and preventing the secondary damage that contributes to RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

In addition to these metabolic effects, AICAR is also expected to attenuate inflammatory responses within the RPE and adjacent retinal tissues. For instance, by modulating the activity of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and reducing the expression of inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and complement components (e.g., C3 and CFB), AICAR would help to create a less pro-inflammatory microenvironment that could further protect RPE cells from damage (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These effects are particularly pertinent given that chronic, low-grade inflammation coupled with complement dysregulation is a recognized component of dry AMD pathogenesis.  

At the cellular level, the outcome of AICAR-induced AMPK activation is expected to manifest as enhanced mitochondrial function, improved energy charge (ATP/AMP ratio), reduced ROS accumulation, and, ultimately, a restoration of normal metabolic and autophagic flux in RPE cells (Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). This improved bioenergetic profile should translate into protection against RPE cell death, potentially slowing or halting the progression of geographic atrophy associated with dry AMD (Yu et al., 2024; Si et al., 2023). Moreover, since RPE dysfunction in AMD also involves a reduction in the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, AICAR’s modulatory effects on autophagy may indirectly help to restore the homeostatic functions of RPE cells, reducing the accumulation of damaging lipofuscin and drusen material (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Sung et al., 2015). In summary, the expected effect is a dual-action benefit—mitigation of oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stresses via improved mitochondrial dynamics and an anti-inflammatory effect stemming from a reduction in complement activation and NF-κB-driven cytokine production (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
AICAR represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its robust and well-characterized mechanism of action via AMPK activation. The strengths of this candidate lie in its dual capacity to modulate critical pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis: on one hand, AICAR enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and promotes the removal of damaged mitochondria through autophagy/mitophagy, and on the other, it attenuates inflammatory cascades that exacerbate RPE cell damage (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hu et al., 2024). The ability of AICAR to upregulate PGC-1α is particularly compelling because mitochondrial dysfunction is now widely recognized as a central element in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have illustrated that dysregulation of mitochondrial function in RPE cells—a decrease in oxidative phosphorylation capacity, increased ROS production, and impaired clearance of damaged organelles—is pivotal in the initiation and progression of AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). Thus, a compound like AICAR that can simultaneously restore mitochondrial health and mitigate inflammatory responses offers a multifaceted approach to disease modification.  

From the therapeutic history perspective, AICAR has been extensively studied in various preclinical models, including those of ocular inflammation and oxidative stress in RPE cells. Its ability to safely activate AMPK in vivo has been demonstrated across multiple species and contexts, including settings that mimic some aspects of AMD-related stress, such as endotoxin-induced uveitis and sodium iodate-induced RPE damage (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chan et al., 2020). Additionally, the compound’s known clinical safety profile in human studies—albeit in contexts outside ophthalmology—provides an encouraging starting point for repurposing it for dry AMD, where no approved therapeutics currently exist (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017).  

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, while AMPK activation is generally beneficial for energy homeostasis and autophagy, certain studies have indicated that AICAR’s effects on RPE cell biology might be context-dependent. For instance, some experimental reports have shown that AICAR can reduce the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments by RPE cells—a process that is essential for retinal health—which may represent a double-edged sword if not carefully titrated (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Yu et al., 2024). In addition, the existence of AMPK-independent effects—such as the direct inhibition of complement factor expression—introduces complexity into the overall mechanism of action and makes it challenging to predict all downstream outcomes. Differential responses have also been observed between healthy and diseased donor RPE cells, implying that “metabolic memory” or cellular adaptation may influence drug responsiveness (Fisher et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2017). These considerations suggest that while the theoretical underpinnings for using AICAR in dry AMD are solid, the translation of these effects into clinical efficacy may require careful optimization of dosing, delivery, and patient selection.  

Another potential limitation is related to its broad mechanism of action. AICAR activates several metabolic pathways that are intertwined with many aspects of cellular physiology. While this pleiotropy provides the therapeutic benefit of addressing multiple dysregulated pathways in AMD simultaneously, it may also increase the risk of off-target effects or metabolic disturbances in tissues outside the retina (Rattan et al., 2005; Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). For instance, systemic administration of AICAR has been associated with shifts in glycolytic flux and modifications of lipid metabolism, and it is therefore imperative that strategies for ocular delivery (such as intravitreal injections or topical formulations) be developed to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic exposure (Chan et al., 2020; Kamoshita et al., 2014).  

Moreover, despite the substantial body of preclinical data supporting the role of AICAR in activating AMPK and restoring mitochondrial function, clinical data specific to dry AMD are lacking. Although related studies have shown benefits in models of retinal inflammation and degeneration, the exact therapeutic window, long-term safety, and efficacy in humans with AMD must be thoroughly evaluated in well-designed clinical trials. It is also worth mentioning that other AMPK activators, such as metformin, have independently demonstrated protective effects in AMD models, thereby lending credence to the approach but also raising questions about whether AICAR offers a distinct advantage over these agents (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

In summary, the overall evaluation of AICAR as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Its well-documented ability to activate AMPK, stimulate PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis, and induce autophagy presents a strong mechanistic rationale for protecting RPE cells from the mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress that drive dry AMD pathogenesis (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2011). The preclinical evidence, gathered from studies in ocular models and other systems, provides encouraging proof-of-concept data that support further investigation (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Hyttinen et al., 2011). Nonetheless, complexities related to AMPK-independent effects, differential responses in healthy versus diseased cells, and potential off-target metabolic changes underscore the need for rigorous preclinical optimization and carefully designed clinical trials before this candidate can be definitively validated for dry AMD treatment (Chung et al., 2017; Fisher et al., 2022; Kirchner et al., 2018).  

Considering all the available literature, the repurposing of AICAR for dry AMD appears to be a promising strategy that merits further investigation. The compound’s ability to simultaneously address mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation positions it as a multifaceted agent with the potential to modify disease progression in a condition that currently lacks effective therapeutic options (Chung et al., 2017; Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Moving forward, it will be critical to further elucidate the detailed cellular and molecular responses to AICAR in human RPE cells, determine the optimal dosing and delivery parameters specific to the ocular environment, and perform in vivo studies that mimic the complex pathobiology of dry AMD. With these additional efforts, AICAR could eventually emerge as a valuable addition to the limited therapeutic arsenal available for managing this debilitating condition.  

In conclusion, AICAR’s robust preclinical profile as an AMPK activator, its well-understood mechanisms of promoting mitochondrial biogenesis and autophagy, and its capacity to mitigate inflammatory responses provide a solid scientific basis for its potential repurposing in dry AMD (Hu et al., 2024; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). However, several challenges remain: the dual nature of its effects (both AMPK-dependent and independent), the possibility of adverse effects on key RPE functions such as phagocytosis, and the need for precise ocular drug delivery methods. Therefore, while AICAR is an exciting candidate with considerable mechanistic appeal, its translation from bench to bedside in the treatment of dry AMD will require further detailed studies to fully map its therapeutic window, safety profile, and efficacy in human subjects (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rego, 2023; Kamoshita et al., 2014). Continued rigorous research and methodical clinical evaluation will determine whether AICAR can be developed into an effective treatment modality for this currently intractable form of macular degeneration.

Proposal for Rapamycin (Abcam #ab120224)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (also known as sirolimus and available as Abcam #ab120224) is a naturally occurring macrolide compound originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus. It belongs to the class of macrocyclic lactones and is known for its potent inhibitory effects on the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). This compound has been extensively used in various contexts such as immunosuppression, cancer therapy, and more recently, as a tool to modulate autophagy in age-related degenerative diseases. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), rapamycin is being explored as a repurposed therapeutic candidate with the hypothesis that mTORC1 inhibition will enhance both general autophagy and selective mitophagy. This clearance of reactive oxygen species (ROS)–generating, damaged mitochondria may alleviate oxidative stress, reduce the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin compounds (including A2E), and ultimately slow the progression of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin was first discovered for its potent immunosuppressive properties and later developed for use in preventing transplant rejection and certain cancers. Its ability to inhibit mTORC1 has made it a valuable tool in research related to aging and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in modulating autophagy and protecting cellular integrity under stress conditions, particularly in the retinal environment. In animal models of retinal degeneration and even some early clinical trials, rapamycin was shown to reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent granules and inflammatory cytokines in the RPE, which are both hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Notably, rapamycin has been administered via diverse routes, including intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, in attempts to treat geographic atrophy or other dry AMD phenotypes, although the clinical outcomes have been mixed. For example, clinical trials such as those referenced in studies with identifiers NCT00766649 and NCT01445548 demonstrated that while rapamycin was generally safe and well-tolerated in ocular applications, its efficacy in slowing down the progression of geographic atrophy and improving visual acuity remained limited (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These historical findings highlight both the promise and the challenges associated with translating rapamycin’s mechanistic benefits into robust clinical outcomes for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of rapamycin involves the formation of a complex with the immunophilin FKBP12. This complex binds to mTORC1 and inhibits its kinase activity, leading to a decrease in the phosphorylation of downstream targets such as ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4EBP1). Under normal circumstances, active mTORC1 suppresses autophagy by phosphorylating these targets, which in turn prevents the formation of autophagosomes. By inhibiting mTORC1, rapamycin effectively removes this blockade, thereby promoting the induction of autophagy as evidenced by increased conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and clearance of the autophagic substrate p62 (Zhang et al., 2015).

Within retinal pigment epithelial cells, this induction of autophagy is particularly important. RPE cells are responsible for the phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments; a process that generates large amounts of cellular debris and metabolic byproducts such as lipofuscin. In dry AMD, impaired autophagic flux leads to the accumulation of these compounds, which, in turn, contributes to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Rapamycin’s inhibition of mTORC1 not only enhances general autophagy but also promotes selective mitochondrial clearance (mitophagy). Key players in the mitophagy pathway include the serine/threonine kinase PINK1 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin, both of which accumulate on depolarized mitochondria and signal their removal via autophagic mechanisms. By stimulating this PINK1/Parkin pathway, rapamycin enhances the clearance of damaged, ROS-generating mitochondria, thus preserving overall mitochondrial health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Additionally, rapamycin’s downstream effects include activation of transcription factors such as TFEB, which regulates lysosomal biogenesis and further enhances the autophagic process. This dual action—promoting both autophagy and lysosomal function—helps to mitigate the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as lipofuscin and A2E in RPE, therefore reducing oxidative stress and inflammation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). Through these biochemical interactions, rapamycin establishes a cellular environment that is more capable of dealing with metabolic challenges and oxidative damage, both of which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed hypothesis, the administration of rapamycin in RPE cells is expected to result in a cascade of beneficial cellular events. In our proposed assay, rapamycin is anticipated to inhibit mTORC1 activity, leading to a measurable increase in autophagic flux. This will be evident from the enhanced lipidation of LC3-II, the clearance of p62 (an autophagy adaptor protein that accumulates when autophagy is impaired), and the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway in response to oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2015).

The specific clearance of damaged mitochondria is particularly critical in the RPE, where mitochondrial dysfunction is a significant contributor to the generation of reactive oxygen species and subsequent cellular damage. By removing these dysfunctional mitochondria, rapamycin is expected to reduce intracellular ROS levels and thereby lower oxidative stress, a driving force in AMD pathology. In parallel, the enhanced autophagic degradation of accumulated lipofuscin and the toxic fluorophore A2E is predicted to further limit the inflammatory and apoptotic cascades triggered by these compounds, thus preserving RPE cell viability and function (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Moreover, the expression of PINK1 and Parkin in RPE cells has been well documented, and their activation is indicative of mitophagic turnover. Their proper functioning is a key determinant in mitochondrial quality control, and rapamycin is expected to potentiate this process, ensuring that mitochondria remain healthy and capable of maintaining cellular energy production and reducing the risk of cell death (Pinelli et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Given that impaired mitochondrial function and the resulting energy production deficits are central to the progression of dry AMD, the expected outcomes from rapamycin treatment would include not only a reduction in oxidative stress markers but also improvements in mitochondrial dynamics and overall cellular homeostasis. Such effects would ideally be reflected in functional assays measuring cell viability, mitochondrial respiration, and reductions in inflammatory cytokine production (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In our comprehensive evaluation of rapamycin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and potential weaknesses emerge that warrant careful consideration. One of the key strengths of rapamycin lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action and its ability to broadly modulate autophagy through mTORC1 inhibition. Preclinical studies have repeatedly demonstrated that rapamycin can induce autophagic flux, leading to the clearance of cellular debris and damaged mitochondria in RPE cells. This is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired autophagy in the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, which are major pathological features of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). The dual-action mechanism—enhancing both autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis via TFEB activation—further supports its potential in addressing multiple aspects of the disease pathology, from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction to inflammation and cellular senescence (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Another strength is the substantial body of preclinical evidence showing that rapamycin not only stimulates autophagy but also improves mitochondrial function. The activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway is particularly relevant since these proteins are indispensable for mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control. By facilitating the removal of ROS-generating, damaged mitochondria, rapamycin could directly impact the cellular energy balance and reduce damaging oxidative insults in the RPE, which is pivotal for maintaining retinal health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Despite its promising mechanistic profile, several significant challenges remain. Clinical studies investigating the use of rapamycin for AMD have yielded mixed results. While the drug has been shown to be safe and tolerable in ocular applications, several clinical trials, such as those involving subconjunctival or intravitreal administration, did not demonstrate significant efficacy in halting the progression of geographic atrophy or improving visual acuity. In some instances, adverse effects such as decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning have been observed, raising concerns about the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential retinal toxicity (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These mixed clinical findings underscore the complexity of modulating mTORC1 in a disease with multifactorial etiology and suggest that the optimal dosage, treatment duration, and patient selection criteria still require refinement.

Furthermore, the variability in response among different donor-derived RPE cells—where only about 50% of AMD donor samples responded positively to rapamycin in certain studies—points to potential issues regarding patient heterogeneity and the need for personalized therapeutic regimens (Ebeling et al., 2020). This heterogeneity may be due to differences in the intrinsic capacity for autophagy, genetic variations affecting mitochondrial quality control, or the extent of existing cellular damage. Such variability complicates the development of standardized treatment protocols and could limit the broad applicability of rapamycin unless predictive biomarkers of response are identified (Zhang et al., 2015).

Another important consideration is the dual nature of autophagy in the context of RPE health. While enhancing autophagy can provide protective benefits by clearing damaged organelles and reducing oxidative stress, excessive autophagic flux under certain stress conditions might paradoxically contribute to cell death. This is especially relevant in advanced stages of dry AMD, where cellular stress is severe and prolonged autophagy induction might tip the balance toward detrimental outcomes rather than recovery (Chang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019). In addition, the potential for rapamycin to interfere with beneficial mTOR signaling under specific conditions (for example, when mTOR activity supports survival pathways via growth factors such as nerve growth factor) further complicates its use, as evidenced by reports that observed mixed effects on retinal ganglion cell survival in different pathological contexts (Wang et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2021).

The delivery method and pharmacokinetics of rapamycin also represent important variables. While nanotechnology-based delivery systems—such as synthetic high-density lipoprotein nanoparticles—have shown promise in achieving more targeted and sustained delivery of rapamycin to the RPE (Mei et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2021), these strategies require further translational studies to assess their safety, efficacy, and scalability in clinical settings. Moreover, the risk of systemic side effects, including metabolic toxicities and immunosuppression, despite the generally favorable ocular safety profile observed in trials, necessitates caution in developing rapamycin-based therapies for chronic conditions like AMD (Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, rapamycin presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its robust mechanism of action—specifically, its capacity to inhibit mTORC1, thereby stimulating both general autophagy and the selective removal of damaged mitochondria via the PINK1/Parkin pathway. Preclinical evidence strongly supports the idea that such modulation can reduce oxidative stress, clear toxic accumulations like lipofuscin/A2E, and ultimately preserve mitochondrial and RPE cellular function (Zhang et al., 2015; Hyttinen et al., 2018). However, the translation of these benefits into clinical improvements remains uncertain, with several trials indicating that while rapamycin is safe and modulates cellular pathways implicated in AMD, its clinical efficacy in terms of preserving visual function has not been conclusively demonstrated. The heterogeneity in patient responses, the potential for adverse outcomes related to excessive autophagy, and the challenges in optimizing dosing and delivery all represent significant hurdles. These considerations suggest that while rapamycin is a promising candidate worthy of further investigation, its ultimate role in the treatment paradigm for dry AMD will depend on our ability to refine treatment regimens, develop predictive biomarkers for patient selection, and perhaps combine mTOR modulation with complementary therapeutic strategies that reinforce its protective effects while mitigating its risks (Wang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2019).

Given the cumulative evidence, our overall recommendation is to continue exploring rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but with a strategic focus on further preclinical investigations that address the dose–response relationships in donor-derived RPE models and the development of advanced drug delivery systems. It will also be important to design future clinical trials with stratified patient populations and integrated biomarkers that can help identify responders. This iterative approach could eventually lead to a carefully balanced regimen where rapamycin’s autophagy-enhancing properties are harnessed to maintain retinal integrity while avoiding the pitfalls of over-inhibition or systemic toxicity. In essence, the promise of rapamycin in modulating autophagy to improve mitochondrial health and reduce oxidative stress in RPE cells is clear at the molecular and cellular levels, but translating these benefits into a safe and effective therapy for dry AMD will require overcoming substantial clinical challenges (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Strengths of rapamycin include its well-established mechanism of action, the significant supportive preclinical data demonstrating improvements in autophagic flux and mitochondrial clearance in RPE models, and its potential to address several key pathological features of dry AMD simultaneously. Weaknesses include the mixed clinical trial outcomes to date, the potential for adverse effects in certain contexts (including decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning), and the observed heterogeneity in therapeutic response among different patient samples. These factors highlight the importance of further mechanistic studies and carefully controlled clinical trials. Overall, rapamycin remains one of the more mechanistically promising candidates for repurposing in dry AMD, yet its future success will depend on how effectively we can tailor its delivery and dosing to maximize protective effects while minimizing risks in the vulnerable RPE of AMD patients (Niu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin’s role as an mTORC1 inhibitor with the capacity to induce autophagy and mitophagy presents an exciting therapeutic avenue for addressing the complex pathology of dry AMD. By alleviating the buildup of toxic metabolites and preserving mitochondrial health in RPE cells, rapamycin could potentially slow disease progression and preserve vision. Nonetheless, the balance between benefit and adverse effects remains delicate, and further research is essential to elucidate how best to leverage rapamycin’s molecular actions in a clinically meaningful way. This comprehensive review supports the continued investigation of rapamycin as a candidate for dry AMD therapy, provided that subsequent studies can address the highlighted challenges and refine the therapeutic strategy to achieve consistent, positive clinical outcomes (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).
