Proposal for Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB; Sigma-Aldrich 389410)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is an endogenous ketone body produced by mitochondrial ketogenesis from fatty-acid–derived acetyl-CoA, classically in hepatocytes but also in extrahepatic cell types including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and several neuronal lineages (enzymatic pathway: ACAT, HMGCS2, HMGCL, and BDH1) (Wang et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). In physiological and nutritional ketosis, circulating BHB rises from baseline (~0.05–0.1 mM) to levels >0.5 mM and up to 5–7 mM with prolonged fasting, providing an alternative oxidative substrate for extrahepatic mitochondria when carbohydrate availability is limited (Wang et al., 2021; Cooper et al., 2023). BHB and acetoacetate are transported into and out of cells via proton-linked monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) such as MCT1 and MCT2 that are expressed at the blood–retinal barrier and in retinal cells, enabling substrate entry into the retina (Yang, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). RPEs robustly express mitochondrial HMGCS2 and can ketogenize palmitate to BHB, secreting BHB via MCT1; retinal cells can take up and metabolize BHB into Krebs-cycle intermediates and amino acids, indicating functional capacity to use BHB as mitochondrial fuel in the outer retina (Yang, 2021). More recent mass spectrometry–based reassessment shows that RPE secretion of BHB is substantially lower than previously estimated by enzymatic kits, that RPE exports BHB to both apical and basal compartments, and that RPE both produces and consumes BHB depending on nutrient state—important considerations for experimental design and therapeutic targeting (Gulette et al., 2024).  

BHB belongs to the class of endogenous metabolic intermediates that function dually as oxidative fuels (via oxidation to acetyl-CoA and entry into TCA cycle) and signaling molecules with paracrine/autocrine receptor and epigenetic actions (e.g., agonism at HCAR2/GPR109A and inhibition of class I/IIa histone deacetylases) (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021). As a therapeutic modality, BHB has been delivered exogenously as salts/esters or induced endogenously through ketogenic diets, fasting, or exercise to support mitochondrial ATP production and alter cellular stress responses in the CNS, heart, and skeletal muscle (Cooper et al., 2023; Kovács et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022). In retinal disease models, ketogenic interventions or exogenous BHB have reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury and improved functional measures, though direct application to dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not yet been clinically tested (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021).  

Therapeutic History  
Ketone biology has a long history in neurology and cardiometabolic research, where BHB has been shown to preserve mitochondrial function, increase ATP production, and blunt oxidative injury in ischemia, neurodegeneration models, and skeletal muscle stress paradigms (Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018). In neural tissues, ketogenic interventions and exogenous ketones prevent synaptic dysfunction induced by respiratory complex inhibitors and increase the brain NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with decreased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Morris et al., 2020). In rat skeletal muscle cells, 5 mM BHB for 24–48 h increased respiratory control, ATP-linked respiration, P:O efficiency, lowered H₂O₂ production, and shifted mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion via DRP1 suppression—consistent with enhanced bioenergetics and decreased oxidative stress (Parker et al., 2018). In primary neurons, BHB maintained oxidative phosphorylation under glutamate workload even when cytosolic NADH transfer via the malate–aspartate shuttle was inhibited, demonstrating that BHB can sustain respiration under conditions that impair glycolytic NADH coupling to mitochondria (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

In the retina and optic nerve, multiple preclinical models show that ketogenic exposures or direct ketone administration reduce oxidative stress and inflammation, preserve function, and limit neuronal death. Intraperitoneal BHB and acetoacetate reduced NMDA-induced retinal ganglion cell (RGC) death in rats, and ketogenic diet attenuated NMDA-induced RGC injury in juvenile rats (Gough, 2021). In ocular blast or optic neuropathy paradigms, ketogenic diet prevented increases in superoxide and IL-1α, preserved visual evoked potentials, and reduced astrocytic hypertrophy and optic nerve death (Gough, 2021). In glaucoma models, ketogenic diet improved RGC soma/axon survival, axonal transport, and reduced gliosis, with increases in NAD and NAD:NADH ratio and upregulation of MCT1/MCT2 in optic nerve (Tribble et al., 2021). AAV-mediated MCT2 overexpression (increasing uptake of lactate/pyruvate/ketones) preserved RGCs and optic nerve axons in ocular hypertension and glaucoma models and elevated markers of mitochondrial biogenesis and function (PGC1α, COX, SDH) and antioxidant defense (SOD2) (Gough, 2021). However, in at least one RGC injury model, daily intraperitoneal BHB or acetoacetate did not replicate ketogenic diet neuroprotection, underscoring differences between exogenous ketone dosing and the systemic/multifactorial effects of ketogenic diets (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Within the RPE compartment specifically, two lines of evidence are relevant: (1) BHB protects ARPE-19 cells from high-glucose–induced injury, improving viability, alleviating cell cycle arrest, and modulating inflammatory mediators (IL-8, IL-17α, MCP-1) at millimolar concentrations achievable with nutritional ketosis or exogenous supplementation (Argentino et al., 2025). (2) HCAR2/GPR109A, a BHB receptor, is robustly expressed by the RPE; BHB agonism reduced retinal leukocyte infiltration in LPS-challenged mice in an HCAR2-dependent manner, and loss of HCAR2 in RPE led to barrier dysfunction (ZO-1 defects) and increased immune cell infiltrates, indicating that BHB–HCAR2 signaling can preserve an immunoinhibitory retinal environment (Powell et al., 2021). In diabetic retinopathy models, systemic BHB activation of HCA2 reduced ER stress and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and ameliorated retinal pathology, establishing anti-inflammatory and ER stress–limiting actions in retina (Trotta et al., 2019).  

In inherited retinal degeneration models, ketogenic interventions delayed photoreceptor degeneration and improved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes and outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in rd10 and Pde6a mice, and a soluble ketogenic formulation partially restored vision and survival in PDH-deficient noir zebrafish—consistent with bypassing PDH to supply acetyl-CoA and support neurotransmitter synthesis (Gough, 2021). Notwithstanding these encouraging signals, the literature consistently notes the absence of clinical trials evaluating ketogenic interventions or BHB in retinitis pigmentosa or AMD patients, and reports potentially adverse effects of ketogenic diets in wild-type mice (decreased ERG amplitudes, altered albumin/weight), highlighting translational uncertainties and the need to distinguish effects of BHB from the broader systemic consequences of diet (Gough, 2021).  

Mechanism of Action  
BHB acts through convergent metabolic, redox, mitochondrial, inflammatory, and epigenetic mechanisms that are mechanistically aligned with the pathophysiology of RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress in dry AMD.  

- Alternative mitochondrial fuel and bioenergetics support. In extrahepatic tissues (including retina), BHB oxidation proceeds via mitochondrial BDH1 (βHB→acetoacetate) followed by SCOT/OXCT1 (AcAc→AcAc-CoA using succinyl-CoA) and acetyl-CoA production for TCA entry and ATP generation, enabling substrate-level maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and oxidative phosphorylation under glucose restriction or impaired glycolytic NADH transfer (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). The retina expresses monocarboxylate transport routes (e.g., MCT1 at the inner blood–retinal barrier; MCT2 in neurons), and RPE expresses MCT1 and can both produce and consume BHB, providing a plausible uptake pathway for exogenous BHB into RPE and neighboring retinal cells (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). In neurons, BHB-supported respiration remains robust when the malate–aspartate shuttle is blocked with AOAA—conditions that decrease glucose-fueled ATP synthesis—indicating that BHB can preserve mitochondrial ATP synthesis and respiratory control when cytosolic NADH transfer is compromised, a scenario relevant to glycolysis-impaired RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

- Redox coupling and ROS control. The interconversion of acetoacetate and BHB by βHB dehydrogenase is linked to NADH/NAD⁺ redox; acetoacetate→BHB requires oxidation of NADH to NAD⁺, and nutritional ketosis in human brain increases NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with reductions in mitochondrial ROS generation (Gough, 2021; Morris et al., 2020). Ketones can inhibit mitochondrial ROS production by increasing NADH oxidation, and ketogenic interventions increase NAD⁺/NADH in vivo, though tissue- and context-dependent effects exist (Morris et al., 2020). Complementary cardiac literature reports that β-OHB can reduce the mitochondrial NAD couple while oxidizing coenzyme Q, emphasizing that BHB modulates both NADH/NAD⁺ and Q/QH₂ redox pairs in mitochondria—with directionality that may depend on prevailing substrate status and respiratory state (Chu et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion models and muscle cells, BHB lowers mitochondrial ROS, decreases mitochondrial swelling, maintains Δψm, and increases ATP production, consistent with direct mitochondrial protection (Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018).  

- Antioxidant transcription (Nrf2) and hormesis. Ketogenic exposures can induce a hormetic redox signal that activates Keap1–Nrf2, increasing transcription of detoxification and antioxidant genes; in retina, ketone body exposure mimicked calorie restriction via fumarate–Nrf2 activation (Gough, 2021; Fu et al., 2020). Preclinical optic/retinal models link these antioxidant transcriptional effects to preserved function and reduced oxidative markers (NOS, MDA, superoxide) (Gough, 2021).  

- Anti-inflammatory signaling via HCAR2/ARRB2 and NLRP3/NF-κB suppression. BHB is a ligand for HCAR1/HCAR2 receptors; HCAR2 is robustly expressed in human RPE and retina, and receptor activation by BHB reduces leukocyte infiltration and preserves RPE barrier integrity in inflammation models (Powell et al., 2021). Downstream, BHB–HCAR signaling recruits β-arrestin-2 (ARRB2) that binds NLRP3 to block inflammasome assembly, decreasing ASC and preventing K⁺ efflux to suppress IL-1β maturation; BHB also activates a COX1/PGD2 cascade that inhibits IKK and NF-κB nuclear translocation, reducing TNF-α and microglial/macrophage activation (Gough, 2021). In diabetic retina, systemic BHB–HCA2 activation suppressed ER stress and NLRP3 inflammasome activity, demonstrating the retinal anti-inflammatory efficacy of this axis (Trotta et al., 2019).  

- Mitochondrial calcium homeostasis and mPTP stabilization. In human iPSC-derived microglia, amyloid-β oligomers increased MCU expression, raised mitochondrial Ca²⁺ ~40%, elevated mtROS, and triggered mPTP opening; BHB normalized MCU, decreased mtCa²⁺/mtROS, and completely reversed mPTP activation, restoring phagocytic function (Jin et al., 2023). Although not conducted in RPE, these mitochondrial-stabilizing effects are mechanistically relevant to post-mitotic cells with high oxidative load.  

- Epigenetic modulation and mitochondrial biogenesis. BHB is an endogenous inhibitor of class I/IIa HDACs at physiological millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and upregulation of FOXO3a and metallothionein genes that encode antioxidant defenses; BHB also increases intracellular acetyl-CoA and supports protein acetylation, and can β-hydroxybutyrylate histones, adding layers of gene regulatory control tied to mitochondrial status (Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021). Through HDAC inhibition and receptor-mediated signaling, BHB increases BDNF via cAMP/PKA/CREB, activates SIRT1/SIRT3 via AMPK/HCA2/NAD⁺ pathways, and promotes PGC1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis and UCP2 expression that collectively improve mitochondrial function and antioxidant capacity (Kovács et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022). In retinal/optic nerve models, ketogenic diet or enhanced monocarboxylate uptake upregulated PGC1α, COX, SDH, and SOD2 while lowering pAMPK/AMPK, linking substrate availability to mitochondrial biogenesis and anti-inflammatory signaling (Gough, 2021).  

- Immunometabolic reprogramming in retina/CNS. Ketogenic interventions increased anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-4, Arginase-1) and M2-like microglia while decreasing IBA-1⁺ macrophage/microglia, consistent with dampened neuroinflammation secondary to improved bioenergetics (reduced AMPK activation) and prevention of NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation (Gough, 2021). BHB also inhibits FFAR3/GPR41, reducing sympathetic activity in mice, indicating broader metabolic signaling roles that could modulate retinal perfusion/metabolism indirectly (Gough, 2021).  

Collectively, these mechanisms—fuel substitution that sustains Δψm and ATP synthesis under glycolytic impairment, improved redox balance with decreased mitochondrial ROS, Nrf2-dependent antioxidant gene induction, NLRP3/NF-κB anti-inflammatory actions via HCAR2/ARRB2, stabilization of mitochondrial Ca²⁺/mPTP, and epigenetic programs that support mitochondrial biogenesis—map directly onto pathologies implicated in RPE degeneration in dry AMD and provide multiple rescue nodes testable in disease-relevant models (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect  
Assay context: The working hypothesis is that exogenous BHB will serve as an alternative mitochondrial substrate in RPE, sustaining Δψm and reducing NADH-driven mitochondrial ROS when glycolysis is impaired—conditions that model bioenergetic stress in geographic atrophy. Mechanistically, this is supported by three converging evidence streams: (1) mitochondrial fuel flexibility to oxidize BHB to acetyl-CoA via BDH1/SCOT, (2) redox modulation that increases NADH oxidation and elevates the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, and (3) multi-layered antioxidant/anti-inflammatory signaling that lowers mitochondrial ROS production and downstream inflammasome/NF-κB activation (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021).  

- Sustained Δψm and ATP under glycolytic impairment. RPE expresses ketogenesis machinery (HMGCS2) and monocarboxylate transport capacity (MCT1) and is capable of both producing and consuming BHB, while inner BRB MCT1 and neuronal MCT2 provide routes for substrate delivery into retinal tissue (Yang, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). In neurons, BHB preserved oxidative phosphorylation and ATP-linked respiration under MAS inhibition, a condition that effectively reduces mitochondrial access to cytosolic NADH from glycolysis; this predicts that, in RPE exposed to glycolytic blockade or high work demand, BHB could maintain Δψm and respiratory control by supplying acetyl-CoA independent of cytosolic NADH shuttling (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). In muscle and cardiac models, BHB improved respiratory control ratios, increased ATP production, and maintained Δψm under stress, providing precedent for Δψm preservation in high-energy post-mitotic cells (Parker et al., 2018; Mierziak et al., 2021).  

- Lowered NADH-driven mtROS and improved redox balance. Nutritional ketosis increases the brain NAD⁺/NADH ratio and ketones inhibit mitochondrial ROS production by increasing NADH oxidation, a shift that is expected to suppress reverse electron transport and semiquinone leak at respiratory complexes under high NADH load (Morris et al., 2020). Although some cardiac literature reports context-dependent changes in the mitochondrial NAD couple under BHB with concurrent oxidation of coenzyme Q, the net effect across neural and muscle studies is reduced mitochondrial ROS generation and improved redox handling, a phenotype also observed in optic/retinal models after ketogenic interventions (Chu et al., 2021; Gough, 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021). These redox improvements are reinforced by Nrf2 activation and increased expression of antioxidant defenses (e.g., SOD2), which increase ROS quenching capacity in retinal and optic tissues (Gough, 2021).  

- Anti-inflammatory and barrier-preserving actions in RPE. BHB agonizes HCAR2 expressed by RPE and retinal microglia, reducing leukocyte infiltration, preserving tight junction integrity (ZO-1), and suppressing inflammasome/NF-κB signaling (Powell et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019). In hyperglycemic ARPE-19, BHB improved viability and cell cycle progression and modulated inflammatory cytokines, consistent with protection under metabolic stress (Argentino et al., 2025). By preserving ATP and lowering AMPK phosphorylation, BHB/ketone availability is expected to block NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation and downstream expression of IL-6 and TNF-α, reducing the chronic para-inflammatory milieu implicated in RPE degeneration (Gough, 2021).  

- Translational considerations for exposure and transport. Systemically delivered BHB can traverse the blood–retinal barrier via MCT1, and RPE’s own MCT1 provides transmembrane transport capacity; nonetheless, quantitative extracellular BHB at RPE surfaces is likely in the low micromolar range under basal conditions, and RPE produces and consumes BHB dynamically, implying that achieving therapeutic mitochondrial utilization in RPE will require millimolar plasma BHB or local delivery (Tribble et al., 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). Nutritional ketosis and exogenous ketone supplementation readily achieve 0.5–2 mM BHB in plasma in rodent and human studies, which are the concentrations used in many in vitro protection assays (Cooper et al., 2023; Argentino et al., 2025).  

Key readouts and validation metrics for the proposed assay should include Δψm (e.g., TMRM/TMRE), OCR/ECAR profiling and ATP-linked respiration (Seahorse), mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX and H₂O₂ flux), NAD⁺/NADH ratio (enzymatic cycling and/or fluorescence lifetime imaging), pAMPK/AMPK and NF-κB p65 nuclear localization, Nrf2 translocation and target gene induction (e.g., SOD2), and inflammasome readouts (ASC specks, IL-1β maturation) (Gough, 2021). Given the measurement pitfalls documented in RPE ketone assays, BHB should be quantified by LC–MS/MS or after removal of high-MW confounders by size exclusion rather than by standard enzymatic kits (Gulette et al., 2024).  
Protein expression considerations support the mechanism in the target cell type. HCAR2/GPR109A is expressed by RPE and retinal microglia/endothelium and mediates anti-inflammatory effects of BHB in vivo, making receptor-dependent components of BHB action directly testable in RPE (Powell et al., 2021). RPE expresses HMGCS2 and MCT1, and retinal cells metabolize BHB into TCA intermediates, consistent with BDH1/SCOT/OXCT1 pathway activity enabling BHB oxidation in retinal tissues; while direct SCOT expression in RPE is not provided here, the metabolic tracing data indicating conversion of BHB to Krebs intermediates in retinal cells justify testing oxidative utilization in RPE (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strength of biological rationale. The core hypothesis—that BHB can act as an alternative mitochondrial fuel to sustain Δψm and lower NADH-driven mitochondrial ROS in glycolysis-impaired RPE—is strongly aligned with BHB’s established roles in extrahepatic tissues and is supported by multiple mechanistic strands in relevant neural and retinal systems (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). BHB oxidation provides acetyl-CoA and maintains respiration when glycolytic NADH transfer is compromised, as demonstrated in primary neurons; BHB reduces mtROS, preserves Δψm, and increases ATP in ischemic muscle/heart models; and nutrient ketosis increases the NAD⁺/NADH ratio and lowers ROS production in brain—effects that would be expected to decrease reverse-electron transport–driven ROS at complex I and stabilize mitochondrial function in stressed RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Mierziak et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020). In retinal tissue, ketogenic interventions and direct ketone administration reduce oxidative injury, preserve function, and enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in RGC/optic nerve models, while anti-inflammatory benefits via HCAR2—expressed by RPE—reduce leukocyte infiltration and preserve barrier integrity (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019). The mitochondrial stabilization effects observed in human microglia—lower MCU/mtCa²⁺, reduced mtROS, prevention of mPTP opening—further support a BHB-mediated mitochondrial resilience phenotype that is likely relevant to RPE (Jin et al., 2023).  

Evidence relevant to the target tissue. RPEs possess ketone-related transport and enzymatic capacity (HMGCS2, MCT1) and can both produce and consume BHB; they are responsive to BHB in vitro under metabolic stress (hyperglycemia) with improved viability and inflammatory marker modulation (Yang, 2021; Argentino et al., 2025). HCAR2-mediated anti-inflammatory and barrier maintenance functions have been demonstrated in RPE/retina, providing a receptor-proximal pathway for BHB to suppress chronic para-inflammation and preserve RPE junctional integrity, both relevant to dry AMD pathobiology (Powell et al., 2021). While direct measurements of BDH1/SCOT activity and NAD⁺/NADH dynamics in human RPE treated with BHB remain to be shown here, the metabolic fate of BHB in retinal cells and robust mitochondrial effects in closely related cell types make the translational experiments technically feasible and mechanistically justified (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Translational gaps and risks. No clinical trials have evaluated ketogenic diets or BHB specifically for RP or AMD, and some ketogenic diet studies reported adverse outcomes in wild-type animals (decreased ERG amplitude, altered serum albumin/weight), emphasizing the need to decouple BHB’s effects from broader dietary/metabolic confounders (Gough, 2021). Direct BHB delivery does not always recapitulate ketogenic diet benefits in RGC injury, suggesting that multi-target effects of diet (e.g., NAD metabolism, mTOR, microbiome) contribute to efficacy; this implies that BHB monotherapy may require combination strategies (e.g., nicotinamide co-therapy) or optimized dosing to achieve comparable benefit (Tribble et al., 2021). Quantification of BHB in RPE experiments is non-trivial due to assay interference; LC–MS/MS or validated size-exclusion protocols must be used to avoid false positives and to measure physiologically relevant, often low-micromolar extracellular BHB in RPE cultures (Gulette et al., 2024). Finally, the directionality of NAD redox effects may be context dependent (reports of both increased NAD⁺/NADH ratio in brain and reduced mitochondrial NAD couple in cardiac models), requiring careful interpretation with compartment-specific assays in RPE (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).  

Development path and decision points. Given the strong mechanistic rationale, retina-focused preclinical evidence, and RPE receptor expression data, BHB is a plausible repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD that merits rigorous, RPE-centric validation. Key go/no-go preclinical criteria should include: (1) demonstration that BHB rescues Δψm and ATP-linked respiration in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE under glycolytic impairment (e.g., 2-deoxyglucose or low glucose plus workload), (2) reduction of mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX/H₂O₂ flux) and elevation of cellular NAD⁺/NADH ratio with BHB, (3) suppression of pAMPK and NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation, induction of Nrf2 target genes, and reduction of NLRP3 activation, (4) persistence of benefits under HCAR2 antagonism/knockdown to parse receptor versus fuel contributions, and (5) confirmation that effects are contingent on monocarboxylate transport (MCT inhibition) and SCOT activity (e.g., OXCT1 knockdown), which would mechanistically link outcomes to BHB oxidation rather than unrelated signaling (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). In vivo, a dry-AMD–relevant RPE degeneration model should test systemic or ocular BHB delivery (dose selection to 0.5–2 mM plasma equivalents) with readouts of RPE mitochondrial structure/function, subretinal inflammation, and lesion progression; blood–retina transport via MCT1 at the inner BRB suggests systemic exposure can reach the retina, though intraocular routes might achieve higher local concentrations (Tribble et al., 2021). Throughout, BHB dosing must be titrated to avoid off-target effects and electrolyte load associated with some salt formulations; direct ketone esters or controlled dietary induction may be considered for translational studies, recognizing model-specific differences seen between exogenous BHB and ketogenic diet (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Strengths  
- Mechanistic breadth and convergence on AMD-relevant pathways: alternative fuel supply to support Δψm/ATP, improved NAD redox and ROS control, Nrf2 antioxidant gene induction, and potent suppression of NLRP3/NF-κB–mediated para-inflammation via HCAR2—each independently linked to retinal/RPE resilience (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Retinal delivery/uptake plausibility: MCT expression at the inner BRB and in RPE, plus RPE’s ability to both produce and consume BHB, establish physiological routes for BHB transit and utilization in target tissues (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Preclinical efficacy signals in retinal and CNS models: reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury, preserved neuronal function, enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis/antioxidant defenses, and receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory actions in retina (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Compatibility with RPE stress biology: BHB improved ARPE-19 survival under metabolic stress and modulated cytokines, and microglial mitochondrial data demonstrate BHB reverses mtCa²⁺/mtROS/mPTP derangements that are mechanistically relevant to RPE degeneration (Argentino et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2023).  

Weaknesses and uncertainties  
- Lack of AMD-specific in vivo data and no clinical trials in AMD/RP; extrapolation from RGC/optic nerve/diabetic models requires confirmation in RPE-targeted systems (Gough, 2021).  
- Measurement pitfalls in RPE ketone studies; reliance on inaccurate enzymatic assays historically confounded interpretation, necessitating MS-based quantitation and careful time-course sampling (Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Context-dependent redox effects; reports differ on NAD couple responses to BHB, indicating the need for compartmentalized NAD⁺/NADH readouts in RPE to avoid misattribution (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).  
- Differences between exogenous BHB and ketogenic diet; some benefits in glaucoma were not reproduced with BHB delivery, suggesting that metabolic co-factors (e.g., NAD boosters) or combinatorial strategies may be required (Tribble et al., 2021).  
- Potential systemic/dietary adverse effects; ketogenic diets can reduce ERG amplitudes and alter systemic biomarkers in wild-type mice—although these are not necessarily attributable to BHB per se, they caution against non-specific dietary induction in frail patients (Gough, 2021).  

Overall, BHB (Sigma-Aldrich 389410) is a compelling repurposed candidate for dry AMD based on strong mechanistic plausibility and retina-relevant preclinical evidence, with direct RPE expression of the key anti-inflammatory receptor HCAR2 and demonstrable RPE responses to BHB under metabolic stress (Powell et al., 2021; Argentino et al., 2025). The major risk is the current absence of AMD-specific in vivo evidence and the historical conflation of diet-level ketosis with BHB pharmacology; these can be addressed by an RPE-centric preclinical plan that uses rigorous ketone quantitation, compartmental redox readouts, transporter/enzyme perturbations (MCT/OXCT1), and in vivo validation in RPE degeneration models. If BHB reproducibly maintains Δψm/ATP, reduces mtROS, and suppresses inflammasome/NF-κB signaling in RPE under glycolytic impairment, it would justify advancement to formulation and delivery optimization for ocular exposure and, subsequently, to early clinical safety/pharmacodynamic studies in dry AMD (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Gough, 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

Proposal for GC4419 (avasopasem manganese)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GC4419 (avasopasem manganese) is a small‐molecule, manganese‐containing superoxide dismutase (SOD) mimetic that was developed by Galera Therapeutics. Its design is based on replicating the catalytic activity of the endogenous mitochondrial enzyme, manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), which naturally detoxifies superoxide radicals by converting them to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen. The compound is formulated as a manganese‐containing macrocyclic ligand complex with a molecular weight of approximately 483, prepared in an aqueous sodium bicarbonate solution (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Originally developed as the enantiomer of M40403, GC4419 belongs to the MnPAM class of SOD mimetics—a subclass of therapeutic agents that have been engineered to overcome the limitations of exogenous SOD proteins, such as immunogenicity and poor pharmacokinetics (Sonis, 2021; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013). SOD mimetics, by virtue of their small molecular weight and catalytic efficiency, have been widely explored clinically as radioprotective agents to mitigate oxidative tissue damage, and they offer an attractive platform for tackling diseases in which oxidative stress is a central pathophysiological driver.

Therapeutic History:  
GC4419 has a well‐documented history in preclinical and clinical settings aimed at ameliorating oxidative tissue injury. Preclinical studies have shown that GC4419 protects against cisplatin‐induced kidney injury in both acute (AKI) and chronic (CKD) murine models by scavenging superoxide radicals and attenuating inflammatory responses (Mapuskar et al., 2024). In the clinical arena, GC4419 has been evaluated in several trials—most notably in Phase 1b/2a and Phase 3 studies—targeting radiation‐induced mucositis in head and neck cancer patients. These trials demonstrated that intravenous infusion of GC4419 not only reduced the incidence and severity of severe oral mucositis but also reduced other therapy‐associated adverse events, such as cisplatin‐induced nephrotoxicity, in a dose‐dependent manner (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021). Despite this extensive history of use in mitigating radiation‐ and cisplatin‐linked toxicities, there have been no direct reports or preclinical studies that have investigated GC4419 in the context of retinal disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Houldsworth, 2024). This lack of prior application in ocular models underscores the novelty of the repurposing hypothesis—to deploy the compound’s antioxidative properties in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells under chronic oxidative stress conditions such as those elicited by drusen accumulation.

Mechanism of Action:  
GC4419 functions by mimicking the natural enzymatic activity of MnSOD, specifically catalyzing the dismutation reaction of superoxide (O2•–) into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and molecular oxygen (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Its reported catalytic rate constant of approximately 1×10^7 per mol per second, while lower than that of native mitochondrial SOD (~1.2×10^9 per mol per second), is nonetheless sufficient to achieve a measurable reduction in superoxide levels in stressed tissues (Mapuskar et al., 2024). This selective removal of superoxide is particularly advantageous because GC4419 does not appreciably interact with other reactive oxygen species such as nitric oxide, peroxynitrite, or hydrogen peroxide, thus ensuring a focused mechanism of action (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013). In preclinical kidney models, treatment with GC4419 has been associated with the restoration of mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) activities, reduced expression of pro-oxidant enzymes like NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4), and a decrease in markers of inflammation (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Although the detailed chemical structure (e.g., the precise coordination geometry of the manganese ion or whether it resembles a classical Mn-salen derivative) has not been fully disclosed, the compound is understood to be a highly stable, low-molecular-weight agent optimized for biological compatibility and effective redox cycling (Sonis, 2021; Mapuskar et al., 2024). Given its intended mechanism as a mitochondrial SOD mimetic, it is hypothesized that GC4419 can enter cells, localize to mitochondria, and thereby directly attenuate mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—a rationale that is central to its anticipated repurposing for dry AMD.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
In dry age-related macular degeneration, the retinal pigment epithelium is subject to chronic oxidative stress resulting from cumulative damage due to drusen deposits and impaired cellular clearance mechanisms. RPE cells are rich in mitochondria and depend heavily on efficient oxidative metabolism; however, over time, excessive production of ROS—particularly superoxide generated by dysfunctional mitochondrial electron transport—can lead to cell death and, consequently, to the progression of dry AMD. The underlying hypothesis for repurposing GC4419 in this context is that, by acting as a mitochondrial SOD mimetic, the compound will convert excess superoxide generated within RPE cells into hydrogen peroxide, which can then be further detoxified by endogenous catalase and glutathione peroxidase systems (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Houldsworth, 2024). This conversion is expected to not only alleviate the oxidative burden but also to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψ_m) and maintain efficient ATP synthesis, which is critical for the survival and function of RPE cells (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Montoro et al., 2023). Furthermore, by reducing superoxide levels, GC4419 may indirectly dampen inflammation mediated by redox-sensitive transcription factors (such as NF-κB), thereby decreasing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines that can exacerbate RPE stress and degeneration (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Houldsworth, 2024). Although direct evidence of GC4419’s efficacy in retinal models has not yet been reported, the known expression of the MnSOD gene (SOD2) in RPE cells and the central role of mitochondrial oxidative damage in dry AMD provide a strong mechanistic rationale for the compound’s potential effectiveness when applied to ocular tissues (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Houldsworth, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
GC4419 presents several compelling strengths as a candidate for repurposing in the management of dry AMD. Its well-characterized mechanism of action, which involves the selective catalytic removal of superoxide, addresses a key pathogenic factor in dry AMD—oxidative stress within the RPE and its mitochondria (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021). The compound’s demonstrated ability to restore mitochondrial function and reduce inflammation in preclinical models of cisplatin-induced kidney injury and radiation-induced mucosal damage underscores its potential utility in any tissue where oxidative stress is a driving factor (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Moreover, the pharmacological profile of GC4419—highlighted by its favorable molecular weight, catalytic properties, and prior progression into clinical trials for other indications—supports its viability as a repurposed drug candidate. By leveraging existing clinical data on safety and efficacy in non-ocular settings, the repurposing effort for dry AMD could benefit from relatively expedited translational development.

Nevertheless, there are also notable weaknesses and uncertainties. First, despite the strong theoretical rationale, no direct preclinical or clinical studies have yet evaluated GC4419 in retinal tissues or in animal models of dry AMD; therefore, its ocular pharmacokinetics, penetrance of the blood–retina barrier, and potential for mitochondrial uptake specifically in RPE cells remain unproven (Houldsworth, 2024). Second, the current formulations of GC4419 are designed for intravenous administration as used in radiation mucositis trials; adapting these formulations for local ocular delivery (e.g., via intravitreal injection or targeted sustained-release systems) may present challenges that need to be carefully addressed. Third, while the mechanism of converting superoxide to hydrogen peroxide is beneficial, it is crucial to ensure that the resultant H2O2 is efficiently cleared by endogenous antioxidant defenses in the RPE; accumulation of H2O2 could itself precipitate oxidative damage if the cellular detoxification capacity is overwhelmed (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Moreover, although GC4419 has been referred to in some contexts as part of the “Mn-salen” or MnPAM families of dismutase mimetics, the precise structural classification has not been fully disclosed, which may affect its predicted bio-distribution and interaction with specific intracellular targets (Sonis, 2021; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013). Lastly, differences in the pathological microenvironments between tissues treated for radiation toxicity versus the RPE in dry AMD could influence the overall efficacy of GC4419; thus, careful preclinical studies in ocular disease models will be necessary to confirm that its antioxidative and anti-inflammatory actions translate effectively to an AMD setting (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021).

In summary, GC4419 (avasopasem manganese) is a well-characterized SOD mimetic that has demonstrated promising protective effects against oxidative stress in non-ocular models, providing a strong biochemical rationale for its potential repurposing as a therapeutic candidate in dry age-related macular degeneration. Its mechanism of selectively dismutating superoxide to hydrogen peroxide could help restore redox balance, preserve mitochondrial integrity, and mitigate inflammatory cascades in the retinal pigment epithelium—a key contributor to dry AMD pathology (Mapuskar et al., 2024). However, the absence of direct evidence in retinal or ocular models and the challenges associated with reformulating a systemically administered drug for local ocular delivery constitute significant hurdles that must be overcome through targeted preclinical research. Overall, while the strengths of GC4419 are notable—with a robust mechanism, supportive preclinical and clinical history in other indications, and a focused approach to counteracting mitochondrial oxidative stress—the weaknesses highlight the need for further investigation into its ocular pharmacodynamics, formulation for targeted delivery, and comprehensive evaluation in dry AMD-specific models before advancing to clinical trials in this indication (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013).

Proposal for Resveratrol (Cayman Chemical #70580)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound belonging to the stilbene class and is structurally defined as 3,5,4′-trihydroxystilbene. It is biosynthesized by plants such as Vitis vinifera (grapes), Japanese Knotweed, and various berries in response to stress factors like injury or pathogen attack, and it is a well‐recognized phytoalexin with a molecular formula of C14H12O3 (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022). Originally isolated from the White Hellebore in the mid-20th century and later found in red wine due to grape skin fermentation, resveratrol has garnered significant attention not only for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties but also for its potential benefits in cardiovascular and neuroprotective contexts (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022). As such, resveratrol—and by extension its commercial version (Cayman Chemical #70580) used in our studies—is classified as a nutraceutical and drug candidate with a long track record of investigative research including applications in aging, inflammation, and ocular health (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
A considerable volume of biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical literature has explored resveratrol’s broad spectrum of activities. Historically, resveratrol has been investigated primarily for its cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects, as well as its anti-aging properties. In the realm of ophthalmology, several in vitro and animal studies have focused on its role in retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic retinopathy (DR), and glaucoma. For instance, its use in RPE cell models has shown promising evidence for ameliorating oxidative stress-induced damage, a central factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Clinical investigations have attempted to translate these findings, as exemplified by the terminated clinical trial NCT02625376 that investigated resveratrol for exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015), highlighting both the potential and the challenges involved in its clinical application (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Beyond ocular applications, resveratrol’s inclusion in various nutraceutical formulations underscores its established safety profile when administered at low-to-moderate doses, although issues pertaining to bioavailability and rapid systemic metabolism have been recurrent themes in the literature (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, resveratrol exerts its effects primarily by modulating multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The central hypothesis we are testing is that resveratrol activates the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a pathway integral to regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and the antioxidant defense system. Activation of SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, by resveratrol increases the deacetylation and activation of its downstream effector, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Once activated, AMPK facilitates the phosphorylation and activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1 alpha (PGC-1α) in the cytoplasm, which subsequently translocates to the nucleus to upregulate the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and antioxidant responses, including the gene encoding superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). This cascade not only improves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and spare respiratory capacity—critical indicators of cellular health under oxidative stress—but also promotes an overall enhancement of cellular resilience against reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bel, 2020; Bryl et al., 2022). Further molecular studies indicate that resveratrol can also modulate extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1/2) and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), contributing additional layers of cytoprotection through anti-apoptotic effects (Pop et al., 2022; Pop et al., 2022). Together, these mechanistic insights provide a comprehensive biochemical framework through which resveratrol is hypothesized to mitigate the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in RPE cells—a primary factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2021; Bryl et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of the proposed assay for dry AMD, our expectation is that resveratrol will exert a multifaceted protective effect on RPE cells under oxidative challenge. Specifically, when RPE cells are exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a model for oxidative stress, resveratrol is anticipated to counteract the resultant mitochondrial dysfunction by upregulating antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, thereby reducing intracellular ROS levels (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Restoration of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a critical endpoint, as it directly reflects cellular energy status and the ability of mitochondria to sustain ATP synthesis under stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024). In addition, an improvement in spare respiratory capacity—the measure of a cell’s ability to respond to increased energy demands—should be evident, reflecting enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and a greater capacity for cellular repair mechanisms (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). These cytoprotective effects have been demonstrated in in vitro studies using ARPE-19 and other human retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, and they resonate with the established role of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in mediating energy metabolism and antioxidative defenses in the retina (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021). Moreover, by decreasing the accrual of oxidative damage, resveratrol is expected to limit apoptotic signaling pathways, which are crucial in slowing the progressive degeneration observed in dry AMD (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from preclinical studies strongly supports the potential of resveratrol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially considering its capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and activate intrinsic antioxidant defenses. The activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis not only augments mitochondrial biogenesis but also enhances the expression of key antioxidant enzymes required to neutralize ROS, thereby directly addressing one of the primary mechanisms underlying AMD pathology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). One of the major strengths of resveratrol is its pleiotropic mode of action; beyond its antioxidant properties, its anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic activities further consolidate its candidacy for chronic conditions like dry AMD (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Bel, 2020). Furthermore, extensive safety data in various preclinical models indicate that resveratrol is well tolerated at certain dose ranges, which is a positive indicator for its potential clinical translation (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020).

However, several limitations remain that warrant careful consideration. The primary challenge with resveratrol is its poor bioavailability and rapid metabolism, which may result in subtherapeutic tissue concentrations despite high oral absorption. This has driven research efforts into advanced drug delivery platforms, such as nanoparticle-based systems and liposomal formulations, aimed at enhancing ocular retention and achieving sustained drug levels in the retina (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Additionally, although the in vitro and animal model data are promising, there exists a dearth of robust clinical trial data specifically addressing dry AMD, as evidenced by the terminated trial in exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015) and the limited clinical evidence in related retinal pathologies (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Another potential weakness is the dose-dependent duality of its mechanism, where low doses predominantly mediate SIRT1-dependent effects, whereas higher doses might trigger SIRT1-independent pathways, possibly leading to off-target effects or toxicity (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such a narrow therapeutic window necessitates a precise optimization of dosing regimens and formulation strategies. Despite these challenges, the overarching trend in preclinical research underscores that with proper formulation and dosing strategies, resveratrol could excel as an adjuvant or even monotherapy for protecting RPE cells from oxidative injury and, consequently, for the management of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In-Depth Analysis of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence:  
Numerous in vitro studies have characterized the effect of resveratrol on retinal pigment epithelial cells, notably ARPE-19 cell lines, under conditions of oxidative stress. Such studies consistently demonstrate that resveratrol treatment leads to a measurable reduction in ROS levels, a decrease in markers of apoptosis, and an overall improvement in mitochondrial parameters including Δψm and spare respiratory capacity (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). These findings are reinforced by experiments showing that resveratrol can mitigate blue light-induced retinal damage and preserve cell viability, further supporting its relevance in ocular pathologies where light-induced oxidative stress is a contributing factor (Bel, 2020). Complementary studies in animal models have shown that resveratrol can reduce inflammatory cytokine secretion and inhibit processes such as choroidal neovascularization, which has implications not only for dry AMD but also for its neovascular (wet) counterpart (Bryl et al., 2022; Bel, 2020).

Moreover, mechanistic investigations into the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis reveal that the deacetylation of PGC-1α is a critical step in the upregulation of mitochondrial genes, which directly correlates with increased cellular ATP production and enhanced resistance to oxidative stress (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Experimental data also show that SOD2 expression is significantly increased following resveratrol treatment, corroborating the compound’s role in boosting the cellular antioxidant capacity (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). These molecular events culminate in an environment that is less conducive to oxidative damage, thereby potentially arresting or even reversing some aspects of RPE degeneration that occur in dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).

From a clinical perspective, the application of resveratrol in ocular disorders has been approached with caution, primarily due to pharmacokinetic challenges. Even though systemic administration of resveratrol has demonstrated efficacy in reducing plasma oxidative markers in diabetic patients and other conditions, the translation to ocular tissue remains hindered by its low aqueous solubility and rapid hepatic metabolism (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Abu-Amero et al., 2016). To overcome these barriers, innovative drug delivery systems such as chitosan-based nanoparticles, polymeric micelles, and liposomal formulations are being actively developed and show promise for achieving therapeutic levels in retinal tissues (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such advanced formulations not only improve bioavailability but also allow for controlled release, which is essential for a chronic condition like dry AMD where sustained therapeutic action is desirable.

Additional mechanistic studies also suggest that resveratrol’s efficacy might be enhanced when used in combination with other therapeutic agents. For instance, its synergistic effects with anti-VEGF treatments in mitigating inflammatory cascades and suppressing angiogenesis have been noted in various preclinical models (Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023; Tong et al., 2022). This combinatorial approach could be particularly valuable in cases where dry AMD transitions toward neovascular complications, thereby broadening the therapeutic window of resveratrol-based interventions.

Challenges in Drug Delivery and Bioavailability:  
While the biochemical rationale for using resveratrol in dry AMD is robust, its clinical development is significantly complicated by pharmacokinetic limitations. The compound is classified as a BCS Class II molecule, meaning that despite having high membrane permeability and lipophilicity, its poor aqueous solubility results in less than 1% bioavailability following oral administration (Kaštelan et al., 2025). As a consequence, only minimal amounts of unchanged resveratrol reach the systemic circulation and, by extension, the ocular tissues. Current research thus prioritizes the optimization of drug delivery vehicles to enhance its stability and target specificity. Nanotechnology-based delivery methods, including polymeric nanoparticles and solid lipid nanoparticles, have demonstrated enhanced tissue penetration and prolonged drug retention in the eye (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). However, these strategies are still in the developmental phase, and their safety, scalability, and reproducibility for routine clinical use remain to be thoroughly validated. The potential for off-target effects and variability in patient-specific pharmacokinetics are additional hurdles that must be addressed in future clinical studies.

Safety and Dosing Considerations:  
Resveratrol has been generally recognized as safe in many preclinical studies, with low-dose regimens showing minimal adverse effects and favorable tolerability profiles (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020). Nonetheless, concerns have been raised regarding gastrointestinal disturbances and other side effects at higher doses, as well as potential interactions with other medications (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Moreover, due to the compound’s rapid metabolism, determining an optimal dosing regimen that achieves effective local concentrations in the retina without inducing systemic toxicity remains challenging. This necessitates further preclinical and early-phase clinical trials to elucidate the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic profiles specific to ocular applications. Tailoring the dosing strategy based on individual metabolic rates and employing controlled-release formulations may help mitigate these issues and maximize therapeutic outcomes (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025).

Strategic Direction and Future Perspectives:  
Given the multifaceted biological activities of resveratrol and the encouraging preclinical evidence in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE damage, it holds considerable promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to modulate the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis and promote mitochondrial biogenesis presents a novel therapeutic approach that directly targets the cellular dysfunctions underlying RPE degeneration. However, the translation of these findings into clinical practice will require addressing the critical challenges of bioavailability, formulation, and dosing.

Future research should focus on (1) developing and rigorously testing advanced drug delivery systems such as nanoparticle encapsulation methods that can bypass first-pass metabolism and target the retina more effectively, (2) conducting detailed pharmacokinetic studies to determine the optimal dosing regimen for achieving sustained therapeutic concentrations in ocular tissues, and (3) exploring combination therapy approaches that integrate resveratrol with conventional treatments such as anti-VEGF agents or other nutraceuticals to provide a comprehensive strategy against AMD progression (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Pop et al., 2022; Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023). Furthermore, expanding the investigative efforts into patient-specific and personalized medicine approaches might allow for tailoring treatment protocols based on individual metabolic and genetic profiles, thereby maximizing efficacy and reducing adverse effects (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, resveratrol emerges as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its extensive preclinical evidence, well-elucidated molecular mechanisms, and potential for modulating critical cellular pathways implicated in retinal degeneration. The strengths of resveratrol are rooted in its natural origin, broad-spectrum antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, and its ability to enhance mitochondrial function through the activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α pathway. These attributes are particularly relevant for combating the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Nonetheless, its clinical utility is hampered by significant challenges related to bioavailability and metabolism, which necessitate innovative formulation and delivery strategies. Moreover, the variable dose-response observed in preclinical studies highlights the need for precise dose optimization before resveratrol can be reliably integrated into clinical practice for AMD treatment (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Although resveratrol has been investigated in clinical trials for ocular conditions, further large-scale, well-designed studies are essential to validate its efficacy, establish an acceptable safety profile, and determine its long-term benefits in human subjects with dry AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015; Pop et al., 2022).

Given the current state of evidence, we recommend that the research team continue to explore resveratrol as a candidate for dry AMD with a dual focus: first, to refine and optimize drug delivery systems that enhance its ocular bioavailability, and second, to design and implement comprehensive dose-escalation and safety studies in relevant preclinical models. Collaborative efforts that integrate insights from molecular biology, pharmacology, and clinical research will be critical in overcoming the translational challenges that have traditionally limited the application of resveratrol in ocular therapeutics (Pop et al., 2022; Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023).

Conclusion:  
Resveratrol represents a promising candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its robust mechanistic rationale and supportive preclinical evidence. Its capacity to activate the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis, promote mitochondrial biogenesis, and enhance antioxidant enzyme expression positions it as a multifaceted agent capable of mitigating oxidative stress in RPE cells—one of the key pathological drivers of AMD (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). While the compound’s safety profile in low-dose regimens is encouraging, its poor bioavailability and rapid metabolism require that future research prioritize advanced drug delivery systems and optimized dosing strategies. With concerted efforts in formulation science, preclinical validation, and clinical evaluation, resveratrol has the potential to become an integral part of a multi-targeted therapeutic approach for dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025).

In conclusion, a comprehensive literature review of resveratrol underscores both its therapeutic potential and the challenges that must be overcome before its clinical application in dry AMD can be realized. The strengths of its molecular mechanisms and established safety in various studies are tempered by pharmacokinetic limitations that necessitate further research. The proposed strategy to focus on enhancing bioavailability via innovative drug delivery systems, coupled with rigorous preclinical safety and efficacy evaluations, will determine whether resveratrol can fulfill its promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bel, 2020). With continued investigation and collaboration across multidisciplinary research teams, resveratrol could offer a novel and effective means to delay or prevent RPE degeneration and the progression of dry AMD, ultimately improving patient outcomes in this challenging and prevalent ocular disease (Bryl et al., 2022; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Given the existing data and the ongoing improvements in nanoparticle and liposome-based delivery systems, our evaluation supports the further development of resveratrol in the context of dry AMD. The integration of this compound as either a monotherapy or as an adjunct to established therapies could provide enhanced protection against oxidative stress, preserve mitochondrial function, and improve retinal cell survival in patients suffering from this debilitating condition. Future research should aim to bridge the gap between promising in vitro efficacy and clinical applicability, ensuring that the dosing, safety, and delivery challenges are adequately addressed through well-designed preclinical and clinical studies (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015).

Overall, our comprehensive evaluation affirms that resveratrol, sourced as Cayman Chemical #70580, holds substantial promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The converging lines of evidence from biochemistry, pharmacology, and early clinical investigations provide a strong rationale for continued development, with a focus on overcoming the pharmacokinetic limitations that have hindered its clinical translation thus far (Bryl et al., 2022; Bel, 2020; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). This proposal is therefore highly recommended for further preclinical optimization and subsequent clinical trial evaluation, establishing resveratrol as a potential cornerstone in the management of dry age-related macular degeneration.

Proposal for Liproxstatin-1 (Selleckchem S7692)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Liproxstatin-1 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of ferroptosis that was originally discovered using phenotypic high-throughput screening in systems where ferroptosis was induced by either genetic deletion of GPX4 or by glutathione depletion with agents like erastin (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69). Its chemical identity is tied to a unique spiroquinoxalinamine scaffold, which places it in the class of aromatic amine radical-trapping antioxidants (RTAs) – compounds well known in industrial settings to protect hydrocarbon products from autoxidation, as well as in biomedical research to block oxidative lipid chain reactions (Scarpellini, 2023, pp. 41–45; Angeli, Shah, Pratt, & Conrad, 2017, pp. 6–8). In contrast to classical phenolic antioxidants such as α-tocopherol, Liproxstatin-1 is designed to operate in the lipid bilayer, where its aminic (or diarylamine) moieties are less hindered by nonproductive hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups, thus allowing rapid hydrogen-atom transfer to lipid peroxyl radicals (Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Although detailed synthetic routes are not provided in the available reports, the discovery process clearly identifies Liproxstatin-1 as a lead candidate that emerged from unbiased cell-based screens aimed at identifying compounds that preserve cell viability in the absence of GPX4 function (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Its categorization as an RTA is significant because this class of compounds has a long history of being used to inhibit free radical–mediated damage in both industrial and biological contexts (Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
The preclinical history of Liproxstatin-1 is rich with evidence supporting its role as a potent inhibitor of ferroptosis. Early studies demonstrated that Liproxstatin-1 acts at low nanomolar concentrations to prevent ferroptotic cell death in mouse embryonic fibroblasts as well as in specialized cells rendered vulnerable by GPX4 inactivation (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Angeli et al., 2014, p. 10). Beyond in vitro cell survival assays, Liproxstatin-1 has been evaluated in vivo where it has shown remarkable protective effects in models of acute tissue injury including genetic GPX4 deficiency, which induces acute renal failure, and in ischaemia/reperfusion models of liver injury (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10). Although its direct clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not been established – with most in vivo data coming from non-ocular models – its success in ameliorating tissue damage by inhibiting lipid peroxidation suggests its potential utility in other degenerative pathologies where oxidative membrane damage drives dysfunction, such as in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration underlying geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–21). Moreover, related compounds, notably Ferrostatin-1, have been tested in various retinal cell models and in some in vivo settings pertaining to retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury and oxygen-induced retinopathy, further bolstering the therapeutic concept of using RTA-type ferroptosis inhibitors in ocular settings (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). While the bulk of Liproxstatin-1’s therapeutic history centers on its role as an anti-ferroptotic agent in cancer, neurodegeneration, and acute organ failure, its mechanistic overlap with key pathological features observed in dry AMD – such as iron accumulation, glutathione depletion and elevated lipid peroxidation in the RPE – supports evaluating it as a repurposed candidate in this context (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which Liproxstatin-1 exerts its cytoprotective effect is rooted in its function as a radical-trapping antioxidant. Specifically, Liproxstatin-1 reacts rapidly with lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate the autoxidation chain reaction in cellular membranes. Experimental data have established that Liproxstatin-1 exhibits an intrinsic reaction rate constant (k_inh) in the range of approximately 2.4 × 10^5 M^−1 s^−1 in organic solvents such as chlorobenzene at 37 °C, which is comparable to industrial diarylamine antioxidants (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9). Although its intrinsic reactivity in homogeneous organic solutions may appear lower than classical phenolic antioxidants like α-tocopherol, its performance in the lipid bilayer is superior due to reduced hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups – a feature that enhances its mobility and reactivity in the lipid environment where ferroptosis is executed (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). The compound functions primarily by donating a hydrogen atom from its arylamine (or diarylamine) N–H group, effectively quenching chain-propagating lipid peroxyl radicals before they can perpetuate lipid hydroperoxide formation (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Kinetic isotope effect studies and computational analyses have confirmed that the N–H bond dissociation enthalpy is sufficiently low in Liproxstatin-1 to enable rapid hydrogen-atom transfer, which is a critical step in its radical-trapping mechanism (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 2–3, 5–7). Importantly, Liproxstatin-1 does not exert significant inhibitory effects on enzymes such as human 15-lipoxygenase-1, thereby ruling out an enzymatic inhibition mechanism and reinforcing that its protective effect is solely attributable to non-enzymatic scavenging of peroxyl radicals (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 201–210). Recent studies have even suggested that Liproxstatin-1 may form a complex with iron in certain cellular compartments (e.g., the lysosome), which could further diminish iron-catalysed radical generation under acidic conditions; however, the predominant and well-characterized mechanism remains its role in intercepting lipid peroxyl radicals (Rodriguez et al., 2024, pp. 1–5; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). On a molecular level, by halting the autoxidation chain reaction, Liproxstatin-1 preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and prevents the deleterious accumulation of lipid hydroperoxides, events that are central to the execution phase of ferroptosis (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Thus, by protecting cellular membranes from oxidative deterioration, Liproxstatin-1 interrupts the cascade of events leading to ferroptotic cell death, a process that is implicated in RPE degeneration seen in geographic atrophy (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy where RPE degeneration is a hallmark, the expected effect of Liproxstatin-1 would be to curtail the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation that underpins ferroptotic cell death. In vitro assays using RPE cell lines such as ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cells have demonstrated that targeting lipid peroxidation – as evidenced by reductions in markers like BODIPY-C11 oxidation and ACSL4 expression – can rescue cells from oxidative stress–mediated death (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23). Liproxstatin-1 is anticipated to mitigate the accumulation of lipid hydroperoxides, thus preserving the integrity of cellular membranes and mitochondrial function in the RPE (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Given that geographic atrophy in dry AMD is associated with iron overload and subsequent iron-catalysed lipid peroxidation, the ability of Liproxstatin-1 to trap peroxyl radicals is particularly significant; by reducing lipid ROS, it is expected to prevent the conversion of polyunsaturated fatty acids into cytotoxic lipid hydroperoxides, thereby maintaining cellular viability (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Moreover, the inhibition of ACSL4-dependent peroxidation pathways – which have been linked to ferroptosis in RPE cells – may also be intercepted by Liproxstatin-1, providing a dual line of defense against ferroptotic signaling (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). On a cellular level, the compound is expected to maintain Δψm and reduce indicators of oxidative stress, as previously demonstrated in models addressing GPX4 inhibition (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). In animal models where ferroptosis contributes to tissue degeneration (such as renal or hepatic ischaemia/reperfusion models), treatment with Liproxstatin-1 resulted in reduced TUNEL-positive cell counts and ameliorated tissue injury; these outcomes provide a rationale for its application in preclinical dry AMD models, where similar pathological processes – including mitochondrial dysfunction, iron dysregulation, and excessive lipid peroxidation – are observed (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Peng et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). In essence, when applied to RPE cells under conditions that mimic dry AMD, Liproxstatin-1 should decrease oxidative markers, prevent cell death, and thereby slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy by restoring the balance between pro-oxidant and antioxidant pathways (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23).

Overall Evaluation:  
Liproxstatin-1 stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent against dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy, given the mechanistic overlap between ferroptosis and RPE cell death observed in dry AMD. One of its principal strengths lies in its potent radical-trapping antioxidant activity, which is not only effective at low nanomolar concentrations but also uniquely suited to the lipid bilayer environment of the RPE (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). This specificity is critical because retinal cells are subject to a high burden of polyunsaturated lipid content and are therefore particularly sensitive to oxidative damage. The fact that Liproxstatin-1 has demonstrated efficacy in protecting cells under ferroptotic stress in other organ systems – including kidney and liver models – further supports its potential viability in ocular applications (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Peng et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). Additionally, the compound’s ability to reduce lipid peroxidation, maintain mitochondrial membrane potential, and possibly engage in secondary iron-inactivating mechanisms (as suggested by lysosomal localization studies) offers multiple avenues through which it may address the multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD (Rodriguez et al., 2024, pp. 1–5; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2).

However, several challenges must be considered. Despite the strong preclinical evidence in non-ocular systems, direct evidence of Liproxstatin-1’s efficacy in models of dry AMD or RPE-specific ferroptosis is still limited relative to other compounds such as Ferrostatin-1 or nanoparticle-delivered ferroptosis inhibitors in retinal models (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23). This gap in ocular preclinical data implies that further dedicated studies using RPE cell models and in vivo dry AMD animal models are necessary to validate its protective effects in the eye. In addition, drug delivery to the retina poses its own set of challenges – the blood-retinal barrier and the unique pharmacokinetic profile required for intravitreal stability must be thoroughly optimized (Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69; Hao, Xu, Zhang, & Xue, 2024, pp. 6–7). Moreover, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease involving not only ferroptosis but also apoptosis, inflammation, and other forms of regulated cell death; therefore, while inhibiting ferroptosis may be beneficial, it is uncertain whether monotherapy with Liproxstatin-1 would be sufficient to arrest disease progression. There is also the matter of safety and tolerability in the context of the ocular environment, as systemic dosing strategies that work in renal or hepatic models may not directly translate to the delicate milieu of retinal tissues (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Finally, considerations regarding the long-term stability, potential off-target effects, and metabolic fate of Liproxstatin-1 in the eye will be crucial parameters in the drug development process.

In summary, the collective literature indicates that Liproxstatin-1 has a well-defined mechanism as a radical-trapping antioxidant that effectively blocks lipid peroxidation and, by extension, ferroptosis. Its discovery through unbiased screening in ferroptosis-susceptible models and its demonstration of efficacy in multiple organ systems provide a strong foundation for its repurposing in dry AMD. The evidence supports that Liproxstatin-1 could counteract the iron-driven ROS amplification and lipid peroxidation that contribute to RPE cell death in geographic atrophy. Nonetheless, while its mechanistic rationale and preclinical promise are substantial, further research – particularly within retinal models – is necessary to fully evaluate its therapeutic potential and address challenges related to ocular delivery and multi-pathway disease components. Taken together, Liproxstatin-1 represents a compelling candidate for further investigation as a targeted inhibitor of ferroptosis in the treatment of dry AMD (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69, 207–210; Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23).
