Proposal for Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me; MedChemExpress HY-15151)

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured in sections that address its origins, therapeutic history, known mechanisms of action, expected effects in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and an overall assessment of its strengths and challenges.

• Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bardoxolone methyl is a semisynthetic derivative belonging to the synthetic oleanane triterpenoid class. Its origin stems from oleanolic acid—a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid abundantly found in various medicinal plants. Early medicinal chemistry programs sought to overcome the modest anti‐inflammatory activity and poor bioavailability of oleanolic acid by introducing targeted modifications. Through chemical derivatization, these programs generated CDDO (2‐cyano‐3,12‐dioxooleana‐1,9‐dien‐28‐oic acid) and subsequently its C‐28 methyl ester, known as Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) (Borella et al., 2019). The synthetic process involves the installation of electrophilic Michael acceptor groups at strategic positions on the oleanane scaffold, such as the addition of an α,β‐unsaturated carbonyl in the A‐ring and further incorporation of a cyano group that substantially increases the compound’s potency relative to its natural precursor (Wong et al., 2016; Zhang & Chapman, 2020). These chemical modifications not only enhance the anti‐inflammatory and anticancer properties but also improve chemical stability and oral bioavailability. The structural design, which incorporates a reversible electrophilic reactivity, underpins the compound’s ability to engage diverse cellular targets (Thomas, 2012; Zhou et al., 2014). Bardoxolone methyl thus represents a chemically advanced, highly potent agent from a class of molecules originally designed to trigger cytoprotective responses via direct electrophilic modulation.

• Therapeutic History  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and early clinical evaluation primarily in fields as disparate as oncology and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Initial studies established that synthetic oleanane triterpenoids, including CDDO and its variants, exert dramatic anti‐inflammatory effects by suppressing inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase (COX‐2) expression in activated macrophages (Gatbonton‐Schwager, 2014). Preclinical studies in multiple mouse cancer models and inflammatory conditions confirmed its potent anticancer activity and cytoprotective properties, which catalyzed its progression into human clinical trials (Borella et al., 2019; Nakagami, 2016).  
In the clinical arena, Bardoxolone methyl was advanced through Phase I cancer trials, where its once‐daily oral dosing regimen and pharmacokinetic profile—with a terminal half‐life of approximately 39 hours—were characterized (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). More notably, its unexpected ability to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patients with advanced renal disease, particularly in diabetic nephropathy, led to its evaluation in large Phase II and Phase III trials, such as the BEAM and BEACON studies (Yagishita et al., 2020; Tanase et al., 2022). However, the BEACON trial was terminated prematurely due to an increased incidence of cardiovascular events, including heart failure, highlighting concerns about the compound’s systemic safety profile when used at higher doses or in populations with comorbidities (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Despite its promising preclinical pharmacology and the breadth of clinical data available in non‐ocular indications, to date there is no direct record in the literature of Bardoxolone methyl being used specifically for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular degenerative conditions (Schiavoni et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the overall safety and pharmacokinetic properties observed in CKD and oncology trials lend valuable insights for considering drug repurposing across therapeutic areas.

• Mechanism of Action  
Bardoxolone methyl is best known for its ability to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway—a master regulator of cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative and electrophilic stress. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is tightly regulated by Kelch‐like ECH‐associated protein 1 (Keap1), which serves as an adaptor for ubiquitin ligases targeting Nrf2 for proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl functions as a potent electrophile and interacts with sulfhydryl groups on critical cysteine residues within Keap1. This covalent or reversible Michael addition reaction disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, thereby stabilizing and allowing Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) in the promoter regions of a host of cytoprotective genes. This transcriptional activation results in the upregulation of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxifying enzymes, including but not limited to heme oxygenase‐1 (HO‐1), NAD(P)H dehydrogenase (quinone 1; NQO1), various glutathione transferases, and glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits (Thomas, 2012; Wong et al., 2016). Studies in non‐ocular tissues have shown that at very low (nanomolar) doses, Bardoxolone methyl robustly engages this cytoprotective program while also exerting dose‐dependent biology wherein intermediate and high doses trigger effects such as modulation of cell differentiation and direct anticancer activity, respectively (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
It is important to note that while the canonical targets of Nrf2 activation are well characterized, Bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic character enables it to interact with multiple regulatory proteins. For example, it can inhibit IκB kinase β (IKKβ), leading to suppression of nuclear factor κB (NF‐κB) signaling and subsequent reduction in proinflammatory cytokine production (Zhou et al., 2014; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the literature does not provide direct experimental evidence that Bardoxolone methyl specifically upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) and peroxiredoxin 3 (PRDX3) in RPE cells, the robust, broad‐spectrum transcriptional response induced by Nrf2 activation strongly suggests that mitochondrial and cytoplasmic components of the antioxidant defense system may also be upregulated (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015). Such upregulation would be consistent with previous findings of increased expression of antioxidant genes and improved cellular redox status upon treatment with similar synthetic triterpenoids (Schiavoni et al., 2025; Sporn et al., 2011).

• Expected Effect in Dry AMD  
The pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration is multifactorial, with chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction playing a central role in the degeneration of the RPE—a critical monolayer that supports photoreceptor health. RPE cells are particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage due to high metabolic activity, exposure to light, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In this context, the proposed mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl, namely activation of the Nrf2/ARE pathway, provides a biologically tenable strategy for neuroprotection and cellular preservation.  
When administered at low doses, Bardoxolone methyl is expected to trigger a cytoprotective transcriptional program in RPE cells. Activation of Nrf2 should lead to the induction of a range of antioxidant enzymes and detoxifying proteins which together help re-establish redox balance in the face of chronic oxidative insult (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012). One key hypothesis is that, in addition to the already well‐documented induction of cytosolic antioxidants such as HO‐1 and NQO1, Bardoxolone methyl may also promote the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3. SOD2 is the primary defense against superoxide radicals within the mitochondria, and PRDX3 plays a critical role in detoxifying hydrogen peroxide produced by mitochondrial respiration. Although direct data in RPE cells are currently lacking, studies in other cellular contexts have demonstrated that activation of Nrf2 results in the upregulation of a broad spectrum of antioxidant genes, and it is plausible that under the oxidative duress typical of dry AMD, similar effects would be observed in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
In vitro models simulating oxidative stress—such as exposure of RPE cells to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)—have shown that compounds with similar electrophilic properties, and indeed other members of the CDDO family like CDDO-Im, reduce the intracellular MitoSOX fluorescence signal, indicative of a reduction in mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Moreover, improvements in mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) have been correlated with such treatments, suggesting that these molecules can help maintain mitochondrial function under stressful conditions (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014). Such outcomes are highly relevant in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE has been implicated in disease progression. The anticipated outcomes, therefore, include a reduction in mtROS, restoration of Δψm, and subsequent preservation of RPE cellular integrity and function.  
Another positive aspect is the compound’s previously established oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic profile. Clinical studies in CKD patients have demonstrated that therapeutic plasma concentrations can be achieved with once-daily dosing. Although systemic administration in ocular diseases is not ideal, these data provide a strong pharmacological starting point for repurposing. In addition, if systemic toxicity remains a concern—as suggested by the cardiovascular signals in CKD trials—an alternative approach might involve localized ocular delivery (for instance, via intravitreal injection or by developing an ocular formulation) to achieve high retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

• Overall Evaluation  
In assessing Bardoxolone methyl for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry AMD, several critical points emerge that underline both its promise and the challenges that must be overcome.

Strengths:  
1. Strong Chemical Rationale and Potency:  
Bardoxolone methyl is a product of sophisticated medicinal chemistry, designed to overcome the limitations of natural triterpenoids like oleanolic acid by installing reactive electrophilic groups that significantly enhance its potency. This design specifically enables the activation of the Nrf2 pathway—a mechanism central to antioxidant defense—at very low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016). The high potency of Bardoxolone methyl as an Nrf2 activator is a significant advantage, particularly when considering that even subtle improvements in cellular antioxidant capacity can have a profound impact on chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD.

2. Broad Cytoprotective Mechanism:  
The mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl involves the disruption of the Keap1-Nrf2 complex via covalent modification of Keap1 cysteine residues, facilitating the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent transcriptional activation of a broad range of antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes (Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012). This broad cytoprotective response is particularly relevant to the RPE, where chronic oxidative stress has been implicated in cellular dysfunction and death. The possibility that Bardoxolone methyl may also induce mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3, although not yet directly confirmed in RPE, is an attractive hypothesis; such an effect would directly address the mitochondrial dysfunction that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).

3. Extensive Clinical Experience and Pharmacokinetic Data:  
Bardoxolone methyl has been evaluated in several clinical trials—most notably in the context of CKD and oncology—yielding a wealth of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and tolerability data. Its oral bioavailability, with a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing, is well documented (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). Although the systemic adverse events observed in these trials (such as cardiovascular-related events) present challenges for broad systemic administration, these data nonetheless offer a useful starting point for repurposing. The established clinical profile can inform dose-escalation studies and safety monitoring protocols should Bardoxolone methyl be advanced into ocular trials.

4. Support from Analogous Preclinical Models:  
Several studies in related models have demonstrated that synthetic triterpenoids can protect retinal tissue from oxidative damage. For example, experiments with CDDO-Im, a closely related analogue, have shown protective effects in retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury, including the attenuation of inflammatory responses and preservation of retinal structure (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Although these studies are not directly with Bardoxolone methyl, the mechanistic commonalities within this compound class support the notion that the same protective pathways can be harnessed in the context of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
1. Lack of Direct Evidence in RPE/Dry AMD Models:  
Despite the strong theoretical rationale, direct evidence that Bardoxolone methyl upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants (SOD2, PRDX3) in RPE cells is currently lacking. Most published data are derived from non-ocular cell types or from studies using other analogues such as CDDO-Im (Cai et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2014). It is therefore essential to perform specific in vitro studies in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress conditions to measure the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes and the functional status of mitochondria (e.g., Δψm, mtROS levels) following treatment with Bardoxolone methyl.

2. Safety Concerns from Prior Clinical Experience:  
A significant challenge in repurposing Bardoxolone methyl stems from its safety profile in systemic indications. The Phase III BEACON trial in CKD patients was halted due to an increased incidence of serious cardiovascular events, including heart failure and increased mortality (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the mechanisms underlying these adverse effects may be related to systemic fluid retention, off‐target reactivity, or other metabolic perturbations, they raise concerns about the safety of systemic administration. For ocular application, it may be necessary to consider alternative dosing strategies or localized delivery methods to avoid systemic exposure while still achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

3. Translational and Formulation Challenges:  
The unique anatomy and physiology of the eye introduce additional obstacles in drug repurposing. RPE cells reside in a relatively immune-privileged, isolated microenvironment behind the blood–retinal barrier. The pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration profiles of Bardoxolone methyl observed in systemic circulation may not directly translate to effective intraocular concentrations. Development of specialized ocular formulations—such as sustained-release intravitreal injections or topical applications that can traverse ocular barriers—will be critical for successful translation (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

4. Multifactorial Nature of AMD Pathogenesis:  
Dry AMD is a complex, multifactorial disease where oxidative stress is only one component of a broader pathogenic network that includes genetic predisposition, inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement system activation. While activation of the Nrf2 pathway can counteract oxidative stress and may have secondary anti-inflammatory effects, it is uncertain whether this single mechanism will be sufficient to alter the course of the disease. A combinatorial therapeutic strategy incorporating Nrf2 activation with other modalities might eventually be required to address the full spectrum of dry AMD pathology (Cheng et al., 2021; Thomas, 2012).

5. Dose-Dependent Effects and Narrow Therapeutic Window:  
Bardoxolone methyl exhibits highly dose-dependent pharmacology. At low doses, it predominantly activates Nrf2 and induces cytoprotective genes; however, as the dose increases, additional actions such as pro-apoptotic and cytotoxic effects emerge (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014). Determining the precise dose that is efficacious in RPE cells without triggering deleterious off-target effects will be crucial. This necessitates rigorous dose-ranging studies in preclinical models to define a therapeutic window that maximizes retinal protection while minimizing risks.

• Overall Evaluation and Recommendation  
In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD thanks to its well-characterized chemical design, potent induction of the Nrf2 pathway, and a broad cytoprotective mechanism that addresses many aspects of the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in RPE degeneration. The extensive clinical data from studies in CKD and oncology provide a valuable foundation for understanding its pharmacokinetics and systemic effects, while the underlying chemistry ensures high potency at low concentrations—features that are highly desirable when targeting a chronic, degenerative condition such as dry AMD (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Nonetheless, significant challenges remain. There is a conspicuous gap in the literature regarding the direct evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl in RPE cells and dry AMD models, particularly concerning its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes like SOD2 and PRDX3 and thereby mitigate mtROS damage. This gap must be addressed through targeted in vitro assays and in vivo animal studies that simulate the retinal environment and its chronic oxidative stress. Safety concerns, as evidenced by the cardiovascular events observed in CKD trials, underscore the need for caution; these risks may be minimized through localized ocular administration, but careful formulation and dosing studies will be required to establish an acceptable safety profile in the ocular context (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
Given the current state of evidence, it is recommended that Bardoxolone methyl be subjected to further preclinical evaluation in the context of dry AMD. Specifically, studies should focus on:  
 – Conducting detailed in vitro experiments in human RPE cell lines to assess whether exposure to Bardoxolone methyl under oxidative stress conditions leads to the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2 and PRDX3) and an associated decrease in mtROS (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
 – Evaluating the effects of Bardoxolone methyl on mitochondrial function (including measurements of Δψm, oxygen consumption rate, and mitochondrial integrity) in these cells.  
 – Adapting ocular-specific formulations that allow high local retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure, potentially using intravitreal or topical delivery methods, and conducting pharmacokinetic studies that establish retinal tissue exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).  
 – Testing the compound in animal models of dry AMD to determine whether the in vitro antioxidant and mitochondrial protective effects translate into preservation of RPE and photoreceptor structure and function over time (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
If these studies yield positive results that confirm the hypothesized upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved RPE function, Bardoxolone methyl could then be advanced to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Such trials would need to incorporate rigorous safety monitoring protocols to mitigate the known systemic adverse effects. A potential strategy may involve administering the drug in a localized manner or at doses that are effective in the eye but low enough to avoid triggering systemic electrophilic toxicity.

Overall, Bardoxolone methyl holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD based on its potent Nrf2-activating properties and the central role of oxidative stress in the disease’s pathogenesis. However, its development for an ocular indication will hinge on its ability to selectively and safely modulate the redox status of RPE cells while avoiding systemic side effects. A stepwise, targeted preclinical program that directly addresses these RPE-specific endpoints is therefore critical before consideration of clinical trials in the dry AMD patient population (Nakagami, 2016).

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl offers a strong mechanistic rationale as an Nrf2 activator with the theoretical capacity to upregulate mitochondrial defenses in RPE cells, further targeted studies are essential. The compound’s repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically attractive given the unmet need for effective therapies in this condition; however, the translational path is complex due to safety concerns observed in systemic trials and the lack of direct ocular data. A rigorous preclinical research plan—encompassing in vitro RPE studies, ocular pharmacokinetic assessments, and animal model validation—will be required to determine whether Bardoxolone methyl can be safely and effectively repurposed to preserve RPE function and slow the progression of dry AMD.

• Summary of Key Supporting Points  
– Bardoxolone methyl is a chemically engineered derivative of oleanolic acid that exploits electrophilic modifications to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016).  
– Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in oncology and CKD, though not in ocular disease, provides important pharmacokinetic and biological safety data that may be leveraged, with modifications, for ocular use (Nakagami, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022).  
– Its mechanism—covalent modification of Keap1 and subsequent nuclear translocation of Nrf2—leads to the transcriptional upregulation of cytoprotective genes, and it is hypothesized that this would include mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2, PRDX3), which are critical for mitigating oxidative damage in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
– Preclinical data with related triterpenoids in retinal models support the concept that Nrf2 activation can ameliorate oxidative stress and preserve retinal integrity, although direct data for Bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD are presently lacking (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
– Key challenges include the translation of systemic dosing to ocular delivery, the need to specifically validate mitochondrial protective effects in RPE cells, and the resolution of safety issues exemplified by prior cardiovascular signals in systemic trials (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

• Final Recommendation  
Based on the current literature review, Bardoxolone methyl emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its potent Nrf2 activation, broad cytoprotective potential, and a well-documented clinical PK profile. However, its repurposing for ocular application must be preceded by targeted preclinical studies that corroborate its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidants in RPE cells and to reduce mtROS while preserving mitochondrial function. These studies should also explore ocular-specific formulations and dosing regimens that minimize systemic exposure. Only after thorough validation in these preliminary investigations can Bardoxolone methyl be considered a credible candidate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. Given these considerations, the candidate warrants further investigation despite the existing translational and safety challenges inherent in repurposing a systemically active electrophilic compound for an ocular indication (Borella et al., 2019; Yagishita et al., 2020; Thomas, 2012).

Proposal for BAM15 (Sigma-Aldrich SML1888)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BAM15 (Sigma-Aldrich SML1888) is a synthetic, lipophilic mitochondrial uncoupling agent that was discovered and subsequently optimized to achieve a mild protonophoric effect on the inner mitochondrial membrane. As a member of the mitochondrial uncoupler class, BAM15 functions by facilitating proton leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane, thereby dissipating the proton motive force (Δψm) in a controlled manner. The key feature of this compound is its ability to reduce electron leakage from the electron transport chain (ETC) at complexes I and III without completely abolishing ATP synthesis. This is achieved by diminishing the mitochondrial membrane potential enough to lower the rate of superoxide generation while still maintaining sufficient ATP production for cellular energetics. Its synthetic nature and lipophilicity enable BAM15 to permeate the mitochondrial membrane rapidly, a property that distinguishes it from earlier, more toxic uncouplers such as 2,4-dinitrophenol or FCCP. The chemical architecture of BAM15 has been tailored to offer high mitochondrial targeting efficiency and a more favorable safety profile compared to traditional uncouplers. Mitochondrial uncouplers have been historically investigated in various research settings ranging from metabolic studies to neurodegenerative disease models, where their capacity to modulate bioenergetics and reduce oxidative stress has been exploited (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Although BAM15 has not yet been directly tested in clinical settings for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), there exists a robust foundational literature supporting the therapeutic targeting of mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. Numerous studies have detailed that mitochondrial defects in RPE are a central mediator of AMD pathogenesis, with evidence pointing to disrupted mitochondrial architecture, decreased mitochondrial mass, and increased mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) damage in human donor tissues (Fisher & Ferrington, 2018). In this context, mitochondrial uncouplers have been explored experimentally to compensate for excessive electron leakage and overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In vitro and in vivo studies using other uncoupling agents such as FCCP have demonstrated that inducing mild uncoupling can stimulate protective mitochondrial quality control pathways including fission, fusion, and mitophagy; these processes have been shown to restore bioenergetic balance in diseased RPE cells (Fisher, 2022; Fisher et al., 2022). In the broader field of drug development, mitochondrial-targeted compounds such as MTP-131 (Elamipretide) have even advanced into early-phase clinical trials for AMD and related retinal neurodegenerative diseases, establishing a strong precedent for targeting the mitochondrial compartment in ocular pathologies (Cousins, 2015; Butcher, 2022). Meanwhile, BAM15 itself has demonstrated therapeutic potential in other disease models including obesity, sepsis, and neurodegeneration, wherein its mild uncoupling properties reduced mitochondrial oxidative stress and improved metabolic and inflammatory parameters (Xiong et al., 2023). However, despite these encouraging attributes and the compelling rationale derived from the role of mtROS in AMD, BAM15’s usage in the context of ocular diseases, particularly dry AMD, remains largely untested to date (Jang et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
BAM15 exerts its effects by acting as a protonophore that facilitates proton translocation across the mitochondrial inner membrane. Under normal conditions, the electron transport chain generates a high proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis; however, this gradient is also responsible for the partial leakage of electrons, which react with molecular oxygen to form superoxide radicals. BAM15’s mechanism is predicated on “mild uncoupling,” which entails a limited dissipation of the proton motive force to reduce the probability of electron slippage at complexes I and III without compromising the entirety of ATP generation. At the molecular level, BAM15 inserts into the mitochondrial inner membrane where its lipophilic and protonophoric properties allow it to shuttle protons from the intermembrane space back into the matrix. This process effectively lowers the mitochondrial membrane potential, diminishing the driving force for electron leakage and concomitant ROS formation (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025).  

Furthermore, BAM15’s action is linked with secondary effects on key intracellular signaling pathways. The reduction in ATP production, while carefully moderated, can activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a critical sensor of cellular energy status. Upon activation, AMPK upregulates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), which is instrumental in driving mitochondrial biogenesis and enhancing overall mitochondrial quality control. These processes are particularly relevant in the context of AMD, where impaired mitophagy and mitochondrial turnover have been well documented in RPE cells (Fisher, 2022). BAM15 has also been shown in other tissues to reduce the release of mtDNA into the cytoplasm—a phenomenon that ordinarily triggers NLRP3 inflammasome activation and the subsequent production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Xiong et al., 2023). With reduced mtROS production and lower inflammasome activation, BAM15 could potentially ameliorate chronic inflammatory responses that exacerbate cellular degeneration in the RPE. Importantly, the uncoupling induced by BAM15 is dose-dependent; the compound must be delivered at concentrations that ensure only a modest reduction in Δψm, thus allowing ATP production to remain functionally intact while still mitigating the adverse effects of excessive ROS (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed experimental paradigm focusing on chronic stress conditions typical of dry AMD, BAM15 is anticipated to exert several beneficial effects on RPE cells. Fundamentally, the agent is hypothesized to lower mitochondrial ROS production by reducing the proton motive force sufficiently to minimize electron leakage without precipitating a full collapse of the energy-transducing gradient. In primary RPE cultures, where mitochondrial dysfunction and bioenergetic deficits have already been documented as key contributors to disease progression (Fisher & Ferrington, 2018; Fisher, 2022), BAM15 is expected to normalize several bioenergetic parameters. The effects should include improved basal respiration and maximal respiratory capacity, as well as better spare respiratory capacity, indicative of a healthier mitochondrial network capable of handling metabolic stress.  

Reduction of ROS levels would likely lead to a decrease in oxidative modifications of lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids within the mitochondria. Given that mtDNA damage is a well-established marker of AMD severity and has been implicated in triggering inflammatory cascades via inflammasome activation, a reduction in mtDNA damage—and its consequent release—would be a direct cellular benefit of BAM15 application (Fisher, 2022). In parallel, the therapeutic intervention is expected to attenuate the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. As studies in AMD have shown that mtROS and mtDNA release can prime inflammasome development and lead to the secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, BAM15’s action could diminish these pro-inflammatory signals. This anti-inflammatory effect is particularly crucial in the context of dry AMD, where chronic sterile inflammation contributes to retinal pigment epithelium loss and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration (Fisher, 2022).  

Moreover, the activation of AMPK and subsequent engagement of PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis may help re-establish cellular homeostasis in RPE cells that have been compromised by prolonged oxidative stress. The fine-tuning of mitochondrial quality control—through enhanced mitophagy and the removal of damaged mitochondria—is expected to contribute to overall cell survival and to slow the progression of AMD pathology. In an in vitro assay, one would anticipate a measurable decrease in ROS levels, reduced markers of inflammasome activation, improved mitochondrial morphology, and increased expression of genes involved in mitochondrial repair and biogenesis. Since the RPE expresses a full complement of metabolic regulators (including AMPK and the NLRP3 inflammasome components) and is highly susceptible to oxidative stress due to its role in photoreceptor support, the expected effect of BAM15 aligns well with the molecular pathology observed in AMD (Fisher & Ferrington, 2018; Fisher, 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of BAM15 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several strengths but also underscores significant areas requiring further investigation. One of the chief strengths of BAM15 is its mechanism of mild mitochondrial uncoupling, which is theoretically suited to ameliorating the bioenergetic deficits and oxidative stress characteristic of AMD. The extensive literature on mitochondrial dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium supports the idea that reducing mtROS production can have a direct, favorable impact on cell survival and function. Studies have repeatedly demonstrated that RPE cells from AMD donors exhibit compromised mitochondrial architecture, increased mtDNA damage, and heightened levels of ROS, all of which contribute to inflammasome activation and chronic inflammation (Fisher & Ferrington, 2018). BAM15’s capacity to modulate these parameters in other tissues—by reducing electron leakage and lowering superoxide generation—provides a sound mechanistic basis for its potential efficacy in the RPE (Xiong et al., 2023). Moreover, the activation of AMPK and the ensuing stimulation of mitochondrial biogenesis represent additional advantages because these processes are crucial for cellular recovery and long-term tissue homeostasis (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025).

Another notable strength lies in BAM15’s relatively favorable safety profile when compared to prototypical uncouplers. Early evidence from studies in hepatocytes, neurons, and other models suggests that BAM15 does not cause dramatic drops in ATP levels or induce significant cytotoxicity, provided that dosing is carefully controlled. This is particularly relevant for the RPE, a cell type with a high energy demand where excessive uncoupling could lead to unintended deleterious effects. In addition, the possibility that BAM15 could mitigate inflammasome activation by curtailing the release of mitochondrial DNA into the cytosol offers an attractive method for diminishing pro-inflammatory cascades known to drive AMD progression (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025).

Despite these advantages, several weaknesses must be acknowledged. Currently, there is a conspicuous lack of direct experimental evidence supporting the use of BAM15 in RPE cells or in in vivo models of dry AMD. While there is compelling rationale derived from studies in other tissues and disease models, the translation of these findings to the ocular environment remains unproven (Jang et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2023). The unique physiology of the retina and the challenges associated with ocular drug delivery—such as achieving sufficient bioavailability in the RPE layer without inducing off-target effects—represent significant hurdles that must be addressed early in preclinical development (Ji et al., 2021; Fisher, 2022).

Another potential limitation is the inherent risk associated with mitochondrial uncoupling. Although BAM15 is designed for mild uncoupling, the fine line between therapeutic and toxic effects is narrow. Overly robust uncoupling could compromise ATP production, leading to energy deficits in RPE cells that are already under metabolic stress due to their high phagocytic activity and constant exposure to photic stress. Therefore, precise dosing regimens and thorough kinetic studies will be critical to ensure that BAM15 exerts its antioxidative benefits without precipitating additional energy crises (Fisher, 2022; Xiong et al., 2023).

Furthermore, while BAM15 has demonstrated promising anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects in other models, the protracted nature of dry AMD necessitates long-term safety and efficacy evaluations. Chronic administration of a mitochondrial uncoupler requires careful monitoring to prevent possible compensatory mechanisms that may reduce efficacy over time or generate unforeseen side effects. In addition, any potential interactions with other cellular pathways in the RPE—such as those regulating lipid metabolism, phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, and the integrity of the blood-retinal barrier—must be investigated comprehensively (Fisher, 2022; Fisher & Ferrington, 2018).

An important consideration in the evaluation of BAM15 is the need for optimization of its ocular delivery. The challenges associated with achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina without systemic exposure may necessitate innovative formulations or localized delivery methods, such as intravitreal injections or sustained-release ocular implants. Such strategies will be essential to ensure that the beneficial mitochondrial effects are confined to the RPE while minimizing the risk of systemic side effects (Ji et al., 2021; Fisher, 2022).

In summary, BAM15 holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its unique mechanism of inducing mild mitochondrial uncoupling. Its ability to reduce mtROS generation, limit subsequent inflammasome activation, and potentially stimulate compensatory mitochondrial biogenesis aligns well with the pathogenic mechanisms underlying RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. The strengths of BAM15 include its favorable efficacy profile in reducing oxidative stress in other models, its potential anti-inflammatory benefits, and the mechanistic rationale provided by extensive studies on mitochondrial dysfunction in AMD. On the other hand, its weaknesses lie in the dearth of direct preclinical evidence in ocular systems, the challenges of ocular drug delivery, and the inherent risks associated with mitochondrial uncoupling if not precisely controlled.

Going forward, it is imperative to initiate a series of targeted in vitro experiments using primary RPE and iPSC-derived RPE models under chronic oxidative stress conditions that mimic dry AMD. These studies should focus on measuring key parameters including mitochondrial membrane potential, ROS production, ATP levels, mitochondrial morphology, and markers of inflammasome activation such as NLRP3 and IL-1β. Concurrently, dose-response studies will be essential to determine the optimal concentration range for BAM15 that affords maximum protective effects without compromising the energetic needs of the cell. Should these initial studies yield favorable results, subsequent in vivo experiments in established animal models of dry AMD would be warranted to evaluate the retinal therapeutic index, ocular tolerability, and long-term benefits of BAM15.

Moreover, given the multifunctional nature of mitochondrial uncoupling, future studies might explore combination approaches wherein BAM15 is administered alongside other mitochondrial-targeted agents (such as SS-31 or antioxidants like N-acetyl-L-cysteine) to synergistically enhance mitochondrial quality control and reduce oxidative stress. Such combination therapies may offer a more comprehensive approach to tackling the complex bioenergetic and inflammatory challenges posed by dry AMD. The incorporation of advanced drug delivery technologies, including nanoparticle-based systems or sustained-release formulations, would further refine the therapeutic potential of BAM15 by enabling localized, precision targeting of the RPE and minimizing systemic exposure.

Overall, while BAM15 is not yet a validated therapy for dry AMD, the compelling theoretical framework and encouraging data from other disease models provide a strong foundation for its further exploration as a mitochondrial-targeted therapeutic. The decision to advance BAM15 into the preclinical pipeline for dry AMD should be accompanied by rigorous, mechanistically driven studies aimed at elucidating its full pharmacological profile in RPE cells. The potential to mitigate mitochondrial oxidative stress and inflammatory cascades through mild uncoupling represents an innovative strategy that could address the central bioenergetic crisis observed in dry AMD pathology (Fisher & Ferrington, 2018; Cousins, 2015).  

In conclusion, BAM15 emerges as an exciting candidate worthy of further investigation owing to its mechanistically sound approach to reducing mitochondrial ROS and dampening inflammasome activation in the context of RPE dysfunction. Key challenges remain, including establishing the appropriate dosing regimen, optimizing ocular delivery, and verifying long-term safety and efficacy in AMD-specific models. Nevertheless, with its favorable molecular profile and the breadth of supporting literature on mitochondrial dysfunction in AMD, BAM15 holds considerable promise as a novel therapeutic approach that may ultimately contribute to preserving retinal function and preventing vision loss in patients with dry AMD (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025; Fisher, 2022).

Proposal for S1QEL-1.1 (Cayman Chemical #25658)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
S1QEL-1.1 is a small synthetic molecule identified as a “suppressor of site IQ electron leak” (S1QEL) that has been developed to target mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production selectively at the quinone‐reaction (IQ) site of Complex I. This compound belongs to a distinct chemical class uncovered through high‐throughput screening efforts of over 635,000 compounds, which yielded two primary structural families: the thiazole‐type S1QEL1 series (of which S1QEL-1.1 is a leading representative) and the piperazine‐type S1QEL2 series (Banba et al., 2019). As a thiazole‐type compound, S1QEL-1.1 was chemically synthesized and subsequently optimized using structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies; derivatives such as S1QEL1.1_D1–D3 were generated to probe the essential chemical features required for function (Banba et al., 2019). In addition, photoaffinity probe derivatives ([125I]S1QEL1.1_PD1 and PD2) have been prepared to map its binding site in Complex I, underscoring both its synthetic tractability and the sophistication of the medicinal chemistry approach used in its development (Banba et al., 2019). As a class, S1QEL compounds have been primarily engineered to modulate mitochondrial ROS by selectively suppressing superoxide production at the IQ site without broad‐spectrum inhibition of electron transfer, a profile that distinguishes them from canonical Complex I inhibitors such as rotenone and piericidin A (Wong et al., 2019). S1QEL-1.1 is commercially available (for example, through Cayman Chemical under catalog number #25658), which not only facilitates its procurement for research but also supports its potential repurposing as a therapeutic candidate—particularly in indications where mitochondrial oxidative stress is regarded as a key pathogenic factor.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, S1QEL compounds have been extensively characterized in biochemical assays using isolated mitochondria and submitochondrial particles. In these studies, S1QEL-1.1 and other members of the class were shown to potently suppress superoxide and hydrogen peroxide production specifically from the IQ site during conditions that favor reverse electron transfer, while sparing forward electron transport and thus preserving overall mitochondrial electron flow and ATP production (Wong et al., 2019). Preclinical studies in in vivo models have demonstrated the protective effects of S1QEL compounds in varied contexts; for instance, stress-induced stem cell hyperplasia in the Drosophila gut was ameliorated by S1QEL application, and in perfused mouse heart preparations, S1QELs reduced ischemia–reperfusion injury (Banba et al., 2019). Although these examples involve cardiac and developmental models, the central concept—that selective suppression of mitochondrial ROS can confer tissue protection—has broad implications for diseases where redox imbalance is a critical driver. Importantly, while there are numerous reports underscoring the utility of S1QELs in modulating mitochondrial ROS in neurons, cardiomyocytes, and skeletal muscle mitochondria (Banba et al., 2019), a direct application of S1QEL-1.1 to ocular disorders such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not yet been documented. However, given that dry AMD is characterized by heightened oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where Complex I activity plays a central role in cellular metabolism and survival, the extension of S1QEL-1.1 into this field is a compelling and logical repurposing avenue (Banba et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, S1QEL-1.1 acts by selectively suppressing the production of superoxide at the Complex I IQ site—a major source of mitochondrial ROS under conditions of reverse electron transfer. Mechanistic studies using bovine heart submitochondrial particles have revealed that S1QEL-1.1 achieves its effect by modulating the redox chemistry in the quinone-binding region while leaving the NADH oxidation (and hence overall electron flux) largely intact (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019). Detailed photoaffinity labeling studies using radiolabeled derivatives ([125I]S1QEL1.1_PD1 and PD2) have mapped its binding to the ND1 subunit of Complex I, particularly near the matrix-side loop connecting transmembrane helices 5 and 6, which is distinct from the canonical quinone-binding pocket typically occupied by classical inhibitors such as rotenone (Banba et al., 2019). This binding does not fully block electron entry nor does it globally inhibit forward electron transfer, because the inhibitory potency for suppressing ROS generation is approximately 1–2 orders of magnitude lower than that required to inhibit basal respiratory activity (Wong et al., 2019). It has been proposed that the binding of S1QEL-1.1 induces subtle conformational changes in Complex I that reduce the probability of electron leakage to oxygen, thereby diminishing superoxide production without altering the essential catalytic cycle of electron transport. Furthermore, the mechanism is direction-dependent: S1QEL-1.1 exhibits significantly stronger inhibition of reverse electron transfer-associated ROS production than forward electron transfer, a property that has been linked to structural differences in the ND1 subunit that influence the flux of electrons under various bioenergetic states (Banba et al., 2019). Notably, competitive studies have demonstrated that the presence of S1QEL-1.1 reduces the inhibitory potency of established quinone-site inhibitors like piericidin A and rotenone, supporting the concept that S1QEL-1.1 interacts directly with, and alters, the conformation of, the quinone-binding region (Wong et al., 2019). Overall, the mechanism of action of S1QEL-1.1 is a fine modulation of the electron leak in Complex I—targeting the very site responsible for superoxide generation—without compromising the bioenergetic integrity of the mitochondrion (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019).

Expected Effect:  
Under the hypothesis proposed by the research team, S1QEL-1.1 is expected to yield significant benefits in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by acting on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) mitochondria. In dry AMD, chronic light exposure, along with inflammatory and complement-mediated stress, leads to persistent mitochondrial dysfunction and escalated ROS production. Since the IQ site of Complex I has been identified as a major source of mitochondrial superoxide production—particularly under conditions of reverse electron transfer—S1QEL-1.1 is anticipated to selectively lower ROS output from this critical site in RPE mitochondria, thereby reducing oxidative damage (Wong et al., 2019).  
In a proposed RPE model of chronic light-induced stress, application of S1QEL-1.1 would be expected to attenuate mitochondrial superoxide formation significantly while preserving forward electron flux, NADH oxidation, and overall mitochondrial ATP synthesis. This preservation of bioenergetic function is crucial because the RPE relies on high levels of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation to support essential cellular functions, including the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and the recycling of visual pigments. Precedents for such effects have been documented in cardiomyocyte and neuronal models, where S1QEL-1.1 efficiently reduced ROS without impairing mitochondrial respiration, thereby contributing to tissue protection under stress (Banba et al., 2019).  
At the molecular level, by binding near the matrix side of the ND1 subunit and inducing conformational changes within the quinone-binding region, S1QEL-1.1 is projected to decrease electron leak from Complex I. This reduction in superoxide generation will likely translate into a lower burden of hydrogen peroxide and peroxynitrite formation, thus mitigating oxidative damage to mitochondrial and cellular components. The expected outcome is a protective effect in RPE cells under constant oxidative assault from light exposure and inflammation, ultimately contributing to the slowing or potential halting of dry AMD progression (Banba et al., 2019).  
Given that RPE cells express all key Complex I subunits, including the ND1 subunit that has been implicated as the binding site for S1QEL-1.1, it is reasonable to extrapolate that the expression profile in RPE cells is conducive to the compound’s mechanism of action (Banba et al., 2019). Moreover, because dysfunction of Complex I and excess mitochondrial ROS production are established features of age-related degeneration in the retina, selectively targeting the IQ site with S1QEL-1.1 represents an attractive strategy to restore redox balance and improve cell survival in the RPE (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
S1QEL-1.1 stands out as a highly promising drug candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its unique ability to selectively suppress mitochondrial ROS production at the Complex I IQ site without impacting the overall electron transport and ATP production. One of the major strengths of S1QEL-1.1 is its mechanism of action, which has been elegantly elucidated: it binds to a region of the ND1 subunit, distinct from the classical quinone-binding pocket, and modulates the rate constants of electron leak specifically associated with superoxide formation. This allosteric mechanism ensures that while pathological ROS production is curtailed, the critical functions of mitochondria—such as NADH oxidation and ATP synthesis—continue without significant perturbation (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019). Such properties are particularly advantageous in the context of dry AMD, where maintaining robust cellular bioenergetics in the RPE is essential to counteract chronic stress from light exposure and inflammation.

Another strength lies in its direction-dependent inhibitory profile. S1QEL-1.1 is capable of exerting a more potent suppression of reverse electron transfer-induced ROS generation compared to forward electron transfer, thereby offering a more refined modulation of mitochondrial activity. This selective action is crucial in tissues such as the RPE that must continuously manage oxidative stress while still performing high levels of metabolic activity (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019).

Furthermore, the extensive preclinical evaluation of S1QEL-1.1 in non-ocular tissues—including models of ischemia–reperfusion injury and stress-induced stem cell hyperplasia—provides a robust foundation for its potential repurposing. Although these studies were conducted in cardiac and developmental systems, the underlying principle—that targeted suppression of mitochondrial ROS can mitigate tissue damage—translates well to the pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD (Banba et al., 2019).  

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. The therapeutic candidate has not yet been evaluated in any ocular or retinal models; therefore, its pharmacokinetics, tissue penetration, and long-term safety within the unique microenvironment of the eye remain to be established. The blood–retina barrier poses a significant hurdle for systemically administered compounds, and specialized delivery methods (such as intravitreal injection or targeted nanoparticle formulations) may be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE (Banba et al., 2019). Additionally, although S1QEL-1.1 exhibits a favorable profile in isolated mitochondria and other cell types, chronic inhibition of mitochondrial ROS could potentially disrupt normal redox signaling mechanisms that are vital for cellular adaptation and homeostasis. Thus, determining the optimal dosing range that provides maximal protective effect without interfering with physiological signaling is critical (Wong et al., 2019).

Another potential limitation is the narrow therapeutic window in which S1QEL-1.1 operates. Preclinical data indicate that while low concentrations effectively suppress pathological superoxide production, higher concentrations may begin to inhibit forward electron transport, which could be deleterious in energy-demanding tissues like the RPE (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019). This necessitates precise dose optimization and comprehensive toxicity studies prior to advancing into clinical trials.

Finally, despite a strong mechanistic rationale and promising biochemical data from non-ocular models, there is still an absence of direct evidence for efficacy in models of dry AMD. Translational research is required to validate whether the selective ROS suppression observed in vitro will translate into measurable therapeutic benefits in the context of retinal degeneration. In particular, the interplay between reduced mitochondrial ROS and the modulation of complement activation or inflammatory cascades in the RPE must be thoroughly investigated (Banba et al., 2019).

In summary, S1QEL-1.1 is a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its robust and selective mechanism of action in reducing mitochondrial ROS production at the Complex I IQ site while preserving oxidative phosphorylation. The strengths of its biochemical profile, including direction-dependent inhibition and a well-characterized binding site on Complex I, provide a strong scientific rationale for its use in a redox-driven degenerative disease. However, significant gaps remain in translating these findings to the ocular context, including challenges related to delivery across the blood–retina barrier, long-term safety in the retina, and the need for dedicated efficacy studies in dry AMD models. Addressing these issues through further in vitro experimentation using RPE cell lines under chronic light-induced stress, followed by targeted in vivo animal studies, will be essential to determine whether S1QEL-1.1 can fulfill its potential as a novel therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019).

Overall, while the existing literature provides a solid foundation in favor of the underlying mechanism and general protective effects of S1QEL-1.1 in reducing mitochondrial ROS, the candidate’s transition into an effective therapy for dry AMD will require extensive further research to ensure ocular efficacy, optimal dosing, and safety over long-term administration. These steps are critical to fully validate S1QEL-1.1 as a viable treatment option in the challenging and complex landscape of age-related macular degeneration (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019).

Proposal for Tat-Beclin 1 peptide (Tocris #4344)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Tat‐Beclin 1 is a synthetic peptide designed to induce autophagy by harnessing a key region of the Beclin 1 protein, which is essential for the initiation of autophagosome formation (He et al., 2022). This candidate was originally derived by fusing a peptide fragment from Beclin 1, typically encompassing residues in the range of 267–284, with the HIV‐1 Tat transduction domain (Saqcena, 2018), thereby rendering it cell‐permeable and capable of entering diverse cell types. The synthesis and design of Tat‐Beclin 1 focus on exploiting the naturally occurring autophagy machinery by facilitating the release of inhibitory factors bound to Beclin 1 and enhancing its interactions with class III PI3K complexes (He et al., 2022). As a member of the therapeutic class of autophagy inducers, Tat‐Beclin 1 shares mechanistic commonalities with other peptides such as the stapled derivatives (e.g., Tat‐SP4) that have been developed to improve binding affinity and structural stability (Gao, 2023; Gao, 2023). This class of compounds has been widely investigated for their ability to promote autophagy in cellular models of cancer, neurodegeneration, and infection, and the peptide’s design rests on principles that have proven effective in enhancing cellular clearance mechanisms in several pathological contexts (He et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Tat‐Beclin 1 has been extensively characterized in preclinical studies as an inducer of autophagy in various cell types including cancer cells, neuronal cells, and immune cells (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). In early studies, it demonstrated potent autophagy‐stimulating effects by enhancing the transformation of LC3‐I to LC3‐II and by decreasing levels of the autophagic substrate p62, thereby leading to augmented autophagic flux (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013). Moreover, experimental applications have shown that Tat‐Beclin 1 can decrease viral titers in infection models such as those involving West Nile virus and chikungunya virus, and it has been explored for promoting autophagic clearance in cancer models, particularly in breast cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma (He et al., 2022; Gao, 2023). Although there is abundant evidence supporting its utility in managing proteotoxic stress and cellular damage in models of neurodegeneration and cancer, direct applications of Tat‐Beclin 1 for treating dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) have not been explicitly reported (Boland et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016). Nevertheless, separate studies indicate that proper autophagy in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is critical for cellular viability and resistance to oxidative stress, where impaired autophagy contributes to the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as A2E and lipofuscin that are implicated in AMD (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Hence, while Tat‐Beclin 1 has not been directly applied in AMD models thus far, its mechanism of promoting clearance of damaged organelles and misfolded proteins provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD treatment.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Tat‐Beclin 1 functions by specifically interacting with Beclin 1, a core component of the Class III PI3K complex that regulates autophagosome nucleation (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). In its inactive state, Beclin 1 is sequestered by negative regulatory proteins such as GAPR‐1, which limits its availability for autophagic initiation. Tat‐Beclin 1 is designed to bind to these inhibitory regulators, thereby liberating Beclin 1 and enabling it to participate in the formation of the PI3K complex necessary for phagophore formation (Ha & Kim, 2016; He et al., 2022). This intervention effectively shifts the balance toward autophagy induction by enhancing the generation of autophagosomes and promoting lysosomal degradation of intracellular cargo. Furthermore, research has demonstrated that Tat‐Beclin 1 increases the conversion of LC3‐I to LC3‐II—a hallmark of autophagosome formation—and has been shown to lower p62 levels, which underscores its role in boosting autophagic flux (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013; Si et al., 2023). Additionally, the peptide’s cell‐penetrating Tat domain facilitates its entry into cells and ensures its functional delivery to intracellular compartments, which is critical for engaging the autophagic machinery even in cells with limited uptake capabilities (Saqcena, 2018; He et al., 2022). Through these molecular interactions, Tat‐Beclin 1 not only enhances general autophagy but has also been reported to drive selective autophagic processes such as mitophagy, thereby promoting the turnover of damaged mitochondria (He et al., 2022; Frost et al., 2014). This mechanistic detail is particularly relevant in conditions of oxidative stress where dysfunctional mitochondria accumulate and contribute to cell death, as has been observed in RPE cells during the progression of dry AMD (Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the therapeutic hypothesis posits that Tat‐Beclin 1 will promote autophagy initiation in RPE cells to facilitate the turnover of damaged organelles—including mitochondria—that accumulate as a result of chronic oxidative stress (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). This enhanced autophagic clearance is expected to mitigate the cytotoxic effects associated with the buildup of toxic aggregates such as A2E and lipofuscin, which are known to drive RPE cell dysfunction and death (Zhang et al., 2015; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Experimental evidence from studies on RPE cells has documented that robust autophagic activity is critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis in the face of oxidative and metabolic insults (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, by increasing autophagic flux, Tat‐Beclin 1 should theoretically lead to a reduction in cellular stress markers and an improvement in mitochondrial quality control mechanisms, thereby preventing the initiation of apoptotic cascades in RPE cells (Saqcena, 2018). In cellular assays, the expected outcome would include an enhanced LC3‐II/LC3‐I ratio, decreased levels of p62, improved lysosomal function, and ultimately enhanced cell viability under oxidative stress conditions (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013; Si et al., 2023). Notably, the efficacy of autophagy induction in rescuing RPE cellular function is supported by literature where pharmacological activation of autophagy—such as through rapamycin or inhibition of mTOR pathways—has been shown to protect RPE cells from degeneration (Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020). Given the inherent ability of Tat‐Beclin 1 to stimulate autophagy in other cellular models, it is reasonable to expect that similar benefits would be observed upon its application to RPE cells, leading to a deceleration of dry AMD pathology by maintaining mitochondrial turnover and preventing the accumulation of deleterious substrates.

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall potential of Tat‐Beclin 1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD lies in its well‐defined mechanism of action, which directly targets the autophagic machinery through interactions with Beclin 1 (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). One of the primary strengths of this candidate is its demonstrated versatility across different disease models, where enhancement of autophagy has led to reduced apoptosis, improved clearance of toxic protein aggregates, and mitigation of cellular stress in both cancer and neurodegenerative contexts (He et al., 2022; Boland et al., 2018). In the specific arena of RPE cell biology, multiple studies have established that autophagic dysfunction is a hallmark of AMD progression and that stimulating autophagy can improve cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, by repurposing Tat‐Beclin 1 for dry AMD, there exists a compelling translational rationale based on mechanistic insights derived from both in vitro and in vivo studies in other systems.

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. Despite extensive preclinical evidence in other domains, there is a lack of direct experimental data demonstrating the efficacy of Tat‐Beclin 1 in ocular models or in RPE-specific assays (He et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2016). This gap in the literature necessitates rigorous validation in relevant RPE cell culture systems and animal models of dry AMD to confirm that the peptide’s autophagy-inducing effects translate to meaningful therapeutic benefits for ocular health. In addition, the potential for overactivation of autophagy poses a safety concern, as excessive autophagic flux can lead to autophagic cell death or unintended degradation of essential cellular components (Pinelli et al., 2025; Peraro et al., 2017). Precise dosing and delivery strategies will therefore be critical to ensure that Tat‐Beclin 1 achieves a balance between sufficient autophagy induction and preservation of RPE cell integrity. 

Pharmacokinetic and biodistribution challenges also remain to be addressed, especially given the unique anatomical barriers of the eye. Although the Tat transduction domain confers robust cell penetration, the stability, half-life, and clearance of the peptide in ocular tissues have yet to be thoroughly investigated (Saqcena, 2018; He et al., 2022). Moreover, the route of administration—potentially through intravitreal injection or topical delivery—must be optimized to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE without eliciting adverse immune responses or off-target effects. It is also important to note that while the autophagy-stimulating effects of Tat‐Beclin 1 have been well documented in various cell types, the specific context of chronic oxidative stress and metabolite accumulation in the aged RPE represents a distinct microenvironment that may influence peptide efficacy (Frost et al., 2014; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Zhang et al., 2015).

Another consideration is the heterogeneity inherent in dry AMD pathology, where oxidative injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammatory processes all contribute to disease progression. Although enhancing autophagy could address multiple facets of the disease, the interplay between autophagic flux and other cellular pathways—such as inflammation and lipid metabolism—remains complex and may necessitate combination therapies for optimal outcomes (Zhang et al., 2020; Pinelli et al., 2025). Nonetheless, leveraging the established protective role of autophagy in RPE cells provides a solid foundation for further research on Tat‐Beclin 1, and its repurposing could represent a novel strategy to counteract the multifactorial stressors associated with dry AMD.

In summary, Tat‐Beclin 1 presents a mechanism-driven approach for inducing autophagy that is grounded in sound biochemical principles and supported by extensive preclinical studies in other disease contexts (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). Its ability to prompt autophagosome formation, enhance mitochondrial turnover, and clear toxic protein aggregates aligns well with the cellular deficits observed in dry AMD, particularly in the RPE. The cumulative literature underscores the therapeutic promise of autophagy-inducing peptides in mitigating oxidative stress and improving cellular viability (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020). However, the lack of direct data in AMD-focused models, potential risks associated with overactivation of autophagy, and the need for refined ocular delivery methods represent critical hurdles that must be overcome through further research. 

Given the potential benefits and the mechanistic rationale underpinning its use, Tat‐Beclin 1 merits further investigation in preclinical RPE models, with attention to dose optimization, delivery strategies, and long-term safety assessments in the context of retinal degeneration. Ultimately, if these challenges can be addressed, Tat‐Beclin 1 could emerge as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD by restoring cellular homeostasis and halting the progression of RPE degeneration. This comprehensive evaluation therefore supports the continued exploration of Tat‐Beclin 1’s therapeutic potential while highlighting the necessity for rigorous validation in ocular-specific experimental paradigms (Frost et al., 2014; Saqcena, 2018; Boland et al., 2018; Frost et al., 2014).
