Proposal for XJB-5-131 (Sigma-Aldrich SML1115)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
XJB-5-131 is a synthetic mitochondria‐targeted nitroxide antioxidant that was developed by conjugating a redox‐active nitroxide moiety (derived from TEMPO, 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl) to a mitochondrial‐targeting peptide fragment derived from gramicidin S (often described in the literature as a hemigramicidin or alkene peptide isostere) (Liu et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012). This design harnesses the properties of the nitroxide, which is capable of catalytically scavenging reactive oxygen and lipid radicals through cycling between its nitroxide, hydroxylamine, and oxoammonium states, and the targeting moiety that enhances its lipid membrane permeability while concentrating the compound specifically in mitochondrial membranes (Wipf et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). The neutral charge of XJB-5-131 confers an advantage because it permits mitochondrial uptake independent of membrane potential, a feature that distinguishes it from the positively charged mitochondria-targeted antioxidants such as MitoQ (Robinson, 2012; Wipf et al., 2022). Moreover, fluorescent derivatives (e.g., BODIPY-labeled analogs) have been used to confirm its preferential accumulation in mitochondria by co-localization with mitochondrial markers, demonstrating an approximately 600-fold enrichment relative to the cytosol in some animal models (Wipf et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). Overall, XJB-5-131 belongs to the class of mitochondria-targeted nitroxides, a class that has been extensively studied for its ability to modulate oxidative stress in cellular and animal models across a variety of tissues (Xun et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, XJB-5-131 has been the subject of preclinical investigation in several models of oxidative stress-related injury. It was originally developed to protect neuronal mitochondria and has been evaluated in models of Huntington’s disease, where it mitigated somatic instability and toxicity by reducing oxidative DNA damage and delaying motor decline (Liu et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). In various studies, XJB-5-131 demonstrated robust efficacy in reducing mitochondrial lipid peroxidation and preserving electron transport chain function in brain, neuronal, and even cardiac cell models (Robinson, 2012; Wipf et al., 2022). Additionally, its use in spinal cord injury models has shown that it can attenuate cardiolipin oxidation and reduce the activation of apoptotic cascades, leading to decreased lesion sizes and improved functional recovery (Ji et al., 2015; Robinson, 2012). There is also evidence of its application in models of ischemia–reperfusion injury, where its ability to blunt the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) was associated with neuroprotection (Xun et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022). Outside of central nervous system paradigms, related mitochondria-targeted nitroxides have been applied in experimental settings addressing ferroptosis and other oxidative stress pathologies (Zhang et al., 2024; Xun et al., 2022). However, despite its established role in neurological and other high-oxidative stress tissues, there is no direct published record – within the context of the available literature – demonstrating that XJB-5-131 has been used to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or any retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)-specific diseases (Wipf et al., 2022). Nonetheless, its pharmacological profile suggests potential applicability in settings where chronic oxidative stress drives pathology.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism by which XJB-5-131 exerts its effects is twofold. First, the nitroxide moiety functions as a redox-active electron scavenger. Under oxidative stress, the nitroxide group readily interconverts with its hydroxylamine and oxoammonium forms; this redox cycling is capable of neutralizing superoxide anions (O2•–) by oxidizing them to molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, effectively mimicking the activity of superoxide dismutase (SOD) (Wipf et al., 2022). Additionally, the hydroxylamine state can donate a hydrogen atom to terminate radical chain reactions, thereby neutralizing lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate lipid peroxidation – a process central to drusen formation and RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Robinson, 2012; Xun et al., 2022). Second, the gramicidin-derived delivery moiety imparts mitochondrial selectivity due to its structural mimicry of naturally occurring cyclic peptides that exhibit high lipid membrane affinity. This results in an efficient and selective accumulation of the antioxidant within the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is particularly important given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage have been implicated in aging and various degenerative diseases (Wipf et al., 2022). Experimental studies have shown that XJB-5-131 can act as a mild uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation, leading to a slight increase in oxygen consumption without detrimentally affecting ATP production; this mild uncoupling may serve to lower the mitochondrial membrane potential, thereby reducing the propensity for electron leakage and subsequent ROS generation (Xun et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024). Furthermore, XJB-5-131’s ability to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels has been documented using both biochemical assays based on Amplex Red for hydrogen peroxide detection and Seahorse assays for oxygen consumption rate (OCR) analysis (Xun et al., 2022). These combined actions—the direct scavenging of radical species and the dampening of ROS-generating processes via mild uncoupling—support a mechanism by which XJB-5-131 could preserve mitochondrial structure (e.g., cristae integrity) and function under chronic oxidative conditions.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD and RPE Context:  
In the context of dry AMD, the pathophysiology is strongly linked to chronic oxidative insult, particularly within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where elevated ROS and lipid peroxidation contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction, accumulation of drusen constituents, and eventual RPE degeneration. The dual mechanism of XJB-5-131 is especially promising for this disease. Given its lipid radical scavenging capabilities, XJB-5-131 is expected to reduce malondialdehyde (MDA) and other markers of lipid peroxidation that are elevated in RPE under chronic UVA or other oxidative stresses (Ji et al., 2015). The compound’s well-documented ability to decrease ROS levels in neuronal and cardiac models, while preserving overall mitochondrial respiration, suggests that similar protective effects can be anticipated in RPE cells, which are highly metabolically active and depend critically on mitochondrial health (Wipf et al., 2022). In preliminary in vitro assays – such as those using pig RPE explants under UVA stress – one would expect XJB-5-131 to reduce MDA-adduct formation and preserve mitochondrial cristae, thereby maintaining cellular homeostasis (the hypothesis provided). At a molecular level, by delivering the nitroxide directly into RPE mitochondria, the compound would catalytically neutralize both superoxide and lipid peroxyl radicals. This dual scavenging effect can interrupt the vicious cycle of chronic oxidative damage that drives RPE dysfunction and drusen accumulation (Liu et al., 2022). Expression studies have demonstrated that genes associated with oxidative stress regulation, such as those encoding SOD and other mitochondrial antioxidants, are active in RPE cells, further supporting the notion that a mitochondria-targeted intervention like XJB-5-131 could restore redox homeostasis in these cells (Wipf et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024). Additionally, by functionally acting as a mild uncoupler, XJB-5-131 may lower mitochondrial membrane potential just enough to reduce electron leakage without compromising adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis, a delicate balance that is particularly important given the high energy requirements of the RPE (Zhou et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2015). Altogether, these effects are anticipated to culminate in the preservation of cristae integrity, reduced oxidative damage, and ultimately improved cell survival—key outcomes that align with the therapeutic goals in treating dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, XJB-5-131 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD owing to several intrinsic strengths. Foremost among these is its robust mitochondrial targeting capability. The incorporation of a gramicidin S-derived peptide moiety ensures that the nitroxide antioxidant is selectively delivered to mitochondria, a critical advantage because mitochondrial dysfunction is central to the pathology of dry AMD (Liu et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012). Its redox cycling properties not only mirror those of enzymatic antioxidants like SOD but also extend protection by neutralizing lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby addressing both protein and lipid oxidation pathways that contribute to drusen formation and RPE cell death (Wipf et al., 2022). Moreover, the reported preclinical successes in neurological and cardiac models, where XJB-5-131 has been shown to mitigate oxidative damage, reduce apoptotic signaling, and improve tissue function, suggest potential translatability of these protective effects to the ocular milieu (Robinson, 2012; Xun et al., 2022). The fact that its use as a mild uncoupler does not compromise ATP production provides an additional safety margin when considering tissues with high energy demands such as the RPE (Xun et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024).

Nevertheless, there are certain limitations and challenges that must be carefully considered before advancing XJB-5-131 into dry AMD studies. Notably, while its efficacy in neuronal, spinal cord, and ischemia-reperfusion models has been well documented, there is a paucity of direct preclinical data demonstrating its benefits specifically in RPE cells or models of retinal degeneration (Wipf et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012). The hypothesis that it can reduce MDA-adduct formation in pig RPE explants under UVA stress is promising; however, this observation must be validated in more comprehensive models of dry AMD that mimic the chronic oxidative environment of the human RPE. Additionally, the complex synthetic route—often reported to involve multiple steps and potentially low water solubility—could pose a challenge for scale-up manufacturing and may necessitate formulation strategies to optimize bioavailability for ocular applications (Wipf et al., 2022; Kaden & Li, 2013). Delivery to the posterior segment of the eye also remains a significant hurdle; while systemic administration has been effective in other animal models, local delivery methods (e.g., intravitreal injection or novel nanocarrier systems) may be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE without off-target effects. Furthermore, despite promising indications of safety in long-term animal studies (with chronic dosing in rodent models showing minimal adverse effects), thorough toxicological investigations will be essential given the sensitive nature of the retinal environment (Wipf et al., 2022; Echeverri-Ruiz et al., 2018). Finally, while the dual scavenging of superoxide and lipid radicals is mechanistically compelling, the risk of interfering with physiological redox signaling must be carefully balanced to avoid unintended consequences on cellular homeostasis (Xun et al., 2022).

In summary, XJB-5-131 represents a highly innovative and mechanistically sound candidate with significant potential for repurposing in dry AMD. Its ability to deliver a nitroxide antioxidant directly to mitochondria, neutralize deleterious ROS, and preserve mitochondrial function aligns well with the current understanding of RPE pathology in dry AMD. The extensive preclinical data in other high-oxidative stress models provide a strong rationale for its further evaluation in ocular-specific models. However, the absence of direct RPE or retinal degeneration studies, formulation and delivery challenges, and the inherent complexity of its synthesis necessitate a cautious and well-planned approach moving forward. Future research should focus on rigorous evaluation in RPE cell culture systems and animal models of dry AMD, optimization of ocular delivery strategies, and comprehensive toxicological assessments to ensure both efficacy and safety in the intended indication (Xun et al., 2022; Bowie, 2018; Wipf et al., 2022). Overall, while challenges remain, the unique pharmacological profile of XJB-5-131 provides a strong basis for considering it as a therapeutic candidate in the fight against dry age-related macular degeneration.

Proposal for Apocynin (Sigma-Aldrich A1788)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Apocynin (Sigma-Aldrich A1788) is a naturally derived, methoxy-substituted catechol originally isolated from the medicinal herb Picrorhiza kurroa, which has a long history of use in traditional Ayurvedic medicine. It is a small molecule with a molecular weight of approximately 166.17 Da and modest lipophilicity (logP ~ 0.83) that allows it to readily cross cellular membranes and even the blood–brain barrier. As a member of the NADPH oxidase (NOX) inhibitor class, it has been historically used to modulate oxidative stress in a variety of preclinical disease models. The compound’s origin is rooted in natural product chemistry, and its attractive small-molecule structure has encouraged detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic investigations in rodent models, where it has been administered intravenously and orally to assess tissue distribution and rapid clearance kinetics. Its chemical profile and natural derivation position it within a class of therapeutic candidates that have been widely evaluated for their antioxidant properties and their ability to attenuate NOX-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory diseases (Liu et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Preclinical studies have evaluated apocynin in a range of animal models that address oxidative stress–related pathologies. In cardiovascular and cerebrovascular research, for example, apocynin has been shown to reduce NADPH oxidase activity and resultant oxidative damage in models of isoproterenol-induced cardiac hypertrophy, diabetic cardiac remodeling, and brain oxidative stress associated with high-fat diets (Liu et al., 2020). Its pharmacokinetic profile in mice indicates a rapid plasma peak and an extremely short half-life of around 3–4 minutes after intravenous dosing, with extensive clearance by the kidneys (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020). In respiratory research, a completed Phase 1 randomized trial in COPD patients demonstrated that nebulized apocynin was well tolerated, produced short-term reductions in exhaled oxidative markers such as hydrogen peroxide and nitrite, and did not affect lung function or systemic safety parameters (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). Despite these encouraging results, there remains limited data on the longer-term systemic safety or adverse-event profiles of apocynin. Importantly, while apocynin has been extensively studied in cardiovascular and respiratory indications, as well as in models of neurodegeneration and hepatic and renal injury, there is minimal direct evidence of its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells such as ARPE-19 (Drummond & Sobey, 2014). Nonetheless, since dry AMD pathogenesis involves oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE, the demonstrated efficacy of apocynin in modulating NADPH oxidase–mediated ROS production in other organs builds a rationale for its repurposing for this indication.

Mechanism of Action:  
The central proposed mechanism by which apocynin exerts its therapeutic effects involves the inhibition of NADPH oxidase, particularly by blocking the assembly of the enzyme complex. NADPH oxidases are multi-subunit enzymatic complexes responsible for the regulated generation of superoxide and downstream reactive oxygen species. In cells, the assembly and activation of NOX, especially isoforms such as NOX2, require the translocation of cytosolic regulatory subunits—most notably p47^phox—to the membrane-bound catalytic core. Early studies reported that apocynin can prevent the translocation of p47^phox to the plasma membrane, thereby inhibiting the assembly of the active NOX2 complex and reducing the production of superoxide, which secondarily lowers the formation of hydrogen peroxide and other ROS (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Drummond & Sobey, 2014).  
However, the molecular pharmacology of apocynin is more complex. Its inhibitory activity appears to be dependent on metabolic activation by myeloperoxidase (MPO) in the presence of hydrogen peroxide. This conversion supposedly generates reactive quinone species or even a dimeric form (diapocynin) that can covalently modify cysteine residues in p47^phox, thus interfering with its function (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018). Some studies, though, have failed to detect diapocynin in vivo, suggesting that other metabolites, such as apocynin glycoconjugates, might instead be responsible for its activity (Liu et al., 2020). Moreover, apocynin has been reported to possess direct antioxidant properties at higher concentrations by scavenging non-radical oxidants such as hypochlorous acid and hydrogen peroxide, independently of its effects on NOX assembly (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018).  
In vitro studies in various cell types have yielded conflicting data regarding whether apocynin primarily functions as a NOX-specific inhibitor or as a broad-spectrum antioxidant. In cell types that are rich in peroxidase activity, such as neutrophils, apocynin’s conversion to an active inhibitor appears robust. In contrast, in cells with lower MPO activity, such as some epithelial or neuronal cells, its efficacy as a NOX inhibitor may be diminished, and observed benefits might be attributable to direct ROS scavenging (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020). Within the context of RPE cells, the candidate hypothesis posits that apocynin will inhibit the translocation of p47^phox during NOX2 activation, thereby reducing cytosolic ROS production while also limiting the spillover of ROS into mitochondria, which would otherwise trigger mitochondrial membrane potential collapse, fragmentation, and reduced oxygen consumption rate (OCR) (Liu et al., 2020; Liu, 2023). This mechanism, if operative in RPE cells such as ARPE-19, would help preserve mitochondrial integrity by preventing excess ROS accumulation and the ensuing mitochondrial dysfunction—a key pathogenic process in dry AMD (Shu et al., 2023; Liu, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism, the use of apocynin in in vitro assays with ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures is expected to yield several beneficial outcomes. First, by blocking p47^phox translocation, apocynin should reduce the assembly of the NOX complex, particularly NOX2, thereby decreasing the production of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. This reduction in ROS should lead to lower levels of oxidative stress markers, as measured by assays such as lucigenin chemiluminescence, dihydroethidium (DHE) fluorescence, and malondialdehyde (MDA) assays (Liu et al., 2020).  
Second, because ROS are known to damage mitochondrial components, it is expected that apocynin treatment will protect against mitochondrial dysfunction. In ARPE-19 cells challenged with hydrogen peroxide or other oxidative stress inducers, apocynin should help preserve the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), prevent mitochondrial fragmentation, and maintain basal oxygen consumption rates (OCR). These mitochondrial endpoints are critical, as disruption of mitochondrial dynamics and energy production is a hallmark of RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Shu et al., 2023; Drummond & Sobey, 2014).  
Furthermore, given that NOX isoforms such as NOX2 and NOX4 have been implicated in the oxidative stress observed in retinal cells exposed to blue light or metabolic insults (Liu et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020), the inhibition of these enzymes with apocynin is expected to attenuate downstream pro-inflammatory signaling cascades. This should result in reduced upregulation of proangiogenic factors like VEGF and a decrease in inflammatory cytokine production that can exacerbate retinal degeneration. In effect, apocynin would act not only to maintain mitochondrial function by limiting local oxidative damage but also to modulate the broader redox environment that contributes to RPE cell dysfunction in dry AMD (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018).  
As a consequence, in the experimental assay proposed by the team, treatment of ARPE-19 cells with apocynin under conditions of induced oxidative stress should demonstrate a measurable preservation of Δψm by fluorescent imaging or flow cytometry using potentiometric dyes, maintenance of basal OCR as measured via Seahorse extracellular flux analysis, and a reduction in mitochondrial ROS accumulation by specific mitochondria-targeted ROS indicators. The reduction in NOX-derived ROS is expected to indirectly prevent mitochondrial fragmentation by mitigating the activation of mitochondrial fission pathways in response to oxidative injury (Liu, 2023; Liu et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
Apocynin represents a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its potential to target a core pathogenic mechanism—the dysregulated production of ROS via NADPH oxidase assembly. One of the strengths of apocynin is its extensive preclinical history demonstrating its capacity to lower oxidative stress in various organs, including the heart, liver, brain, and lung, with documented rapid distribution to tissues and a well-characterized pharmacokinetic profile in animal models (Liu et al., 2020; Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014). Its observed safety in a small Phase 1 clinical study in COPD patients further bolsters the case for its safety on at least short-term administration in humans (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). Moreover, its chemical simplicity as a natural product and its relatively low molecular weight make it attractive for further formulation studies in ocular indications.  
Nevertheless, significant weaknesses and challenges must be addressed. A major issue is the ongoing debate regarding the exact mechanism of action of apocynin. While some studies support its role as a NOX inhibitor via prevention of p47^phox translocation, others have demonstrated that its activity may be largely due to its direct antioxidant properties or require metabolic activation by MPO—a process that may not be robust in retinal pigment epithelial cells (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014). This mechanistic ambiguity raises concerns about its efficacy and specificity in the RPE, where the peroxidase activity necessary for conversion to an active form may be limited.  
Furthermore, the extremely short plasma half-life (approximately 3–4 minutes) observed in rodent models indicates that apocynin is rapidly cleared, which could limit its therapeutic window and necessitate frequent dosing or the development of modified formulations such as a sustained-release ocular implant or a mitochondria-targeted derivative (e.g., mito-apocynin) to achieve prolonged local concentrations in the retina (Liu et al., 2020; Liu, 2023). This rapid clearance could also complicate the translation of in vivo results to a clinical setting for a chronic disease such as dry AMD.  
Another concern is that, despite the general rationale for reducing oxidative stress in the RPE, there is a paucity of direct evidence from ARPE-19 or primary RPE models showing that apocynin effectively prevents mitochondrial fragmentation, preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), or maintains basal oxygen consumption rates. Although some studies have demonstrated that NOX inhibition can reduce ROS levels in retinal cells, apocynin’s specific action in the context of dry AMD has not been rigorously documented (Shu et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2020). Additionally, the variability of its effects across different cell types—dependent on the presence or absence of peroxidase activity—suggests that its efficacy in the RPE may be inconsistent, thereby necessitating further targeted studies.  
There is also the possibility of off-target effects. Because apocynin has been reported to act as a general antioxidant rather than a highly specific NOX inhibitor, it might interfere with normal redox signaling that is essential for cell survival and immune defense, particularly when applied systemically. Caution must be exercised to ensure that suppression of NOX activity does not inadvertently impair protective immune responses or lead to unwanted toxicity, even if short-term clinical data appears reassuring (Drummond & Sobey, 2014; Casas et al., 2015).  
In summary, while the mechanistic rationale behind using apocynin to inhibit NOX assembly in RPE cells is compelling, particularly given the central role of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis, several critical questions remain. These include the precise mechanism by which apocynin exerts its effects in the RPE, the consistency of its efficacy in protecting mitochondrial function in ARPE-19 cells, its pharmacokinetic limitations, and its potential off-target effects. Overall, apocynin has strengths as a natural antioxidant with a history of reducing systemic oxidative stress in preclinical models and demonstrating short-term safety in human trials. However, its mechanism remains controversial, and its rapid clearance, potential variability in retinal cells, and limited direct evidence in AMD models represent significant weaknesses that must be overcome through further targeted biochemical, in vitro, and in vivo studies before advancing into clinical trials for dry AMD (Liu et al., 2020; Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010; Shu et al., 2023; Rohowetz et al., 2018; Liu, 2023).  
Given these considerations, further investigation into apocynin’s effects on mitochondrial protection and NOX inhibition in RPE cells is warranted. Such studies should include detailed assessments of p47^phox translocation in ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress, measurement of mitochondrial membrane potential (using dyes such as JC-1 or TMRE), and evaluations of OCR using Seahorse analysis. Moreover, efforts to optimize its pharmacokinetic profile—perhaps through formulation modifications or conversion to a mitochondria-targeted analogue—would address one of its key limitations. Only with these additional data can we determine whether apocynin holds sufficient promise to justify its repurposing for the treatment of dry AMD.

Proposal for S3QEL-2 (Cayman Chemical #26918)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
S3QEL-2 is a synthetic small‐molecule member of the S3QEL (Suppressors of Superoxide production from mitochondrial Complex III) class, originally discovered through a high‐throughput screen of approximately 635,000 small molecules using isolated mitochondria and an Amplex UltraRed H₂O₂ detection assay (Orr et al., 2015). In this screening paradigm, compounds were rigorously selected for their ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation arising from the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III without impairing oxidative phosphorylation or altering the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Orr et al., 2015). The discovery approach involved counterscreens that monitored Δψm changes, respiration rates, and markers of cellular viability, ensuring that S3QEL-2 exhibits specificity in mitigating reactive oxygen species (ROS) production rather than acting as a nonspecific antioxidant or uncoupler (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 was sourced from commercial screening collections—for example, vendors such as Chemdiv—and its powder-stock purity was confirmed by HPLC–MS analysis (Orr et al., 2015). As a member of a structurally diverse chemotype group, S3QEL-2 belongs to a new class of mitochondrial ROS-targeted modulators that differ fundamentally from classical Complex III inhibitors such as antimycin A or myxothiazol; unlike these inhibitors, S3QELs do not block the electron transfer chain or impair ATP production, but rather reduce the electron leak from the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site (Orr et al., 2015). In general, compounds in the S3QEL class have been used experimentally as probes to decouple pathological ROS generation from normal bioenergetic function in diverse cell types, with applications ranging from studies on hypoxia-induced transcription (e.g., HIF-1α signaling) to experiments investigating ROS-mediated cell stress in pancreatic β-cells (Orr et al., 2015). The commercial catalog number Cayman Chemical #26918 identifies S3QEL-2 for research purposes, which suggests that this compound is available for repurposing studies beyond its initial characterization in nonocular systems (Orr et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Although S3QEL-2 was originally developed as a novel chemical probe to selectively suppress Complex III-derived superoxide production, its preclinical evaluation has been extensive within the context of cellular models evaluating ROS-mediated signaling and cell stress responses (Orr et al., 2015). In cellular assays, S3QEL-2 has demonstrated the ability to reduce H₂O₂ production in isolated mitochondria, lower HIF-1α transcription in hypoxia-challenged HEK-293 cells, and protect pancreatic β-cells from oxidative stress-induced apoptosis during islet isolation and culture (Orr et al., 2015). Notably, in studies where cells were exposed to concentrations up to 20× the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC₅₀) determined for site IIIQo superoxide production, S3QEL-2 did not impair basal or uncoupled respiration, nor did it compromise mitochondrial viability (Orr et al., 2015). Additionally, S3QEL-2 has been employed as a pharmacological tool in experiments on human monocyte-derived macrophages, where it contributed to demonstrating that inhibition of mitochondrial ROS can reduce inflammasome activation and subsequent IL-18 secretion upon stimulation by the complement membrane attack complex (MAC) (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). However, despite its utility in these nonocular systems—where mitochondrial ROS inhibition was linked to attenuation of inflammatory cytokine pathways—there is little to no published preclinical or clinical data directly evaluating S3QEL-2 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or in other ocular disease contexts (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2015). While the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of dry AMD, particularly those involving chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and associated inflammasome activation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, are well documented (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), a direct therapeutic history for S3QEL-2 in retinal or AMD models remains absent in the current literature (Korhonen, 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Thus, S3QEL-2 represents a promising repurposing candidate that has been validated in other contexts of ROS-related cellular stress but has not yet been explicitly applied to the treatment of dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of S3QEL-2 is based on its capacity to selectively suppress superoxide generation originating at the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III. Under normal conditions, the electron transport chain (ETC) can leak electrons during the reduction of oxygen, particularly at the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site, resulting in the formation of superoxide—a primary reactive oxygen species (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 does not act as a general ROS scavenger; rather, it modulates the rate constant for the electron transfer from the semiquinone to molecular oxygen without significantly altering the steady-state levels of semiquinone species or the redox poise of the ubiquinone (Q) pool (Orr et al., 2015). This selective inhibition of ROS generation is achieved through an allosteric modulation of protein conformation within Complex III, specifically targeting the Qo site to reduce electron leak while sparing the remainder of the electron transport processes (Orr et al., 2015). By decreasing superoxide production, S3QEL-2 effectively reduces the downstream formation of H₂O₂ as detected by Amplex UltraRed assays, a finding that has been consistently reproduced in isolated mitochondrial studies (Orr et al., 2015). Moreover, because S3QEL-2 does not interfere with the overall electron flux or the maintenance of Δψm, it preserves the bioenergetic capacity of the mitochondria—a critical factor in tissues with high metabolic demands such as the RPE (Orr et al., 2015). On a molecular level, the compound’s activity at nanomolar to low micromolar concentrations (with a reported mean IC₅₀ around 1.7 μM for S3QEL-2) suggests a highly potent modulation of the ROS generation pathway that is independent of the mitochondrial matrix redox state (Orr et al., 2015). This targeted approach is further distinguished from classical Complex III inhibitors like myxothiazol and antimycin A, which disrupt the entire electron transport process and can lead to a collapse in mitochondrial function; in contrast, S3QEL-2 specifically mitigates the pathological component of ROS production while maintaining ATP synthesis and cellular energy homeostasis (Orr et al., 2015). In macrophages and other cell types, the reduction in mitochondrial ROS production by S3QEL-2 has been shown to blunt ROS-dependent signaling pathways, such as the stabilization of the transcription factor HIF-1α under hypoxic conditions, and to decrease the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Toma et al., 2021). Thus, the molecular interactions of S3QEL-2 within Complex III position it as a potential modulator of redox signaling pathways that are implicated in inflammatory and degenerative processes, including those observed in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Based on its established mechanism of action, the use of S3QEL-2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is expected to selectively reduce mitochondrial ROS generated at the Complex III Qo site. In dry age-related macular degeneration, one of the prevailing hypotheses attributes disease progression to chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE, leading to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and subsequent secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The selective inhibition of ROS by S3QEL-2 should therefore interrupt this pathological signaling cascade. In an in vitro assay using RPE cells—cells that have been shown to express components of the NLRP3 inflammasome and are especially vulnerable to oxidative insults—the drug is anticipated to lower ROS markers, as measured by fluorescent dyes (for example, oxidized carboxy-H₂DCFDA), without compromising the cells' mitochondrial respiration or Δψm (Orr et al., 2015). With less mitochondrial ROS available to act as secondary messengers, the downstream stabilization of HIF-1α under stress conditions is expected to be reduced, and the inflammatory response mediated by inflammasome assembly will likely be attenuated (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Orr et al., 2015). Given that multiple studies have demonstrated the role of mitochondrial ROS in directly or indirectly activating NLRP3 inflammasome signaling in both macrophages and RPE cells (Gao et al., 2015; Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Piippo, 2019), the hypothesis is that S3QEL-2 will break this mtROS–NLRP3 axis. In a therapeutic assay, one would expect that RPE cells treated with S3QEL-2 under conditions of complement dysregulation (a known contributor to dry AMD pathology) would demonstrate not only reduced markers of oxidative stress and inflammasome activation but also improved cellular viability, decreased apoptosis, and maintenance of proper metabolic function (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Furthermore, if S3QEL-2 can lower the intracellular superoxide burden, it might also reduce the formation of oxidized lipids and other damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that contribute to the progression of AMD (Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Toma et al., 2021). Overall, the strategic downregulation of mitochondrial ROS production should translate into a protective phenotype in RPE cells by interrupting the signaling mechanisms that lead to chronic inflammation and cell death in the context of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
S3QEL-2 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique pharmacological profile and precision in targeting mitochondrial ROS production. One of the key strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation at the Complex III Qo site without impairing the overall electron transport chain function or disrupting mitochondrial membrane potential (Orr et al., 2015). This high degree of specificity is particularly valuable in a disease such as dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to pathogenesis yet preserving the RPE’s bioenergetic capacity is essential for retinal health (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The preclinical data available for S3QEL-2 in nonocular systems—ranging from hypoxia-induced HIF-1α modulation to protection of pancreatic β-cells and dampening of inflammasome activation in macrophages—suggest that its mechanism of action may well translate to the RPE, a cell type that is similarly sensitive to mitochondrial oxidative stress (Orr et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Moreover, the ability of S3QEL-2 to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels without interfering with ATP production positions it as a promising agent for interrupting the mtROS–NLRP3 inflammasome axis that is proposed to drive inflammatory responses in the geographic atrophy observed in dry AMD (Orr et al., 2015; Orr et al., 2015).

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. Despite the encouraging preclinical data in cell culture and isolated mitochondrial systems, there is currently no direct evidence linking S3QEL-2 to therapeutic benefit in retinal models or in dry AMD specifically (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2015). The candidate has been primarily evaluated in nonocular models, and the complex microenvironment of the retina—including the blood-retinal barrier, immune cell interactions, and local complement dysregulation—may pose significant challenges in translating in vitro efficacy to in vivo benefit (Korhonen, 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Furthermore, while S3QEL-2 has been shown to reduce ROS-mediated signaling in macrophages and pancreatic islets, the pharmacokinetic properties, tissue distribution, and long-term safety profile of this compound in ocular tissues remain to be determined (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Orr et al., 2015). Delivery of S3QEL-2 to the retina may require formulation strategies that overcome solubility and permeability barriers inherent in drug delivery to the posterior segment of the eye. Another concern is the potential for off-target effects that, while not evident in the isolated systems tested so far, may manifest in the complex in vivo environment or with chronic administration (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Orr et al., 2015).

In addition, the exact molecular site of action on Complex III is not yet fully delineated at the atomic level, meaning that while the compound has been shown to modulate ROS production, the precise binding interactions and potential variability between different cell types or individuals remain uncertain (Orr et al., 2015). This incomplete mechanistic detail could complicate structure-activity relationship (SAR) explorations, as well as efforts to optimize the compound further for better efficacy or reduced toxicity in an ocular setting.

From a therapeutic perspective, the hypothesis that S3QEL-2 can reduce inflammasome activation by lowering mitochondrial ROS is strongly supported by data in other cell types, particularly where a reduction in ROS has been correlated with lower levels of IL-1β and IL-18 secretion (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Given the well-established involvement of mitochondrial ROS and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), S3QEL-2 holds promise as a tool to dissect and potentially therapeutically modulate this axis. However, concrete evidence in AMD-relevant models, especially primary RPE cells derived from patients or appropriate animal models, is necessary before advancing this compound further in the drug development pipeline (Korhonen, 2024; Macchioni et al., 2020).

In summary, the strengths of S3QEL-2 lie in its high selectivity for Complex III-derived ROS suppression, preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, and the proven ability to modulate ROS-dependent inflammatory pathways in several preclinical settings (Orr et al., 2015). Its repurposing for dry AMD is biochemically plausible and aligns with the current understanding of the disease, where chronic low-level oxidative stress and inflammasome activation play central roles in RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). Conversely, weaknesses include the absence of direct preclinical evidence in ocular models, potential pharmacokinetic and delivery challenges, and an incomplete elucidation of its binding mechanism at the atomic level. Considering these factors, S3QEL-2 represents a highly promising candidate that merits further investigation through targeted preclinical studies in retinal and RPE models, including assessments of its delivery, efficacy in reducing NLRP3-driven cytokine release, and long-term safety in ocular tissues (Gao et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Ultimately, while S3QEL-2 is supported by robust biochemical data in nonocular systems and has a compelling mechanism that could translate into therapeutic benefit for dry AMD, additional focused research in AMD-relevant models is essential to validate its potential as a repurposed drug candidate for this challenging indication.

Proposal for SRT1720 (Sigma-Aldrich SML0260)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SRT1720 is a fully synthetic small molecule initially discovered through high‐throughput screening by Sirtris Pharmaceuticals, which sought potent alternatives to the naturally occurring polyphenol resveratrol. Unlike resveratrol—which suffers from low bioavailability, poor metabolic stability, and broad non‐selective target interactions—SRT1720 belongs to the class of synthetic Sirtuin Activating Compounds (STACs) designed to selectively activate the NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylase SIRT1. Chemically, SRT1720 is based on an imidazo[1,2-b]thiazole scaffold and was optimized for its potency; studies have indicated that it is approximately 1000× more potent than resveratrol, with an EC1.5 value of around 0.16 μM and impressive maximal activation percentages in vitro (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Chang et al., 2024). The synthetic origins of SRT1720 represent a deliberate medicinal chemistry effort aimed at overcoming the limitations of natural SIRT1 activators. In the broader context, compounds in this class have been used as investigational drugs targeting pathways involved in metabolism, aging, inflammation, and stress tolerance, thereby establishing a framework for repurposing efforts across various disease areas (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
Preclinical studies of SRT1720 have predominantly focused on its metabolic effects in rodent models characterized by diet-induced obesity, insulin resistance, and other forms of metabolic dysfunction. In these studies, administration of SRT1720 resulted in significant improvements in insulin sensitivity, reduction of plasma glucose levels, and enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis across metabolic tissues such as skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissues (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Donmez, 2012). Moreover, in genetically obese and high-fat diet animal models, SRT1720 has been demonstrated to improve mitochondrial function, as indicated by increased ATP production, elevated expression of mitochondrial proteins such as ATP synthase β and NDUFB8, and enhanced oxidative metabolism (Funk et al., 2010). This modulatory effect on mitochondrial biogenesis and function is thought to be mediated via the SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway—a mechanism that has garnered attention in age-related diseases where mitochondrial dysfunction is central. Although SRT1720 has not been directly investigated in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or explicitly in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, the underlying pathogenic processes in dry AMD—namely, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysregulation—share significant overlap with the tissues previously demonstrated to benefit from SRT1720 treatment (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009). This cross-tissue efficacy provides a compelling rationale to explore SRT1720’s repurposing for dry AMD. Additionally, related compounds in this class (e.g., SRT2104) have advanced into clinical development for other indications, further suggesting that the pharmacological modulation of SIRT1 is a viable therapeutic approach (Hoppner et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action:  
The underlying mechanism of action of SRT1720 centers on its ability to allosterically activate SIRT1, a key regulator of cellular energy metabolism and stress responses. SIRT1 is an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase that modulates the activity of various transcription factors and co-regulators, notably PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1-α), which is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. SRT1720 binds to an allosteric site on the SIRT1 enzyme-peptide substrate complex, situated amino terminal to the enzyme’s catalytic domain. This binding facilitates a conformational change in SIRT1 that lowers the Michaelis constant (K_m) for the acetylated substrates, thereby enhancing the rate of deacetylation (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Wan, 2021). Biochemical assays have demonstrated that SRT1720 increases SIRT1 deacetylase activity in a dose-dependent manner, leading to reduced acetylation of PGC-1α and thus promoting its transcriptional activity in driving mitochondrial gene expression (Funk et al., 2010). In addition to PGC-1α, SRT1720-mediated SIRT1 activation influences the acetylation status of several other proteins involved in stress responses and apoptosis, including FOXO1 and PPARγ, which collectively contribute to improved cellular resilience against oxidative damage (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Hoppner et al., 2014). Of note, many studies have confirmed that the beneficial effects observed with SRT1720 are abrogated in the presence of SIRT1 inhibitors such as nicotinamide and sirtinol, providing strong evidence for a SIRT1-dependent mode of action (Funk et al., 2010; Djouadi & Bastin, 2019). However, it is important to acknowledge that there has been some controversy regarding whether SRT1720 and its structural relatives directly interact with SIRT1 or exert off-target effects; nonetheless, the preponderance of kinetic and biophysical data supports the view that SRT1720 is primarily a SIRT1 activator (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) accompanied by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and an overall decline in cellular energy homeostasis. The hypothesis for repurposing SRT1720 in this context is based on its well-documented ability to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and enhance oxidative capacity in multiple tissue types. In the RPE, which is a post-mitotic and metabolically demanding cell layer critical for photoreceptor survival, mitochondrial dysfunction is a key pathological feature that contributes to the progression of dry AMD. By activating SIRT1, SRT1720 is expected to promote deacetylation of PGC-1α, thereby upregulating a transcriptional program that enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and repair. This, in turn, would improve oxidative phosphorylation, reduce the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), and bolster the cells’ ability to cope with the chronic oxidative stress that underlies dry AMD pathology (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Furthermore, studies in other tissues, such as aged skeletal muscle and hepatocytes, have shown that SRT1720 reduces mtROS and restores cellular ATP levels by increasing mitochondrial number and function (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010). It is reasonable to extrapolate that similar benefits could be achieved in RPE cells, where preserved mitochondrial function is essential for maintaining retinal integrity and preventing progression to geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry AMD. Expression analyses have demonstrated that both SIRT1 and PGC-1α are expressed in RPE cells, and their activities are critical for retinal health; thus, modulation of the SIRT1–PGC-1α axis by SRT1720 offers a mechanistic basis for its expected protective effects in the RPE (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009). It is anticipated that in assays using RPE cell cultures, treatment with SRT1720 will lead to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis—as evidenced by increased mitochondrial DNA content, elevated levels of mitochondrial proteins, and improved cellular ATP production—while concurrently attenuating markers of oxidative stress. These effects would collectively improve the oxidative resilience of RPE cells, thereby potentially slowing or halting the progression of dry AMD (Funk et al., 2010; Hoppner et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation:  
There are several compelling strengths associated with the use of SRT1720 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, its synthetic design has led to a compound that is remarkably more potent than resveratrol, addressing one of the key limitations of natural SIRT1 activators. This enhanced potency, coupled with a clearly elucidated mechanism of action involving allosteric activation of SIRT1, provides a robust biochemical rationale for its efficacy. The observed effects in metabolic, hepatic, and renal systems—where SRT1720 has demonstrated significant improvements in mitochondrial biogenesis and reductions in oxidative stress—are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells plays a central role (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Another strength is the extensive preclinical data supporting the involvement of the SIRT1-PGC-1α axis in regulating mitochondrial function and cellular energy homeostasis. Since RPE cells share similar reliance on these pathways for maintaining cellular function and resisting oxidative injury, it is plausible that SRT1720 can be effectively translated into a therapeutic for dry AMD. Moreover, the fact that SRT1720’s effects are abrogated by SIRT1 inhibitors reinforces the notion that its beneficial actions are directly linked to SIRT1 activation rather than resulting from non-specific off-target activities, a point underscored by multiple biochemical studies (Wan, 2021; Funk et al., 2010).

However, there are also notable weaknesses and uncertainties that warrant consideration. Although SRT1720 has a well-characterized profile in terms of metabolic and mitochondrial effects in other tissue types, there is a paucity of data directly pertaining to ocular tissues or RPE cells. The retinal environment possesses unique pharmacokinetic and physiological characteristics, and the ability of SRT1720 to reach effective concentrations in the RPE upon systemic or local administration remains to be determined. Moreover, while the SIRT1-PGC-1α axis is a promising target, some studies have raised controversies concerning whether SRT1720 truly acts as a direct SIRT1 activator or if its effects might be partially mediated by off-target pathways, which could complicate both efficacy and safety profiles (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024). There is also the broader issue of translating findings from systemic models of mitochondrial dysfunction to the highly specialized context of the eye, which may require careful consideration of formulation, dosing regimen, and potential adverse effects that are specific to ocular tissues.

The overall evaluation suggests that SRT1720 has a strong scientific foundation based on its potent SIRT1 activation, its capacity to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis, and its demonstrated ability to mitigate oxidative stress in multiple preclinical models (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010). These characteristics are directly relevant to addressing the molecular pathogenesis of dry AMD, where impaired mitochondrial function in the RPE is a key contributor to disease progression. Nevertheless, the gaps in the existing literature, particularly the lack of direct ocular studies, necessitate additional targeted preclinical research. Rigorous in vitro studies in RPE cell cultures and subsequent in vivo models of dry AMD will be essential to validate the therapeutic potential of SRT1720 in the ocular setting. Such studies should also focus on optimizing delivery mechanisms to ensure that effective drug levels are achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Future investigations should include detailed pharmacokinetic assessments in ocular tissues, evaluation of the specific effects on RPE mitochondrial dynamics, and analyses of potential off-target effects that could compromise safety. Additionally, given the controversies around whether compounds such as SRT1720 function solely via SIRT1 activation, complementary studies using genetic knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of SIRT1 in RPE cells would help to unequivocally determine the mechanism by which SRT1720 exerts its effects. Ultimately, while the translational rationale appears strong, careful attention must be paid to the unique biological milieu of the eye and to the rigorous design of preclinical studies that directly address the therapeutic endpoints relevant to dry AMD (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

In conclusion, SRT1720 is a promising candidate for repurposing as a treatment for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its potent SIRT1 activation, demonstrated effects on mitochondrial biogenesis, and its ability to reduce oxidative stress, which is central to the pathology observed in RPE cells. The synthetic origin and high potency of SRT1720 distinguish it from natural agents like resveratrol and suggest that it might overcome many of the pharmacokinetic and specificity issues that have historically limited the success of SIRT1 activators in clinical settings. However, given that most of the existing evidence arises from non-ocular models, systematic studies focusing on the ocular pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of SRT1720 are imperative before clinical translation can be considered. If future studies can confirm that SRT1720 effectively reaches the RPE in therapeutic concentrations and modulates the SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway without deleterious off-target effects, it could represent a significant advancement in our ability to protect the RPE against oxidative stress and slow the progression of dry AMD (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010; Hoppner et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation Summary:  
Strengths of SRT1720 include its exceptional potency compared to natural SIRT1 activators, robust preclinical evidence demonstrating mitochondrial biogenesis and reduced oxidative stress in multiple tissues, and a well-elucidated mechanism involving allosteric activation of SIRT1 with consequent deacetylation of PGC-1α. These attributes are particularly relevant given the central role of mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD. The SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway is a validated target in several preclinical models of aging and metabolic disease, and its modulation is anticipated to offer significant protection in RPE cells (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010).

Weaknesses center on the current lack of direct evidence in retinal cells or animal models of AMD, the need for ocular pharmacokinetic data, and some lingering controversies regarding the specificity of SRT1720’s mechanism of action. The translation of metabolic benefits observed in liver, muscle, and kidney to the RPE requires further study, and potential off-target effects or issues with drug delivery to ocular tissues remain concerns that necessitate additional research (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024).

Based on the review of the available biochemical, preclinical, and mechanistic literature, SRT1720 shows promise as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. However, its application in this context should proceed with careful preclinical evaluation in relevant ocular models to address the outstanding issues related to tissue-specific pharmacokinetics and potential mechanistic ambiguities. This comprehensive evaluation supports the inclusion of SRT1720 in the research team’s pipeline for further investigation, provided that subsequent studies are designed to directly assess its efficacy and safety in the RPE and in vivo models of dry AMD (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Hoppner et al., 2014).

Proposal for Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA; Sigma-Aldrich D2534)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a naturally occurring long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (LC-PUFA) that has been isolated from marine sources, such as fish oil, and is commercially available in a highly purified form (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich D2534). DHA is synthesized via metabolic elongation and desaturation of dietary alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) in mammals; however, this endogenous conversion is limited, and direct dietary intake is critical for maintaining adequate retinal DHA levels (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14). Belonging to the omega-3 class of fatty acids, DHA has long been recognized for its important roles in maintaining membrane structure and function, particularly in neural tissues and the retina where it is highly concentrated in photoreceptor outer segments and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) membranes (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3). Its polyunsaturated nature—with six cis double bonds—confers unique biophysical properties, enabling DHA to increase membrane fluidity and participate in critical signaling cascades. The compound has been used extensively as a nutritional supplement and has been incorporated in various formulations aimed at cardiovascular health, cognitive function, and ocular protection, establishing a robust safety profile over decades of human use (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Skowronska-Krawczyk & Chao, 2019, pp. 3–4).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, extensive research has explored the role of DHA and related omega-3 fatty acids in maintaining retinal function and potentially preventing age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Epidemiologic studies have consistently demonstrated an inverse association between dietary fish and high omega-3 fatty acid intake and the risk of developing AMD, suggesting that populations with higher DHA consumption tend to exhibit a lower incidence of both early and, to some extent, advanced forms of the disease (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). In clinical settings, large-scale randomized controlled trials, such as AREDS2, incorporated DHA (and EPA) into a multi-nutrient formula designed originally for AMD, though the overall randomized trial outcomes have been mixed, with some studies finding no statistically significant benefit for progression to late AMD (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Pilot clinical trials and observational cohort studies, including NAT-1 and NAT-2, have assessed DHA supplementation in subjects with drusenoid lesions or early-stage AMD; while some of these studies have shown promising improvements in blood biomarkers (e.g., increased red blood cell DHA levels) and correlations with reduced AMD progression, the clinical efficacy remains under debate (Querques et al., 2016, pp. 2–4; Querques et al., 2011, pp. 7–8). Notably, evidence from animal models suggests that dietary DHA may protect against light-induced retinal degeneration and reduce the accumulation of deleterious lipid peroxidation products, although some preclinical studies also caution that DHA’s susceptibility to oxidation could, under certain conditions, worsen retinal injury (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for using DHA in dry AMD is based on its predicted ability to incorporate into the mitochondrial membranes of RPE cells, thereby enhancing membrane fluidity and protecting against oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes. Under normal cellular conditions, DHA—owing to its multiple methylene-interrupted cis double bonds—integrates into phospholipid bilayers and modulates biophysical properties such as fluidity, permeability, and thickness (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). In mitochondrial membranes, this incorporation is thought to replace more saturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid, ultimately reducing lipid peroxidation and mitigating oxidative stress that is deleterious to ETC function (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9). In vitro studies have shown that DHA supplementation in retinal cell cultures can decrease markers of apoptosis and preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity, with a concomitant increase in anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g., Bcl-2) (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4).  
In addition, DHA is enzymatically converted under conditions of oxidative stress into neuroprotective docosanoids, such as neuroprotectin D1 (NPD1), which can inhibit pro-inflammatory gene expression and reduce cell death in RPE and photoreceptor cells (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). This conversion not only contributes to countering local inflammation but also supports cellular health by modulating intracellular signaling pathways, particularly those involving NF-κB and other transcription factors critical for managing oxidative stress (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that direct, quantitative evidence detailing DHA’s incorporation specifically into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its precise effects on mitochondrial cristae structure, malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, or oxygen consumption rate (OCR) remains limited in the current literature (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). Several reviews and preclinical reports acknowledge the theoretical framework while emphasizing the need for more detailed mechanistic studies that directly measure these mitochondrial endpoints (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic hypothesis, DHA supplementation is expected to yield several beneficial effects in retinal cells, particularly within the RPE, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In an ideal in vitro or ex vivo assay, DHA would incorporate into RPE cell membranes—including the mitochondrial inner membrane—increasing fluidity and enabling better diffusion of substrates and electron carriers necessary for efficient ATP production. Enhanced mitochondrial membrane fluidity should help reduce the susceptibility of the electron transport chain to oxidative damage, thereby lowering the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the subsequent production of lipid peroxidation byproducts such as MDA (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Furthermore, preservation of mitochondrial cristae structure is anticipated to maintain optimal alignment and function of ETC complexes, leading to an improved oxygen consumption rate (OCR) that is directly linked to cellular energy metabolism and overall cell viability (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4; Souied et al., 2016, p. 8).  
At a molecular level, the increased presence of DHA in mitochondrial membranes is expected to initiate a cascade of protective events: reduced oxidative stress and inflammation via inhibition of NF-κB activation, promotion of the antioxidant response through NFE2L2 (NRF2) pathway activation, and enhanced autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and organelles through upregulation of SQSTM1 (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 1–2; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, p. 3). Consequently, these effects should translate into preservation of RPE cell function, reduced apoptosis, and maintenance of photoreceptor health—an effect that could help slow the progression of dry AMD by stabilizing the retinal environment and preventing drusen accumulation and other degenerative changes (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5). Additionally, because genes encoding crucial direct mediators of DHA uptake such as Mfsd2a are expressed in RPE cells and photoreceptors, the target tissue is particularly well-positioned to benefit from increased dietary or supplementary DHA (Fathima et al., 2023, p. 8). However, it is also recognized that despite the strong rationale, direct experimental confirmation of these outcomes—specifically measured improvements in MDA levels, cristae ultrastructure integrity, and OCR in human RPE cells—is still pending, and the observed epidemiologic correlations are not yet unequivocally supported by randomized clinical trial data (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposition to repurpose DHA for dry AMD is underpinned by compelling mechanistic rationale and epidemiologic associations, yet it is not without its challenges and limitations. One clear strength is DHA’s established role as an essential component of retinal cell membranes. Its high concentration in photoreceptors and the RPE is functionally integral to maintaining visual function and cellular homeostasis, lending strong biological plausibility to its protective potential in AMD (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). Its ability to modulate membrane fluidity, serve as a precursor to neuroprotective mediators like NPD1, and exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions provide multiple mechanistic pathways through which it may mitigate the cellular stressors implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14).  
From a therapeutic history perspective, DHA is well understood in the context of nutritional supplementation, and numerous epidemiologic studies point toward a lower risk of AMD with higher dietary DHA intake (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). The safety profile of DHA is also well established, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing. However, the clinical trial data to date (including large-scale studies such as AREDS2 and smaller trials like NAT-2) have not consistently demonstrated a clear benefit in altering the progression of advanced AMD, and it remains uncertain whether observed benefits in intermediate AMD or specific cellular endpoints translate into clinically meaningful outcomes in the dry form of the disease (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8).  
A significant weakness in the current body of research is the lack of direct mechanistic studies that quantitatively document DHA incorporation into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its subsequent effects on mitochondrial parameters. In our hypothesis, improved mitochondrial function is key, with expected reductions in MDA levels, preservation of cristae structure, and enhancement of OCR serving as biomarkers of efficacy. Yet, while several in vitro studies and animal experiments have suggested that DHA can reduce markers of oxidative stress and improve mitochondrial integrity in retinal models, the literature provided does not include rigorous, high-resolution measurements of these specific parameters in human RPE cells (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Jiang et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). This gap in the direct evidence would need to be addressed through targeted preclinical assays employing electron microscopy, lipidomics, and mitochondrial respirometry to validate the proposed mechanism.  
Furthermore, the mode of formulation and bioavailability of DHA is a critical factor that may contribute to the mixed findings in clinical trials; DHA administered as an ethyl ester may have different absorption and incorporation profiles compared to its triglyceride-bound form, and the optimal dosing necessary to achieve sufficient retinal or mitochondrial enrichment remains unclear (Souied et al., 2016, pp. 6–7; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Potential pro-oxidant effects of DHA in settings where oxidation is excessive must also be carefully monitored, as some animal studies have reported that under specific conditions DHA accumulation may even exacerbate oxidative damage (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).  
In summary, while the epidemiologic literature and preclinical studies provide an encouraging backdrop for the repurposing of DHA as a therapeutic agent in dry AMD—by showing that high DHA intake is associated with a reduced risk of AMD and that DHA can confer mitochondrial and anti-oxidative benefits in retinal models—the critical mechanistic endpoints that support our specific hypothesis are not yet fully substantiated in the published literature. The overall evaluation is that DHA has substantial mechanistic promise, safety, and historical use as a nutritional supplement; however, further robust mechanistic studies and carefully designed clinical trials are necessary to validate its specific effects on mitochondrial function in RPE cells and to determine whether these biochemical improvements translate into a clinically significant slowing of dry AMD progression (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).
